Yunus ibn Ubayd said: al-Hasan held that the imam should supplicate in the qunut (a prayer of supplication in the standing posture) while those behind him say "amin" without raising the voice, and Yunus recited: "when he called upon his Lord with a secret call." Ibn al-Arabi said: Malik made the qunut silent, while al-Shafi'i made it audible, and saying it audibly is more excellent, because the Prophet (ﷺ) used to supplicate with it aloud.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 19, verses 1–15 (part 2 of 4):

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿He said, "My Lord, indeed my bones have weakened within me"﴾. In this verse there are two issues [[So in the manuscripts, though it should read "three", so the text has "two issues".]]:

The first: His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿He said, "My Lord, indeed [my bones] have weakened"﴾. It is read *wahana* with all three vowel patterns, meaning he became weak. It is said: *wahana yahinu wahnan* when one becomes weak, so he is *wahin*. Abu Zayd said: it is said *wahana yahinu* and *wahina yawhanu*. He mentioned the bone (*'azm*) because it is the pillar (*'amud*) of the body, by which it stands, and it is the foundation of its structure. When it weakens, the rest of its strength collapses and falls away. It is also because it is the hardest and firmest part of the body, so when it weakens, what is beyond it is weaker still. He used the singular because the singular denotes the generic sense: his intent was that this kind, which is the pillar and support, and the strongest of what the body is composed of, has been struck by weakness. Had he used the plural, he would have intended another meaning, namely that not some of his bones had weakened but all of them.

The second: His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿and the head has blazed with grey hair﴾. Abu 'Amr assimilated the *sin* into the *shin*. This is among the finest metaphors in the speech of the Arabs. *Al-ishti'al* is the spreading of the light of fire, and the spreading of white hair over the head is likened to it. He says: "I have grown old and weakened." He attributed the blazing to the place where the hair grows, which is the head. He did not mention "the head" explicitly, relying on the listener's knowledge that it was the head of Zakariyya, peace be upon him. As for *shaybань* (*shayban*, "grey hair") in its accusative case, there are two views: the first is that it is a verbal noun (*masdar*), because the meaning of *ishta'ala* is *shāba* (grew grey). This is the view of al-Akhfash. Al-Zajjaj said it is in the accusative of specification (*tamyiz*). Al-Nahhas said: the view of al-Akhfash is preferable, because the verb is derived from *fa'ala*, so the verbal noun is more appropriate to it. *Shayb* is the mixing of black hair with white.

The third: The scholars said: it is recommended for a person, in his supplication, to mention the blessings of God Most High upon him and what befits humility, because His saying, may He be exalted, "my bones have weakened within me," is a manifestation of humility. And his saying, ﴿and I have never been unsuccessful in my prayer to You, my Lord﴾, is a manifestation of His customary bounty in answering his supplications, meaning: I have never been unsuccessful in my calling upon You; You have never disappointed my supplication whenever I called upon You, that is, You had already accustomed me to being answered in the past. It is said: *shaqiya bi-kadha* meaning he toiled at it and did not attain his aim. It is related from some of them that a needy man asked him and said: "I am the one whom you favoured at such-and-such a time." He said: "Welcome to one who has sought an intercession through us to us," and he fulfilled his need.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And indeed I fear my relatives after me, and my wife is barren, so grant me from Yourself an heir﴾. In it there are seven issues:

The first: His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿And indeed I fear my relatives (*al-mawali*)﴾. 'Uthman ibn 'Affan, Muhammad ibn 'Ali, 'Ali ibn al-Husayn, and Yahya ibn Ya'mur, may God be pleased with them, read: *khaffat* with a fatha on the *kha'*, a shadda on the *fa'*, a kasra on the *ta'*, and a sukun on the *ya'* of *al-mawali*, because it is in the nominative case as the subject of *khaffat*; its meaning is "they ceased" (*inqata'at*) by death. The rest read *khiftu* with a kasra on the *kha'*, a sukun on the *fa'*, a damma on the *ta'*, and a fatha on the *ya'* of *al-mawaliya*, because it is in the accusative case as the object of *khiftu*. Here *al-mawali* means relatives, paternal cousins and the agnates who are nearest to him in lineage. The Arabs call paternal cousins *al-mawali*. The poet said:

"Gently, O sons of our paternal uncle, gently, O our *mawali*,
Do not dig up between us what has been buried."

Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Qatada said: he feared that they would inherit his wealth, and that his estate would pass to *al-kalala* (collateral heirs), so he was apprehensive that someone other than a child would inherit it. Another group said: his relatives were merely neglectful of the religion, so he feared that upon his death the religion would be lost, and he sought an heir who would uphold the religion after him. Al-Zajjaj related this view, and according to it he did not ask for someone to inherit his wealth, because prophets are not inherited from. This is the sounder of the two views regarding the interpretation of the verse. He, upon him be blessings and peace, intended the inheritance of knowledge and prophethood, not the inheritance of wealth, because it is established from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "We, the company of prophets, are not inherited from; what we leave behind is charity." And in the book of Abu Dawud: "Indeed the scholars are the heirs of the prophets, and indeed the prophets did not bequeath dinar or dirham; they bequeathed knowledge."

More detail on this will come under His saying, "who will inherit me."

The second: This hadith falls within the category of tafsir supported by a chain of transmission (*al-tafsir al-musnad*), because of His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿And Sulayman inherited David﴾ [[See vol. 13, p. 163.]], and it is an expression of Zakariyya's words, "grant me from Yourself an heir who will inherit me and inherit from the family of Ya'qub," and a specification of the general sense in that matter: Sulayman did not inherit from David any wealth that David left behind after him; he inherited from him only wisdom and knowledge. Likewise Yahya inherited from the family of Ya'qub. This is what the people of knowledge of the Qur'an's interpretation have said, except the Rafidites. As for what is related from al-Hasan, that he said: "who will inherit me" refers to wealth, "and inherit from the family of Ya'qub" refers to prophethood and wisdom, every view that contradicts the saying of the Prophet ﷺ is rejected and abandoned, as said by Abu 'Umar. Ibn 'Atiyya said: most of the exegetes hold that Zakariyya intended only the inheritance of wealth, and the Prophet's saying ﷺ, "We, the company of prophets, are not inherited from," may be understood as not meaning it in a general sense, but as describing their usual condition. So reflect on this. The more apparent and more fitting view for Zakariyya, peace be upon him, is that he intended the inheritance of knowledge and religion, so the inheritance is used metaphorically. Do you not see that when he asked for an heir he did not specify a son, and God granted his hope in the most perfect way? Abu Salih and others said: his words "from the family of Ya'qub" mean knowledge and prophethood.

The third: His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿from after me (*min warā'i*)﴾. Ibn Kathir read with *madd* (lengthening), *hamz* (glottal stop), and a fatha on the *ya'*. It is also related from him that he read it short (*maqsur*), with a fatha on the *ya'*, like *'asaya*. The rest read it with *hamz*, lengthening, and a sukun on the *ya'*. The readers read *khiftu* as they read *nimtu*, except what we mentioned from 'Uthman. This is an anomalous reading, very remote, to the extent that some scholars claimed it is not permissible. [They say:] How can one say "the relatives became few after me," meaning after my death, while he is still alive? Al-Nahhas said: the interpretation of it is that by His saying "from after me" he does not mean after my death, but "from behind me at that time." This too is remote and requires evidence that they became few and reduced at that time. God has already informed us of something that indicates abundance when they said, "Which of them will take charge of Maryam?" [[See vol. 4, pp. 85 and 79.]]. Ibn 'Atiyya: "from after me" means after me in time; it is the sense of *warā'* as explained earlier in *al-Kahf* [[See p. 34 and following of this part.]].

The fourth: His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿and my wife has been barren﴾. His wife was Ishā' daughter of Faqudha son of Qabil, and she was the sister of Hannah daughter of Faqudha, according to al-Tabari. Hannah was the mother of Maryam, as explained earlier in *Al 'Imran* [[See vol. 4, pp. 85 and 79.]]. Al-Qutabi said: the wife of Zakariyya was Ishā' daughter of 'Imran. According to this view, Yahya would be the true maternal cousin of 'Isa, peace be upon them both. According to the other view, he would be the cousin of his mother. In the hadith of the Night Journey the Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "I met the two maternal cousins, Yahya and 'Isa," which is evidence for the first view [[The "first view" here refers to the view of al-Qutabi.]]. And God knows best.

The barren woman (*al-'aqir*) is the one who does not bear children because of her advanced age, and its explanation has already passed in *Al 'Imran*. *Al-'aqir* among women also refers to the one who does not bear children without being old. From this is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿and He makes whom He wills barren﴾ [[See vol. 16, p. 48.]] [al-Shura: 50]. Likewise *al-'aqir* among men, and from this is the saying of 'Amir ibn al-Tufayl:

"Wretched is the youth if I am one-eyed and barren,
Cowardly, so what excuse have I before every gathering?"

The fifth: His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿so grant me from Yourself an heir﴾. This is a request and a supplication. He did not state "a son" explicitly, because of what he knew of his own condition and his distance from it on account of his wife. Qatada said: this matter happened to him when he was in his seventies. Muqatil said: when he was ninety-five, and this is more likely, for it had come to be his strong expectation that he would not have children because of his old age, and for this reason he said, "and I have indeed reached extreme old age." Another group said: rather, he sought a child, and then he sought that the answer be in his living until he would inherit him, lest the answer come as a child who would be unsuitable, and the purpose would not be achieved from him.

The sixth: The scholars said: Zakariyya's supplication, peace be upon him, concerning a child was only to manifest his religion, to revive his prophethood, and to multiply his reward, not for the sake of this world. His Lord had accustomed him to being answered, and for this reason he said, "and I have never been unsuccessful in my prayer to You, my Lord," meaning in my calling upon You. This is a good means: to seek intercession through His blessings and to draw His bounty through His generosity. It is related that Hatim al-Ta'i, famed for generosity, was met by a man who asked him, and Hatim said to him: "Who are you?" He said: "I am the one to whom you did good the year before." He said: "Welcome to one who has sought intercession with us through ourselves." If it is asked: how did Zakariyya proceed to ask for something that breaks the customary order without permission? The answer is that this is permissible in the time of the prophets, and the Qur'an contains what uncovers this meaning, for He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿Whenever Zakariyya entered upon her in the sanctuary, he found provision with her. He said, "O Maryam, from where is this for you?" She said, "It is from God; indeed God provides for whom He wills without account"﴾ [Al 'Imran: 37]. When he saw the extraordinary sign, his hope in the answering of his supplication became firm, so He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿There Zakariyya called upon his Lord, saying, "My Lord, grant me from Yourself good offspring"﴾ [[See vol. 4, p. 72 and following.]] [Al 'Imran: 38], and so on.

The seventh: If someone says: this verse indicates the permissibility of supplicating for a child, while God, glory be to Him and exalted, has warned us against the calamities of wealth and children, and alerted us to the corruptions arising from them, saying: ﴿Indeed, your wealth and your children are a trial﴾ [[See vol. 18, p. 140 and following.]] [al-Taghabun: 15], and ﴿Indeed, among your spouses and your children are enemies to you, so beware of them﴾ [[See vol. 18, p. 140 and following.]] [al-Taghabun: 14]. The answer is that supplicating for a child is established from the Book and the Sunnah, as explained earlier in *Al 'Imran* [[See vol. 4, p. 72 and following.]]. Then Zakariyya, peace be upon him, took precaution, saying: "good offspring," and he said: "and make him, my Lord, one with whom You are pleased." A child who has this quality benefits his parents in this world and the next, and passes from the boundary of enmity and trial to the boundary of joy and blessing. The Prophet ﷺ supplicated for Anas, his servant, saying: "O God, increase his wealth and his children, and bless him in what You have given him." He supplicated for him for blessing, as a precaution against the ruin to which abundance may lead. Thus let the servant humbly beseech his Master for the guidance of his child and his salvation in this world and the next, following the example of the prophets, peace be upon them, and the virtuous. [Al-Awliya' [[From manuscripts J, K and Y.]]] Its explanation has already been given in *Al 'Imran* [[See vol. 4, p. 72 and following.]].

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 19, verse 1–15 (part 3 of 4):

Allah's words: ﴿He will inherit me and inherit from the family of Ya'qub; and make him, my Lord, one with whom You are pleased.﴾ In this there are four issues.

The first issue: Allah's words ﴿He will inherit me﴾. The people of the two sanctuaries (Makkah and Madinah), al-Hasan, 'Asim and Hamzah read "yarithuni wa yarithu" with a raised (marfu') ending in both places. Yahya ibn Ya'mar, Abu 'Amr, Yahya ibn Wathhab, al-A'mash and al-Kisa'i read both with a jussive (majzum) ending. According to the view of Sibawayh, these two are not the answer (jawab) to "hab" (grant); rather, its implied sense is "in tahabhu yarithuni wa yarith" (if You grant him, he will inherit me and inherit). The first reading is more correct in meaning, because he was asking for a specified heir, meaning: grant me from You the guardian who has this condition and description, since among the guardians (awliya') there are some who do not inherit. So he said: grant me one who will be my heir. This is what Abu 'Ubayd said, and he rejected the jussive reading, saying: its meaning would be "if You grant, he inherits," and how would Allah, Mighty and Majestic, inform of this when He knows it better than he does? Al-Nahhas said: this is a well-established argument, because the answer to an imperative (jawab al-amr) in the view of the grammarians carries the meaning of a condition and a consequence. You say: "Obey Allah, Exalted, and He will admit you to Paradise," meaning: if you obey Him, He will admit you to Paradise.

The second issue: Al-Nahhas said: as for the meaning of "He will inherit me and inherit from the family of Ya'qub," scholars have three interpretations. It has been said: it is the inheritance of prophethood. It has been said: it is the inheritance of wisdom. It has been said: it is the inheritance of wealth. As for their saying "inheritance of prophethood," it is impossible, because prophethood is not inherited; if it were inherited, someone would say: people trace their lineage to Nuh, peace be upon him, and he was a messenger prophet. The inheritance of knowledge and wisdom is a good view, and in a hadith: "The scholars are the heirs of the prophets." As for the inheritance of wealth, it is not impermissible, although some people have denied it, because of the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "We (prophets) do not leave inheritance; what we leave is charity." This has no proof in it, because one person may speak of himself in plural form. It may also be interpreted to mean: "We do not leave an inheritance of what we leave, which is charity," because the Prophet ﷺ did not leave anything to be inherited from him; what Allah, Mighty and Majestic, permitted him in his lifetime, by His saying, blessed is His name: ﴿And know that whatever you acquire of spoils, a fifth of it is for Allah and for the Messenger﴾ [al-Anfal: 41], because the meaning of "for Allah" is for the cause of Allah, and of the cause of Allah is what serves the interest of the Messenger ﷺ as long as he lives. If it is said: in some narrations, "We prophets do not leave inheritance; what we leave is charity," then both interpretations apply to it: that "ma" means "that which," and the other that "he who is in this condition is not inherited from." Abu 'Umar said: The scholars differed regarding the interpretation of his saying, peace be upon him: "We do not leave inheritance; what we leave is charity," into two views. One of them, which is the more common and held by the majority, is that the Prophet ﷺ is not inherited from, and what he leaves is charity. The other is that our Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, was not inherited from, because Allah, Exalted, specially made all his wealth charity, as an increase in his virtue, just as he was singled out in marriage with things He permitted to him and forbade to others. This view was held by some people of Basra, among them Ibn 'Ulayyah, while the rest of the scholars of the Muslims hold the first view.

The third issue: Allah's words ﴿from the family of Ya'qub﴾. It has been said: it is Ya'qub ibn Ishaq. Zakariyya was married to the sister of Maryam daughter of 'Imran, and her lineage goes back to Ya'qub, since she was of the descendants of Sulayman ibn Dawud, who was of the descendants of Yahudha ibn Ya'qub, and Zakariyya was of the descendants of Harun, brother of Musa, and Harun and Musa were of the descendants of Lawi ibn Ya'qub, and prophethood was in the tribe of Ya'qub ibn Ishaq. It has also been said: the meaning of Ya'qub here is Ya'qub ibn Matan, brother of 'Imran ibn Matan, father of Maryam; the two were brothers from the offspring of Sulayman ibn Dawud, peace be upon them both, because Ya'qub and 'Imran were sons of Matan, and the sons of Matan were chiefs of the Children of Israel. This was said by Muqatil and others. Al-Kalbi said: the family of Ya'qub were his maternal uncles, namely Ya'qub ibn Matan, and rulership was among them, and Zakariyya was of the descendants of Harun ibn 'Imran, brother of Musa. Qatadah narrated that the Prophet ﷺ said: "May Allah, Exalted, have mercy on Zakariyya; what did he have to do with his heirs?" Ya'qub is not declined because he is non-Arabic (a'jami).

The fourth issue: Allah's words ﴿and make him, my Lord, one with whom You are pleased﴾, that is, one who is pleasing in his character and actions. It has been said: one who is content with Your decree and destiny. It has been said: a righteous man with whom You are pleased. Abu Salih said: a prophet, just as You made his father a prophet.

Allah's words: ﴿O Zakariyya﴾. There is an omission in the speech, meaning: so Allah answered his supplication and said: "O Zakariyya, We give you good news of a boy whose name is Yahya." This good news comprised three things: first, the answering of his supplication, which is an honour. Second, the giving of a son, which is strength. Third, that he be singled out by his naming; the meaning of his naming Yahya has already been mentioned in "Al 'Imran" (see vol. 4, p. 75 onward). Muqatil said: He named him Yahya because he was made to live (hayiya) between an aged father and an old mother. This is questionable, given what has preceded, that his wife was barren and could not bear. And Allah knows best.

Allah's words: ﴿We have not made for him before, any namesake﴾, that is, We have not named anyone before Yahya with this name. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, Qatadah, Ibn Aslam and al-Suddi. He was blessed by Allah, Exalted, in that his naming was not left to his parents. Mujahid and others said: "samiyyan" means a like and an equal, and it is like His saying, Exalted: ﴿Do you know anyone of similar name to Him?﴾ [Maryam: 65], meaning a like and equal. It is as if it derives from "musamah" and "sumuw" (height). This is far-fetched, because he is not preferred over Ibrahim and Musa, except in specific matters such as nobility and chastity, as has already been explained in "Al 'Imran" (vol. 4, pp. 74 and 79). Ibn 'Abbas also said: the meaning is that barren women did not bear a son like him. It has been said: Allah, Exalted, stipulated "before," because He intended to create after him one more excellent than him, who is Muhammad ﷺ. In this verse there is evidence and proof that beautiful names (al-asami al-sung) are worthy of preference, and it was for these that the Arabs aimed in naming, because they are more distinguished and more free from reproach (nabz), until a poet said:
"Beautiful names, wearing red garments
That touch the ground with their fringes."
Ru'bah said to the genealogist al-Bakri, when he asked him about his lineage: "I am the son of al-'Ajjaj." He said: "You have fallen short and made yourself known."

Allah's words: ﴿He said: My Lord, how can I have a boy when my wife is barren and I have reached extreme old age?﴾ 40. This is not in the sense of denying what Allah, Exalted, has informed of, but in the manner of wonder at the power of Allah, Exalted, to bring forth a child from a barren woman and an aged old man. It has been said: other than this, which has been explained earlier in "Al 'Imran" (vol. 4, pp. 74 and 79).

(And I have indeed reached extreme old age) meaning the utmost in old age, dryness and desiccation. Similar to it is "al-'usiyy." Al-Asma'i said: "'asa al-shay'" (the thing) dries and hardens, "'asa'" (with extended vowel) means it dried and became hard, and "qad 'asa al-shaykh ya'su 'usiyyan" means the old man became decrepit and aged, like "ata." It is said: "'ata al-shaykh ya'tu 'utuwwan wa 'itiyyan" means the old man aged and became decrepit, and "'atawta ya fulan ta'tu 'utuwwan wa 'itiyyan." The original form is "'utuww," since it is from the roots with waw, so they changed the waw into ya', because it is its cognate and lighter than it, and the verses are on ya' endings. Whoever says "'itiyyan" dislikes the damma with the kasra and the ya'. The poet said:
"Only the youth is excused, and not
he who was in the time 'itiyyan."
Ibn 'Abbas read "'usiyyan," and it is so in the codex of Ubayy. Yahya ibn Wathhab, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Hafs read "'itiyyan" with a kasra on the 'ayn, and likewise "jithiyyan" and "siliyyan" wherever they occur. Hafs alone read "bukiyyan" with a damma, and the rest read all of them with a damma; both are dialects. It has been said: "'itiyyan" means "qasiyyan" (hard), as one says: "malik 'at" (a tyrannical king) when he is hard-hearted.

Allah's words: ﴿He said: Thus [it is]; your Lord says: It is easy for Me﴾. That is, the angel said to him: "Thus your Lord says," and the kaf is in the place of nominative, meaning: the matter is thus, as it was said to you: "It is easy for Me." Al-Farra' said: His creating him is easy for Me.

(And I created you before, when you were nothing) meaning: before Yahya. This is the reading of the people of Madinah, Basra and 'Asim. The rest of the Kufans read "wa qad khalaqnahu" with nun and alif in the plural form of majesty. The first reading is more consistent with the written text (al-sawad).

(And you were not a thing) meaning: just as Allah created you after non-existence, when you were not a thing existing, so He is capable of creating Yahya and bringing him into being.

Allah's words: ﴿He said: My Lord, make for me a sign﴾. He asked for a sign, to be carried by her (fi jamlih) after the angels' good news to him, and after Allah's words: "And I created you before, when you were nothing," as added reassurance, meaning: complete the favour by making for me a sign, and let that sign be an increase in favour and honour. It has also been said: he asked for a sign that would show him the good news of Yahya came from Him and not from Satan, because Satan had cast that thought into him. This was said by al-Dahhak, and it is the meaning of al-Suddi's view. This is questionable, given Allah's report that the angels called out to him, as has preceded in "Al 'Imran" (vol. 4, p. 80 onward).

(He said: Your sign is that you will not speak to people for three nights while being sound) 10. Its explanation has preceded in "Al 'Imran" (vol. 4, p. 80 onward), so there is no point in repeating it.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 19, verses 1–15 (part 4 of 4):**

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿So he came out to his people from the prayer niche (mihrab), and signaled to them to glorify [Allah] morning and evening﴾. In this there are five issues.

**The first issue:** His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So he came out to his people from the prayer niche﴾, meaning he appeared before them from the place of prayer (al-musalla). The *mihrab* (prayer niche) is the highest place and the most honorable seat, and they used to make *mihrabs* in what was raised from the ground. The evidence for this is the *mihrab* of Dawud, peace be upon him, as will come. People differed about its derivation. One group said: it is derived from *al-harb* (war), as if its occupant wages war (yuharib) against Satan and desires. Another group said: it is derived from *al-harab* (with a fatha on the ra'), as if its occupant encounters from it war (harab), weariness and fatigue.

**The second issue:** This verse indicates that it was legislated among them in their prayer for the imam to be raised above the congregation. The jurists of the cities differed on this matter. Imam Ahmad [ibn Hanbal [[from manuscripts J and K.]]] and others permitted it, holding to the story of the pulpit (minbar). Malik prohibited it when the elevation is great, but not when it is slight, and his companions justified the prohibition by fear of arrogance on the part of the imam. I say: this is open to scrutiny. The best that has been said on this is what Abu Dawud related from Hammam: that Hudhayfa led the people in prayer at al-Mada'in standing on a raised platform (dukkan), and Abu Mas'ud took hold of his garment and pulled him, and when he had finished his prayer he said: "Did you not know that they used to forbid this?" Or: "they used to forbid that!" He said: "Yes, I remembered when you pulled me." It is also related from Adi ibn Thabit al-Ansari, who said: A man related to me that he was with Ammar ibn Yasir at al-Mada'in, and the prayer was established, and Ammar ibn Yasir went forward and stood on a raised platform to pray while the people were below him. Hudhayfa came forward and took hold of his hands, and Ammar followed him until Hudhayfa brought him down. When Ammar had finished his prayer, Hudhayfa said to him: "Did you not hear the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say: 'When a man leads the people in prayer, he should not stand in a place higher than their station,' or words to that effect?" Ammar said: "For that I followed you when you took hold of my hands." I say: these are three of the Companions who reported the prohibition of this, and none of them argued against the other with the hadith of the pulpit. This indicates that it has been abrogated (mansukh). Among what indicates its abrogation is that it involves an additional action in the prayer, namely descending and ascending, so it was abrogated just as speech and greeting (during prayer) were abrogated. This is better than what our companions have offered as an excuse, that the Prophet ﷺ was protected from arrogance, because many imams are found to have no arrogance in them, and some of them justified it by saying that the elevation of the pulpit was slight. And Allah knows best.

**The third issue:** His saying, the Exalted: ﴿and He revealed to them that they should glorify [Him] morning and evening﴾. Al-Kalbi, Qatada and Ibn Munabbih said: *awha* means he signaled (ashara). Al-Qutabi said: he gestured (awma'a) [in manuscripts J and K: he instructed (awsa)]. Mujahid said: he wrote on the ground. Ikrima said: he wrote in a book. Revelation (al-wahy) in the speech of the Arabs means writing, and from it is the saying of Dhu al-Rummah:

*Except the four dark-colored ones, as if they were*
*A remnant of revelation in the bellies of the pages.*

And Antara said:

*Like the writing of pages from the era of Kisra,*
*Which he sent as a gift to a non-Arab, mumbling (tamtami).* [[al-tamtami: the non-Arab who does not speak clearly.]]

"Morning and evening" (bukratan wa 'ashiyyan) are two adverbs of time. Al-Farra' claimed that *al-ashi* is feminine, but it may be masculinized when left indefinite. He said: *al-'ashi* may also be the plural of *'ashiyya*.

**The fourth issue:** The ruling on signaling has already been mentioned in Al 'Imran [[see vol. 4, p. 81.]]. Our scholars differed regarding one who swears not to speak to a person and then writes to him a letter, or sends a messenger to him. Malik said: he breaks his oath, unless he intends to speak to him face to face. Then he retracted and said: he is not believed regarding the letter, and he breaks the oath unless he retrieves the letter before it reaches him. Ibn al-Qasim said: if he reads the letter he breaks the oath, and likewise if the one who swore reads the letter of the one sworn against. Ashhab said: he does not break the oath if he reads it, and this is clear, because he has not spoken to him nor initiated speech with him, unless he intends that he should not know the meaning of his speech, in which case he breaks it; and Ibn al-Qasim's view is to be understood in this way. If he swears that he will certainly speak to him, he is not fulfilling it except by speaking to him face to face. Ibn al-Majishun said: if he swears "if I come to know of such-and-such, I will certainly inform him or report it to him," and then he writes to him or sends a messenger to him, he fulfills the oath; but if they both come to know it together, he does not fulfill it until he informs him, because their knowledge differs.

**The fifth issue:** Malik, al-Shafi'i and the Kufans agreed that if a mute person writes a divorce with his own hand, it is binding upon him. The Kufans said: except if a man has been silenced for days and then writes, in which case nothing of that is valid. Al-Tahawi said: muteness (al-kharas) differs from temporary silence, just as inability to have intercourse that is caused by illness or the like for a day or so differs from the permanent impotence that one despairs of, such as insanity, in the chapter on the wife's option regarding separation.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿O Yahya, take the Scripture with determination﴾. There is an ellipsis in the speech, the meaning being: a child was born to him, and Allah the Exalted said to the newborn: "O Yahya, take the Scripture with determination." This is an abbreviation that the context indicates. "The Scripture" is the Torah, without disagreement. "With determination" means with earnestness and diligence, as Mujahid said. It was also said: [it means] knowing it, memorizing it, and acting upon it, which is adherence to its commands and refraining from its prohibitions; Zayd ibn Aslam said this. It has already been discussed in al-Baqarah [[see vol. 1, p. 437.]].

[His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And We gave him judgment while still a child﴾ [[from manuscripts J and K.]]: It was said: judgment means legal rulings and knowledge of them. Ma'mar related that the children said to Yahya: "Come, let us go and play," and he said: "I was not created for play." So Allah the Exalted revealed: "And We gave him judgment while still a child." Qatada said: he was two or three years old. Muqatil said: he was three years old. "Sabiyyan" (as a child) is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (hal). Ibn 'Abbas said: whoever recites the Qur'an before reaching puberty is among those who were given judgment as children. It is related in the explanation of this verse, by way of 'Abdullah ibn 'Umar, from the Prophet ﷺ, that he said: "Every son of Adam will come on the Day of Resurrection carrying a sin, except Yahya ibn Zakariyya." Qatada said: Yahya, peace be upon him, never disobeyed Allah [[from manuscript K.]] the Exalted, neither in a minor sin nor a major one, and he never even desired a woman. Mujahid said: the food of Yahya, peace be upon him, was grass, and there were permanent channels of tears on his cheeks.]

The discussion of the meaning of His saying: ﴿and a leader and chaste﴾ [Al 'Imran: 39] has already passed in Al 'Imran [[see vol. 4, p. 86.]].

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿and compassion from Us﴾. "Hananan" (compassion) is conjoined with "al-hukm" (judgment). It is related from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "By Allah, I do not know what 'al-hanan' is." The majority of the exegetes said: al-hanan is tenderness, mercy and love, and it is one of the actions of the soul. Al-Nahhas said: regarding the meaning of al-hanan from Ibn 'Abbas there are two statements. The first: he said: Allah the Mighty and Majestic showed him tenderness with mercy. The second statement is what was given to him of the mercy of people, to the extent that he delivered them from disbelief and polytheism [[in manuscript J: "the evil."]]. Its origin is from the yearning (haniin) of the she-camel for her offspring. It is said: *hanaanaka* and *hanaaniyka*; it was said these are two dialects with the same meaning, and it was said *hanaaniyka* is the dual of *al-hanan*. Abu 'Ubayda said: the Arabs say: "Hanaanaka, O Lord" and "Hanaaniyka, O Lord" with the same meaning, meaning Your mercy. Imru' al-Qays said:

*And the sons of Shamaji ibn Jarm grant them*
*Their goats, [saying] "Your mercy, O Merciful One" (hanaanaka dha al-hanan).* [[Hanaanaka dha al-hanan means: Your mercy, O Merciful. The narration in Lisan: "yamna'uha" (withhold).]]

Tarafa said:

*O father of Mundhir, you have destroyed us, so spare some of us,*
*Have mercy (hanaaniyka), for some evil is less harmful than some other evil.*

Al-Zamakhshari said: "hananan" means mercy toward his parents and others, tenderness and compassion. Sibawayh recited:

*She said: "Hanan, what brought you here?*
*Are you of lineage, or are you one who knows the tribe?"*

Ibn al-A'rabi said: al-Hanan (with a shadda), as an attribute of Allah the Exalted, means the Compassionate; al-Hanan (without shadda) means tenderness and mercy, and al-hanan also means provision and blessing. Ibn 'Atiyya said: al-hanan in the speech of the Arabs also means what is great among matters concerning the Essence of Allah the Exalted, and from it is the saying of Zayd ibn 'Amr ibn Nufayl in the hadith of Bilal: "By Allah, if you kill this servant, I will certainly take his grave as a hanan (sanctuary)." Al-Harawi related this report and said: in the hadith of Bilal, when Waraqa ibn Nawfal passed by him while he was being tortured, he said: "By Allah, if you kill him, I will certainly take him as a hanan," meaning: I will certainly not stop touching him (la amsahanna bihi). Al-Azhari said: it means: I will certainly not show tenderness toward him nor have mercy upon him, because he is among the people of Paradise. I say: so al-hanan is tenderness, and Mujahid also said this. "Hananan" means tenderness from Us toward him, or from him toward creation. Al-Hutay'a said:

*Show me compassion (tahannan), may the King guide you,*
*For every station has its speech.*

Ikrima said: it means love. And the wife of a man is called *hunna* because of their mutual affection. The poet said:

*She said: "Hanan, what brought you here?*
*Are you of lineage, or are you one who knows the tribe?"*

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿and purity﴾. "Zakat" means purification, blessing, and growth in all forms of goodness and righteousness; that is, We made him blessed for the people, guiding them. It was also said: the meaning is that We purified him by giving him good praise, as witnesses commend a person. It was also said: "zakatan" means charity given on his behalf to his parents, said by Ibn Qutayba.

(And he was pious) meaning obedient to Allah the Exalted; for this reason he did not commit a sin and did not approach one.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿and dutiful to his parents﴾. "Barr" is in the sense of "barr" (dutiful), which is one who is abundantly dutiful. And ﴿tyrannical﴾ means arrogant. This is a description of Yahya, peace be upon him, in gentleness of manner and lowering of the wing (humility).

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And peace be upon him the day he was born﴾. Al-Tabari and others said: its meaning is safety (aman). Ibn 'Atiyya said: in my view the more evident meaning is the customary greeting, which is more honorable and more striking than safety, because safety is attained for him through the absence of disobedience from him, and that is the least of his ranks; rather, the honor lies in that Allah the Exalted greeted him with peace and saluted him in the situations in which a person is in utmost weakness, need, lack of resources, and poverty before Allah the Exalted, [and in manuscripts J and K: and the magnitude of the terror] before the Mighty Power.

I say: this is a good statement. We have already mentioned its meaning from Sufyan ibn 'Uyayna in the chapter of Subhan [[see vol. 10, p. 220.]] [al-Isra': 1], regarding the killing of Yahya. Al-Tabari related from al-Hasan that 'Isa and Yahya met, and they were cousins through their mothers. Yahya said to 'Isa: "Pray to Allah for me, for you are better than me." 'Isa said to him: "Rather, you pray to Allah for me, for you are better than me. Allah greeted you with peace, and I greeted myself with peace." Some scholars derived from this verse concerning the greeting that 'Isa is superior, saying: his greeting upon himself indicates his rank with Allah the Exalted, which required that, when he is established in the Mighty Book, he is greater in station than to be greeted upon. Ibn 'Atiyya said: each has its own perspective.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 19, verses 1–15 (part 1 of 4)**

It is a Meccan surah by consensus (ijma'). It has ninety-eight verses.

When the Battle of Badr took place, and Allah killed the leaders of the disbelievers in it, the disbelievers of Quraysh said: "Your vengeance is in the land of Abyssinia. So make a gift to the Negus (al-Najashi), and send to him two men of your opinion, so that perhaps he will hand over to you those of Quraysh who are with him, and you may kill them in return for those of you who were killed at Badr." The disbelievers of Quraysh sent 'Amr ibn al-As and Abdullah ibn Abi Rabi'a. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) heard of their dispatch, so he sent 'Amr ibn Umayya al-Damri and wrote a letter with him to the Negus. He arrived before the Negus and read the letter of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Then the Negus summoned Ja'far ibn Abi Talib and the emigrants (muhajirun), and he sent for the monks and the priests and gathered them. Then he ordered Ja'far to recite the Qur'an to them, so he recited Surah Maryam, "Kaf-Ha-Ya-'Ayn-Sad," and they stood up with their eyes flowing with tears. They are the ones concerning whom Allah the Exalted revealed: ﴿And you will surely find the nearest of them in affection to those who believe the ones who say, "We are Christians." That is because among them are priests and monks, and because they are not arrogant﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 82]. He recited up to His words: "the witnesses" [see vol. 6, p. 285 ff.]. This was related by Abu Dawud. In the biography (sira) it is also reported: the Negus said, "Do you have with you anything of what he has brought from Allah?" Ja'far said, "Yes." The Negus said to him, "Recite it to me." So he recited "Kaf-Ha-Ya-'Ayn-Sad," and by Allah the Negus wept until his beard was wet, and their bishops wept until their beards were wet when they heard what was being recited to them. Then the Negus said: "Indeed this and what Moses brought come from one niche (mishkat). Go, for by Allah I will never hand them over to you." He mentioned the rest of the report.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

1. Kaf-Ha-Ya-'Ayn-Sad.
2. A mention of the mercy of your Lord to His servant Zakariya,
3. when he called upon his Lord with a secret call.
4. He said: "My Lord, indeed my bones have weakened and my head has glistened with grey hair, and I have never been unsuccessful in my supplication to You, my Lord.
5. And indeed I fear my relatives after me, and my wife is barren, so grant me from Yourself an heir,
6. who will inherit me and inherit from the family of Ya'qub, and make him, my Lord, pleasing."
7. "O Zakariya, indeed We give you good news of a boy whose name is Yahya; We have not given this name to anyone before."
8. He said: "My Lord, how can I have a son when my wife is barren and I have reached extreme old age?"
9. He said: "So it will be. Your Lord says, 'It is easy for Me, and I created you before, when you were nothing.'"
10. He said: "My Lord, appoint for me a sign." He said: "Your sign is that you will not speak to people for three nights, while sound."
11. So he came out to his people from the prayer niche (mihrab) and inspired them to glorify Him morning and evening.
12. "O Yahya, take the Scripture with determination." And We gave him wisdom while still a boy,
13. and compassion from Us and purity, and he was devout,
14. and dutiful to his parents, and he was not a tyrant or disobedient.
15. And peace be upon him the day he was born, the day he dies, and the day he is raised alive.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Kaf-Ha-Ya-'Ayn-Sad﴾. The discussion of the opening letters of surahs has already preceded [see vol. 1, p. 154 ff.]. Ibn Abbas said concerning "Kaf-Ha-Ya-'Ayn-Sad": the Kaf is from *Kafin* (Sufficient), the Ha from *Hadin* (Guide), the Ya from *Hakim* (Wise), the 'Ayn from *'Alim* (All-Knowing), and the Sad from *Sadiq* (Truthful). Ibn 'Aziz related it. Al-Qushayri reported from Ibn Abbas that its meaning is: Sufficient for His creation, Guide for His servants, His hand is above their hands, Knowing of them, Truthful in His promise. Al-Tha'labi mentioned it from al-Kalbi, al-Suddi, Mujahid and al-Dahhak. Al-Kalbi also said: the Kaf is from *Karim* (Generous), *Kabir* (Great) and *Kafin*; the Ha from *Hadin*; the Ya from *Rahim* (Merciful); the 'Ayn from *'Alim* (Knowing) and *'Azim* (Mighty); the Sad from *Sadiq*; and the meaning is one. Also from Ibn Abbas: it is one of the names of Allah the Exalted. From Ali (may Allah be pleased with him): it is the name of Allah the Mighty and Majestic, and he used to say, "O Kaf-Ha-Ya-'Ayn-Sad, forgive me." Al-Ghaznawi mentioned it. Al-Suddi said: it is the Greatest Name of Allah, by which when He is asked He gives, and when He is called upon He answers. Qatada said: it is one of the names of the Qur'an, related by Abd al-Razzaq from Ma'mar from him. It has also been said: it is the name of the surah, and this is the choice of al-Qushayri regarding the opening letters. On this view it has been said that the sentence is complete at His words "Kaf-Ha-Ya-'Ayn-Sad," as if it is an announcement of the name of the surah, just as you say "the book of such-and-such" or "the chapter of such-and-such" and then begin the intended subject. Abu Ja'far recited these letters separately, and the rest connected them. Abu 'Amr inclined the Ha and pronounced the Ya with a fatha; Ibn 'Amir and Hamza did the reverse; al-Kisa'i, Abu Bakr and Khalaf inclined both. Ahl al-Madina, Nafi' and others, recited them between the two sounds. The rest pronounced both with a fatha. It is related from Kharija that al-Hasan used to pronounce the Kaf with a damma, and another reported that he used to pronounce the Ha with a damma, and Isma'il ibn Ishaq related that he used to pronounce the Ya with a damma. Abu Hatim said: it is not permissible to pronounce the Kaf, the Ha or the Ya with a damma. Al-Nahhas said: the reading of the people of Madina is among the best of what has been said on this, and inclining is permissible in *ha-ya*. As for the reading of al-Hasan, it confused a group, so that they said it is not permissible, among them Abu Hatim. The correct view on it is what Harun al-Qari explained. He said: al-Hasan used to give the sound of the *damma* (*ishmam al-raf'*), meaning that he would merely indicate it, just as Sibawayh reported that some Arabs say *al-salat wa al-zakat* while indicating the *waw*, and for this reason they are written in the Mushaf with a *waw*. Nafi', Ibn Kathir, 'Asim and Ya'qub made the *dal* of the spelling of *Sad* clear, and this is the choice of Abu 'Ubayd, while the rest assimilated it.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿A mention of the mercy of your Lord to His servant Zakariya. When he called upon his Lord with a secret call.﴾ In this there are three issues.

The first issue: His words ﴿A mention of the mercy of your Lord﴾. Concerning the *raf'* of *dhikr* there are three views. Al-Farra' said: it is in the nominative governed by "Kaf-Ha-Ya-'Ayn-Sad." Al-Zajjaj said: this is impossible, because "Kaf-Ha-Ya-'Ayn-Sad" is not something Allah has informed us of concerning Zakariya, and Allah has told us about him and what he was given good news of, and "Kaf-Ha-Ya-'Ayn-Sad" is not part of his story. Al-Akhfash said: the sense is, "in what is recounted to you is the mention of the mercy of your Lord." The third view: the meaning is "this which is recited to you is the mention of the mercy of your Lord." It has also been said: "dhikru rahmati rabbika" is in the nominative by an implied subject, i.e. "this is the mention of the mercy of your Lord." Al-Hasan read "dhikra rahmati rabbika," meaning "this recited portion of the Qur'an mentioned the mercy of your Lord." It was also read "dhakkir" as an imperative. The word *rahmat* is written and stopped on with a *ha*, and likewise everything similar to it; there is no disagreement about this among the grammarians. They gave as the reason that this *ha* marks the feminine of nouns, distinguishing them from verbs.

The second issue: His words ﴿his servant﴾. Al-Akhfash said it is in the accusative governed by "rahmat," and "Zakariya" is an apposition to it, just as you say "this is the mention of the striking of Zayd 'Amr," where "'Amr" is in the accusative governed by the striking, just as "his servant" is in the accusative governed by the mercy. It has also been said that it is by inversion, meaning: "the mention of your Lord to His servant Zakariya with mercy," so "his servant" is in the accusative governed by the mention. This was reported by al-Zajjaj and al-Farra'. Some read "'abduhu Zakariya" in the nominative, and this is the reading of Abu al-'Aliya. Yahya ibn Ya'mur read "dhakara" in the accusative, in the sense that "this Qur'an mentioned the mercy of His servant Zakariya." The languages and the readings concerning "Zakariya" have already been discussed in Surah Al 'Imran [see vol. 4, p. 70].

The third issue: His words ﴿When he called upon his Lord with a secret call﴾. This is like His words: ﴿Call upon your Lord humbly and in secret; indeed He does not like the transgressors﴾ [al-A'raf: 55], which has already preceded [see vol. 7, p. 223 ff.]. *Nida'* means supplication and desire. That is, he communed with his Lord in this way in his prayer niche. The evidence is His words: ﴿So the angels called to him while he was standing in prayer in the mihrab﴾ [Al 'Imran: 39]. This shows that He answered him in his prayer, just as he called out in the prayer. Scholars differed about his concealing this call. It has been said: he concealed it from his people, so that he would not be blamed for asking for a child in old age, and because it was a worldly matter; if it was answered he would obtain his desire, and if it was not answered no one would know of it. It has been said: he was sincere in it, and none but Allah the Exalted knew of it. It has been said: since hidden deeds are more excellent and further from ostentation, he concealed it. It has been said: "khafiyyan" means secretly, away from his people, in the middle of the night. All of these are possible, and the first is more apparent, and Allah knows best. It has already been stated that the recommended way of supplication is in secret, in Surah al-A'raf, and this verse is explicit on that, because Allah praised Zakariya for it. Isma'il related, saying: Musaddad related to us, saying: Yahya ibn Sa'id related to us from Usama ibn Zayd, from Muhammad ibn Abd al-Rahman, who is Ibn Abi Ka'bsha, from Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Indeed the best remembrance is the hidden one, and the best sustenance is that which suffices." This is general in application. Yunus ibn Ubayd said: al-Hasan held that the imam should supplicate in the qunut (a prayer of supplication in the standing posture) while those behind him say "amin" without raising the voice, and Yunus recited: "when he called upon his Lord with a secret call." Ibn al-Arabi said: Malik made the qunut silent, while al-Shafi'i made it audible, and saying it audibly is more excellent, because the Prophet (ﷺ) used to supplicate with it aloud.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 19, verses 1–15 (part 2 of 4):

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿He said, "My Lord, indeed my bones have weakened within me"﴾. In this verse there are two issues [[So in the manuscripts, though it should read "three", so the text has "two issues".]]:

The first: His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿He said, "My Lord, indeed [my bones] have weakened"﴾. It is read *wahana* with all three vowel patterns, meaning he became weak. It is said: *wahana yahinu wahnan* when one becomes weak, so he is *wahin*. Abu Zayd said: it is said *wahana yahinu* and *wahina yawhanu*. He mentioned the bone (*'azm*) because it is the pillar (*'amud*) of the body, by which it stands, and it is the foundation of its structure. When it weakens, the rest of its strength collapses and falls away. It is also because it is the hardest and firmest part of the body, so when it weakens, what is beyond it is weaker still. He used the singular because the singular denotes the generic sense: his intent was that this kind, which is the pillar and support, and the strongest of what the body is composed of, has been struck by weakness. Had he used the plural, he would have intended another meaning, namely that not some of his bones had weakened but all of them.

The second: His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿and the head has blazed with grey hair﴾. Abu 'Amr assimilated the *sin* into the *shin*. This is among the finest metaphors in the speech of the Arabs. *Al-ishti'al* is the spreading of the light of fire, and the spreading of white hair over the head is likened to it. He says: "I have grown old and weakened." He attributed the blazing to the place where the hair grows, which is the head. He did not mention "the head" explicitly, relying on the listener's knowledge that it was the head of Zakariyya, peace be upon him. As for *shaybань* (*shayban*, "grey hair") in its accusative case, there are two views: the first is that it is a verbal noun (*masdar*), because the meaning of *ishta'ala* is *shāba* (grew grey). This is the view of al-Akhfash. Al-Zajjaj said it is in the accusative of specification (*tamyiz*). Al-Nahhas said: the view of al-Akhfash is preferable, because the verb is derived from *fa'ala*, so the verbal noun is more appropriate to it. *Shayb* is the mixing of black hair with white.

The third: The scholars said: it is recommended for a person, in his supplication, to mention the blessings of God Most High upon him and what befits humility, because His saying, may He be exalted, "my bones have weakened within me," is a manifestation of humility. And his saying, ﴿and I have never been unsuccessful in my prayer to You, my Lord﴾, is a manifestation of His customary bounty in answering his supplications, meaning: I have never been unsuccessful in my calling upon You; You have never disappointed my supplication whenever I called upon You, that is, You had already accustomed me to being answered in the past. It is said: *shaqiya bi-kadha* meaning he toiled at it and did not attain his aim. It is related from some of them that a needy man asked him and said: "I am the one whom you favoured at such-and-such a time." He said: "Welcome to one who has sought an intercession through us to us," and he fulfilled his need.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And indeed I fear my relatives after me, and my wife is barren, so grant me from Yourself an heir﴾. In it there are seven issues:

The first: His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿And indeed I fear my relatives (*al-mawali*)﴾. 'Uthman ibn 'Affan, Muhammad ibn 'Ali, 'Ali ibn al-Husayn, and Yahya ibn Ya'mur, may God be pleased with them, read: *khaffat* with a fatha on the *kha'*, a shadda on the *fa'*, a kasra on the *ta'*, and a sukun on the *ya'* of *al-mawali*, because it is in the nominative case as the subject of *khaffat*; its meaning is "they ceased" (*inqata'at*) by death. The rest read *khiftu* with a kasra on the *kha'*, a sukun on the *fa'*, a damma on the *ta'*, and a fatha on the *ya'* of *al-mawaliya*, because it is in the accusative case as the object of *khiftu*. Here *al-mawali* means relatives, paternal cousins and the agnates who are nearest to him in lineage. The Arabs call paternal cousins *al-mawali*. The poet said:

"Gently, O sons of our paternal uncle, gently, O our *mawali*,
Do not dig up between us what has been buried."

Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Qatada said: he feared that they would inherit his wealth, and that his estate would pass to *al-kalala* (collateral heirs), so he was apprehensive that someone other than a child would inherit it. Another group said: his relatives were merely neglectful of the religion, so he feared that upon his death the religion would be lost, and he sought an heir who would uphold the religion after him. Al-Zajjaj related this view, and according to it he did not ask for someone to inherit his wealth, because prophets are not inherited from. This is the sounder of the two views regarding the interpretation of the verse. He, upon him be blessings and peace, intended the inheritance of knowledge and prophethood, not the inheritance of wealth, because it is established from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "We, the company of prophets, are not inherited from; what we leave behind is charity." And in the book of Abu Dawud: "Indeed the scholars are the heirs of the prophets, and indeed the prophets did not bequeath dinar or dirham; they bequeathed knowledge."

More detail on this will come under His saying, "who will inherit me."

The second: This hadith falls within the category of tafsir supported by a chain of transmission (*al-tafsir al-musnad*), because of His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿And Sulayman inherited David﴾ [[See vol. 13, p. 163.]], and it is an expression of Zakariyya's words, "grant me from Yourself an heir who will inherit me and inherit from the family of Ya'qub," and a specification of the general sense in that matter: Sulayman did not inherit from David any wealth that David left behind after him; he inherited from him only wisdom and knowledge. Likewise Yahya inherited from the family of Ya'qub. This is what the people of knowledge of the Qur'an's interpretation have said, except the Rafidites. As for what is related from al-Hasan, that he said: "who will inherit me" refers to wealth, "and inherit from the family of Ya'qub" refers to prophethood and wisdom, every view that contradicts the saying of the Prophet ﷺ is rejected and abandoned, as said by Abu 'Umar. Ibn 'Atiyya said: most of the exegetes hold that Zakariyya intended only the inheritance of wealth, and the Prophet's saying ﷺ, "We, the company of prophets, are not inherited from," may be understood as not meaning it in a general sense, but as describing their usual condition. So reflect on this. The more apparent and more fitting view for Zakariyya, peace be upon him, is that he intended the inheritance of knowledge and religion, so the inheritance is used metaphorically. Do you not see that when he asked for an heir he did not specify a son, and God granted his hope in the most perfect way? Abu Salih and others said: his words "from the family of Ya'qub" mean knowledge and prophethood.

The third: His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿from after me (*min warā'i*)﴾. Ibn Kathir read with *madd* (lengthening), *hamz* (glottal stop), and a fatha on the *ya'*. It is also related from him that he read it short (*maqsur*), with a fatha on the *ya'*, like *'asaya*. The rest read it with *hamz*, lengthening, and a sukun on the *ya'*. The readers read *khiftu* as they read *nimtu*, except what we mentioned from 'Uthman. This is an anomalous reading, very remote, to the extent that some scholars claimed it is not permissible. [They say:] How can one say "the relatives became few after me," meaning after my death, while he is still alive? Al-Nahhas said: the interpretation of it is that by His saying "from after me" he does not mean after my death, but "from behind me at that time." This too is remote and requires evidence that they became few and reduced at that time. God has already informed us of something that indicates abundance when they said, "Which of them will take charge of Maryam?" [[See vol. 4, pp. 85 and 79.]]. Ibn 'Atiyya: "from after me" means after me in time; it is the sense of *warā'* as explained earlier in *al-Kahf* [[See p. 34 and following of this part.]].

The fourth: His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿and my wife has been barren﴾. His wife was Ishā' daughter of Faqudha son of Qabil, and she was the sister of Hannah daughter of Faqudha, according to al-Tabari. Hannah was the mother of Maryam, as explained earlier in *Al 'Imran* [[See vol. 4, pp. 85 and 79.]]. Al-Qutabi said: the wife of Zakariyya was Ishā' daughter of 'Imran. According to this view, Yahya would be the true maternal cousin of 'Isa, peace be upon them both. According to the other view, he would be the cousin of his mother. In the hadith of the Night Journey the Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "I met the two maternal cousins, Yahya and 'Isa," which is evidence for the first view [[The "first view" here refers to the view of al-Qutabi.]]. And God knows best.

The barren woman (*al-'aqir*) is the one who does not bear children because of her advanced age, and its explanation has already passed in *Al 'Imran*. *Al-'aqir* among women also refers to the one who does not bear children without being old. From this is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿and He makes whom He wills barren﴾ [[See vol. 16, p. 48.]] [al-Shura: 50]. Likewise *al-'aqir* among men, and from this is the saying of 'Amir ibn al-Tufayl:

"Wretched is the youth if I am one-eyed and barren,
Cowardly, so what excuse have I before every gathering?"

The fifth: His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿so grant me from Yourself an heir﴾. This is a request and a supplication. He did not state "a son" explicitly, because of what he knew of his own condition and his distance from it on account of his wife. Qatada said: this matter happened to him when he was in his seventies. Muqatil said: when he was ninety-five, and this is more likely, for it had come to be his strong expectation that he would not have children because of his old age, and for this reason he said, "and I have indeed reached extreme old age." Another group said: rather, he sought a child, and then he sought that the answer be in his living until he would inherit him, lest the answer come as a child who would be unsuitable, and the purpose would not be achieved from him.

The sixth: The scholars said: Zakariyya's supplication, peace be upon him, concerning a child was only to manifest his religion, to revive his prophethood, and to multiply his reward, not for the sake of this world. His Lord had accustomed him to being answered, and for this reason he said, "and I have never been unsuccessful in my prayer to You, my Lord," meaning in my calling upon You. This is a good means: to seek intercession through His blessings and to draw His bounty through His generosity. It is related that Hatim al-Ta'i, famed for generosity, was met by a man who asked him, and Hatim said to him: "Who are you?" He said: "I am the one to whom you did good the year before." He said: "Welcome to one who has sought intercession with us through ourselves." If it is asked: how did Zakariyya proceed to ask for something that breaks the customary order without permission? The answer is that this is permissible in the time of the prophets, and the Qur'an contains what uncovers this meaning, for He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿Whenever Zakariyya entered upon her in the sanctuary, he found provision with her. He said, "O Maryam, from where is this for you?" She said, "It is from God; indeed God provides for whom He wills without account"﴾ [Al 'Imran: 37]. When he saw the extraordinary sign, his hope in the answering of his supplication became firm, so He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿There Zakariyya called upon his Lord, saying, "My Lord, grant me from Yourself good offspring"﴾ [[See vol. 4, p. 72 and following.]] [Al 'Imran: 38], and so on.

The seventh: If someone says: this verse indicates the permissibility of supplicating for a child, while God, glory be to Him and exalted, has warned us against the calamities of wealth and children, and alerted us to the corruptions arising from them, saying: ﴿Indeed, your wealth and your children are a trial﴾ [[See vol. 18, p. 140 and following.]] [al-Taghabun: 15], and ﴿Indeed, among your spouses and your children are enemies to you, so beware of them﴾ [[See vol. 18, p. 140 and following.]] [al-Taghabun: 14]. The answer is that supplicating for a child is established from the Book and the Sunnah, as explained earlier in *Al 'Imran* [[See vol. 4, p. 72 and following.]]. Then Zakariyya, peace be upon him, took precaution, saying: "good offspring," and he said: "and make him, my Lord, one with whom You are pleased." A child who has this quality benefits his parents in this world and the next, and passes from the boundary of enmity and trial to the boundary of joy and blessing. The Prophet ﷺ supplicated for Anas, his servant, saying: "O God, increase his wealth and his children, and bless him in what You have given him." He supplicated for him for blessing, as a precaution against the ruin to which abundance may lead. Thus let the servant humbly beseech his Master for the guidance of his child and his salvation in this world and the next, following the example of the prophets, peace be upon them, and the virtuous. [Al-Awliya' [[From manuscripts J, K and Y.]]] Its explanation has already been given in *Al 'Imran* [[See vol. 4, p. 72 and following.]].

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 19, verse 1–15 (part 3 of 4):

Allah's words: ﴿He will inherit me and inherit from the family of Ya'qub; and make him, my Lord, one with whom You are pleased.﴾ In this there are four issues.

The first issue: Allah's words ﴿He will inherit me﴾. The people of the two sanctuaries (Makkah and Madinah), al-Hasan, 'Asim and Hamzah read "yarithuni wa yarithu" with a raised (marfu') ending in both places. Yahya ibn Ya'mar, Abu 'Amr, Yahya ibn Wathhab, al-A'mash and al-Kisa'i read both with a jussive (majzum) ending. According to the view of Sibawayh, these two are not the answer (jawab) to "hab" (grant); rather, its implied sense is "in tahabhu yarithuni wa yarith" (if You grant him, he will inherit me and inherit). The first reading is more correct in meaning, because he was asking for a specified heir, meaning: grant me from You the guardian who has this condition and description, since among the guardians (awliya') there are some who do not inherit. So he said: grant me one who will be my heir. This is what Abu 'Ubayd said, and he rejected the jussive reading, saying: its meaning would be "if You grant, he inherits," and how would Allah, Mighty and Majestic, inform of this when He knows it better than he does? Al-Nahhas said: this is a well-established argument, because the answer to an imperative (jawab al-amr) in the view of the grammarians carries the meaning of a condition and a consequence. You say: "Obey Allah, Exalted, and He will admit you to Paradise," meaning: if you obey Him, He will admit you to Paradise.

The second issue: Al-Nahhas said: as for the meaning of "He will inherit me and inherit from the family of Ya'qub," scholars have three interpretations. It has been said: it is the inheritance of prophethood. It has been said: it is the inheritance of wisdom. It has been said: it is the inheritance of wealth. As for their saying "inheritance of prophethood," it is impossible, because prophethood is not inherited; if it were inherited, someone would say: people trace their lineage to Nuh, peace be upon him, and he was a messenger prophet. The inheritance of knowledge and wisdom is a good view, and in a hadith: "The scholars are the heirs of the prophets." As for the inheritance of wealth, it is not impermissible, although some people have denied it, because of the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "We (prophets) do not leave inheritance; what we leave is charity." This has no proof in it, because one person may speak of himself in plural form. It may also be interpreted to mean: "We do not leave an inheritance of what we leave, which is charity," because the Prophet ﷺ did not leave anything to be inherited from him; what Allah, Mighty and Majestic, permitted him in his lifetime, by His saying, blessed is His name: ﴿And know that whatever you acquire of spoils, a fifth of it is for Allah and for the Messenger﴾ [al-Anfal: 41], because the meaning of "for Allah" is for the cause of Allah, and of the cause of Allah is what serves the interest of the Messenger ﷺ as long as he lives. If it is said: in some narrations, "We prophets do not leave inheritance; what we leave is charity," then both interpretations apply to it: that "ma" means "that which," and the other that "he who is in this condition is not inherited from." Abu 'Umar said: The scholars differed regarding the interpretation of his saying, peace be upon him: "We do not leave inheritance; what we leave is charity," into two views. One of them, which is the more common and held by the majority, is that the Prophet ﷺ is not inherited from, and what he leaves is charity. The other is that our Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, was not inherited from, because Allah, Exalted, specially made all his wealth charity, as an increase in his virtue, just as he was singled out in marriage with things He permitted to him and forbade to others. This view was held by some people of Basra, among them Ibn 'Ulayyah, while the rest of the scholars of the Muslims hold the first view.

The third issue: Allah's words ﴿from the family of Ya'qub﴾. It has been said: it is Ya'qub ibn Ishaq. Zakariyya was married to the sister of Maryam daughter of 'Imran, and her lineage goes back to Ya'qub, since she was of the descendants of Sulayman ibn Dawud, who was of the descendants of Yahudha ibn Ya'qub, and Zakariyya was of the descendants of Harun, brother of Musa, and Harun and Musa were of the descendants of Lawi ibn Ya'qub, and prophethood was in the tribe of Ya'qub ibn Ishaq. It has also been said: the meaning of Ya'qub here is Ya'qub ibn Matan, brother of 'Imran ibn Matan, father of Maryam; the two were brothers from the offspring of Sulayman ibn Dawud, peace be upon them both, because Ya'qub and 'Imran were sons of Matan, and the sons of Matan were chiefs of the Children of Israel. This was said by Muqatil and others. Al-Kalbi said: the family of Ya'qub were his maternal uncles, namely Ya'qub ibn Matan, and rulership was among them, and Zakariyya was of the descendants of Harun ibn 'Imran, brother of Musa. Qatadah narrated that the Prophet ﷺ said: "May Allah, Exalted, have mercy on Zakariyya; what did he have to do with his heirs?" Ya'qub is not declined because he is non-Arabic (a'jami).

The fourth issue: Allah's words ﴿and make him, my Lord, one with whom You are pleased﴾, that is, one who is pleasing in his character and actions. It has been said: one who is content with Your decree and destiny. It has been said: a righteous man with whom You are pleased. Abu Salih said: a prophet, just as You made his father a prophet.

Allah's words: ﴿O Zakariyya﴾. There is an omission in the speech, meaning: so Allah answered his supplication and said: "O Zakariyya, We give you good news of a boy whose name is Yahya." This good news comprised three things: first, the answering of his supplication, which is an honour. Second, the giving of a son, which is strength. Third, that he be singled out by his naming; the meaning of his naming Yahya has already been mentioned in "Al 'Imran" (see vol. 4, p. 75 onward). Muqatil said: He named him Yahya because he was made to live (hayiya) between an aged father and an old mother. This is questionable, given what has preceded, that his wife was barren and could not bear. And Allah knows best.

Allah's words: ﴿We have not made for him before, any namesake﴾, that is, We have not named anyone before Yahya with this name. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, Qatadah, Ibn Aslam and al-Suddi. He was blessed by Allah, Exalted, in that his naming was not left to his parents. Mujahid and others said: "samiyyan" means a like and an equal, and it is like His saying, Exalted: ﴿Do you know anyone of similar name to Him?﴾ [Maryam: 65], meaning a like and equal. It is as if it derives from "musamah" and "sumuw" (height). This is far-fetched, because he is not preferred over Ibrahim and Musa, except in specific matters such as nobility and chastity, as has already been explained in "Al 'Imran" (vol. 4, pp. 74 and 79). Ibn 'Abbas also said: the meaning is that barren women did not bear a son like him. It has been said: Allah, Exalted, stipulated "before," because He intended to create after him one more excellent than him, who is Muhammad ﷺ. In this verse there is evidence and proof that beautiful names (al-asami al-sung) are worthy of preference, and it was for these that the Arabs aimed in naming, because they are more distinguished and more free from reproach (nabz), until a poet said:
"Beautiful names, wearing red garments
That touch the ground with their fringes."
Ru'bah said to the genealogist al-Bakri, when he asked him about his lineage: "I am the son of al-'Ajjaj." He said: "You have fallen short and made yourself known."

Allah's words: ﴿He said: My Lord, how can I have a boy when my wife is barren and I have reached extreme old age?﴾ 40. This is not in the sense of denying what Allah, Exalted, has informed of, but in the manner of wonder at the power of Allah, Exalted, to bring forth a child from a barren woman and an aged old man. It has been said: other than this, which has been explained earlier in "Al 'Imran" (vol. 4, pp. 74 and 79).

(And I have indeed reached extreme old age) meaning the utmost in old age, dryness and desiccation. Similar to it is "al-'usiyy." Al-Asma'i said: "'asa al-shay'" (the thing) dries and hardens, "'asa'" (with extended vowel) means it dried and became hard, and "qad 'asa al-shaykh ya'su 'usiyyan" means the old man became decrepit and aged, like "ata." It is said: "'ata al-shaykh ya'tu 'utuwwan wa 'itiyyan" means the old man aged and became decrepit, and "'atawta ya fulan ta'tu 'utuwwan wa 'itiyyan." The original form is "'utuww," since it is from the roots with waw, so they changed the waw into ya', because it is its cognate and lighter than it, and the verses are on ya' endings. Whoever says "'itiyyan" dislikes the damma with the kasra and the ya'. The poet said:
"Only the youth is excused, and not
he who was in the time 'itiyyan."
Ibn 'Abbas read "'usiyyan," and it is so in the codex of Ubayy. Yahya ibn Wathhab, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Hafs read "'itiyyan" with a kasra on the 'ayn, and likewise "jithiyyan" and "siliyyan" wherever they occur. Hafs alone read "bukiyyan" with a damma, and the rest read all of them with a damma; both are dialects. It has been said: "'itiyyan" means "qasiyyan" (hard), as one says: "malik 'at" (a tyrannical king) when he is hard-hearted.

Allah's words: ﴿He said: Thus [it is]; your Lord says: It is easy for Me﴾. That is, the angel said to him: "Thus your Lord says," and the kaf is in the place of nominative, meaning: the matter is thus, as it was said to you: "It is easy for Me." Al-Farra' said: His creating him is easy for Me.

(And I created you before, when you were nothing) meaning: before Yahya. This is the reading of the people of Madinah, Basra and 'Asim. The rest of the Kufans read "wa qad khalaqnahu" with nun and alif in the plural form of majesty. The first reading is more consistent with the written text (al-sawad).

(And you were not a thing) meaning: just as Allah created you after non-existence, when you were not a thing existing, so He is capable of creating Yahya and bringing him into being.

Allah's words: ﴿He said: My Lord, make for me a sign﴾. He asked for a sign, to be carried by her (fi jamlih) after the angels' good news to him, and after Allah's words: "And I created you before, when you were nothing," as added reassurance, meaning: complete the favour by making for me a sign, and let that sign be an increase in favour and honour. It has also been said: he asked for a sign that would show him the good news of Yahya came from Him and not from Satan, because Satan had cast that thought into him. This was said by al-Dahhak, and it is the meaning of al-Suddi's view. This is questionable, given Allah's report that the angels called out to him, as has preceded in "Al 'Imran" (vol. 4, p. 80 onward).

(He said: Your sign is that you will not speak to people for three nights while being sound) 10. Its explanation has preceded in "Al 'Imran" (vol. 4, p. 80 onward), so there is no point in repeating it.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 19, verses 1–15 (part 4 of 4):**

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿So he came out to his people from the prayer niche (mihrab), and signaled to them to glorify [Allah] morning and evening﴾. In this there are five issues.

**The first issue:** His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So he came out to his people from the prayer niche﴾, meaning he appeared before them from the place of prayer (al-musalla). The *mihrab* (prayer niche) is the highest place and the most honorable seat, and they used to make *mihrabs* in what was raised from the ground. The evidence for this is the *mihrab* of Dawud, peace be upon him, as will come. People differed about its derivation. One group said: it is derived from *al-harb* (war), as if its occupant wages war (yuharib) against Satan and desires. Another group said: it is derived from *al-harab* (with a fatha on the ra'), as if its occupant encounters from it war (harab), weariness and fatigue.

**The second issue:** This verse indicates that it was legislated among them in their prayer for the imam to be raised above the congregation. The jurists of the cities differed on this matter. Imam Ahmad [ibn Hanbal [[from manuscripts J and K.]]] and others permitted it, holding to the story of the pulpit (minbar). Malik prohibited it when the elevation is great, but not when it is slight, and his companions justified the prohibition by fear of arrogance on the part of the imam. I say: this is open to scrutiny. The best that has been said on this is what Abu Dawud related from Hammam: that Hudhayfa led the people in prayer at al-Mada'in standing on a raised platform (dukkan), and Abu Mas'ud took hold of his garment and pulled him, and when he had finished his prayer he said: "Did you not know that they used to forbid this?" Or: "they used to forbid that!" He said: "Yes, I remembered when you pulled me." It is also related from Adi ibn Thabit al-Ansari, who said: A man related to me that he was with Ammar ibn Yasir at al-Mada'in, and the prayer was established, and Ammar ibn Yasir went forward and stood on a raised platform to pray while the people were below him. Hudhayfa came forward and took hold of his hands, and Ammar followed him until Hudhayfa brought him down. When Ammar had finished his prayer, Hudhayfa said to him: "Did you not hear the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say: 'When a man leads the people in prayer, he should not stand in a place higher than their station,' or words to that effect?" Ammar said: "For that I followed you when you took hold of my hands." I say: these are three of the Companions who reported the prohibition of this, and none of them argued against the other with the hadith of the pulpit. This indicates that it has been abrogated (mansukh). Among what indicates its abrogation is that it involves an additional action in the prayer, namely descending and ascending, so it was abrogated just as speech and greeting (during prayer) were abrogated. This is better than what our companions have offered as an excuse, that the Prophet ﷺ was protected from arrogance, because many imams are found to have no arrogance in them, and some of them justified it by saying that the elevation of the pulpit was slight. And Allah knows best.

**The third issue:** His saying, the Exalted: ﴿and He revealed to them that they should glorify [Him] morning and evening﴾. Al-Kalbi, Qatada and Ibn Munabbih said: *awha* means he signaled (ashara). Al-Qutabi said: he gestured (awma'a) [in manuscripts J and K: he instructed (awsa)]. Mujahid said: he wrote on the ground. Ikrima said: he wrote in a book. Revelation (al-wahy) in the speech of the Arabs means writing, and from it is the saying of Dhu al-Rummah:

*Except the four dark-colored ones, as if they were*
*A remnant of revelation in the bellies of the pages.*

And Antara said:

*Like the writing of pages from the era of Kisra,*
*Which he sent as a gift to a non-Arab, mumbling (tamtami).* [[al-tamtami: the non-Arab who does not speak clearly.]]

"Morning and evening" (bukratan wa 'ashiyyan) are two adverbs of time. Al-Farra' claimed that *al-ashi* is feminine, but it may be masculinized when left indefinite. He said: *al-'ashi* may also be the plural of *'ashiyya*.

**The fourth issue:** The ruling on signaling has already been mentioned in Al 'Imran [[see vol. 4, p. 81.]]. Our scholars differed regarding one who swears not to speak to a person and then writes to him a letter, or sends a messenger to him. Malik said: he breaks his oath, unless he intends to speak to him face to face. Then he retracted and said: he is not believed regarding the letter, and he breaks the oath unless he retrieves the letter before it reaches him. Ibn al-Qasim said: if he reads the letter he breaks the oath, and likewise if the one who swore reads the letter of the one sworn against.
