The answer is that supplicating for a child is established from the Book and the Sunnah, as explained earlier in *Al 'Imran* [[See vol. 4, p. 72 and following.]]. Then Zakariyya, peace be upon him, took precaution, saying: "good offspring," and he said: "and make him, my Lord, one with whom You are pleased." A child who has this quality benefits his parents in this world and the next, and passes from the boundary of enmity and trial to the boundary of joy and blessing. The Prophet ﷺ supplicated for Anas, his servant, saying: "O God, increase his wealth and his children, and bless him in what You have given him." He supplicated for him for blessing, as a precaution against the ruin to which abundance may lead. Thus let the servant humbly beseech his Master for the guidance of his child and his salvation in this world and the next, following the example of the prophets, peace be upon them, and the virtuous. [Al-Awliya' [[From manuscripts J, K and Y.]]] Its explanation has already been given in *Al 'Imran* [[See vol. 4, p. 72 and following.]].

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 19, verse 1–15 (part 3 of 4):

Allah's words: ﴿He will inherit me and inherit from the family of Ya'qub; and make him, my Lord, one with whom You are pleased.﴾ In this there are four issues.

The first issue: Allah's words ﴿He will inherit me﴾. The people of the two sanctuaries (Makkah and Madinah), al-Hasan, 'Asim and Hamzah read "yarithuni wa yarithu" with a raised (marfu') ending in both places. Yahya ibn Ya'mar, Abu 'Amr, Yahya ibn Wathhab, al-A'mash and al-Kisa'i read both with a jussive (majzum) ending. According to the view of Sibawayh, these two are not the answer (jawab) to "hab" (grant); rather, its implied sense is "in tahabhu yarithuni wa yarith" (if You grant him, he will inherit me and inherit). The first reading is more correct in meaning, because he was asking for a specified heir, meaning: grant me from You the guardian who has this condition and description, since among the guardians (awliya') there are some who do not inherit. So he said: grant me one who will be my heir. This is what Abu 'Ubayd said, and he rejected the jussive reading, saying: its meaning would be "if You grant, he inherits," and how would Allah, Mighty and Majestic, inform of this when He knows it better than he does? Al-Nahhas said: this is a well-established argument, because the answer to an imperative (jawab al-amr) in the view of the grammarians carries the meaning of a condition and a consequence. You say: "Obey Allah, Exalted, and He will admit you to Paradise," meaning: if you obey Him, He will admit you to Paradise.

The second issue: Al-Nahhas said: as for the meaning of "He will inherit me and inherit from the family of Ya'qub," scholars have three interpretations. It has been said: it is the inheritance of prophethood. It has been said: it is the inheritance of wisdom. It has been said: it is the inheritance of wealth. As for their saying "inheritance of prophethood," it is impossible, because prophethood is not inherited; if it were inherited, someone would say: people trace their lineage to Nuh, peace be upon him, and he was a messenger prophet. The inheritance of knowledge and wisdom is a good view, and in a hadith: "The scholars are the heirs of the prophets." As for the inheritance of wealth, it is not impermissible, although some people have denied it, because of the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "We (prophets) do not leave inheritance; what we leave is charity." This has no proof in it, because one person may speak of himself in plural form. It may also be interpreted to mean: "We do not leave an inheritance of what we leave, which is charity," because the Prophet ﷺ did not leave anything to be inherited from him; what Allah, Mighty and Majestic, permitted him in his lifetime, by His saying, blessed is His name: ﴿And know that whatever you acquire of spoils, a fifth of it is for Allah and for the Messenger﴾ [al-Anfal: 41], because the meaning of "for Allah" is for the cause of Allah, and of the cause of Allah is what serves the interest of the Messenger ﷺ as long as he lives. If it is said: in some narrations, "We prophets do not leave inheritance; what we leave is charity," then both interpretations apply to it: that "ma" means "that which," and the other that "he who is in this condition is not inherited from." Abu 'Umar said: The scholars differed regarding the interpretation of his saying, peace be upon him: "We do not leave inheritance; what we leave is charity," into two views. One of them, which is the more common and held by the majority, is that the Prophet ﷺ is not inherited from, and what he leaves is charity. The other is that our Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, was not inherited from, because Allah, Exalted, specially made all his wealth charity, as an increase in his virtue, just as he was singled out in marriage with things He permitted to him and forbade to others. This view was held by some people of Basra, among them Ibn 'Ulayyah, while the rest of the scholars of the Muslims hold the first view.

The third issue: Allah's words ﴿from the family of Ya'qub﴾. It has been said: it is Ya'qub ibn Ishaq. Zakariyya was married to the sister of Maryam daughter of 'Imran, and her lineage goes back to Ya'qub, since she was of the descendants of Sulayman ibn Dawud, who was of the descendants of Yahudha ibn Ya'qub, and Zakariyya was of the descendants of Harun, brother of Musa, and Harun and Musa were of the descendants of Lawi ibn Ya'qub, and prophethood was in the tribe of Ya'qub ibn Ishaq. It has also been said: the meaning of Ya'qub here is Ya'qub ibn Matan, brother of 'Imran ibn Matan, father of Maryam; the two were brothers from the offspring of Sulayman ibn Dawud, peace be upon them both, because Ya'qub and 'Imran were sons of Matan, and the sons of Matan were chiefs of the Children of Israel. This was said by Muqatil and others. Al-Kalbi said: the family of Ya'qub were his maternal uncles, namely Ya'qub ibn Matan, and rulership was among them, and Zakariyya was of the descendants of Harun ibn 'Imran, brother of Musa. Qatadah narrated that the Prophet ﷺ said: "May Allah, Exalted, have mercy on Zakariyya; what did he have to do with his heirs?" Ya'qub is not declined because he is non-Arabic (a'jami).

The fourth issue: Allah's words ﴿and make him, my Lord, one with whom You are pleased﴾, that is, one who is pleasing in his character and actions. It has been said: one who is content with Your decree and destiny. It has been said: a righteous man with whom You are pleased. Abu Salih said: a prophet, just as You made his father a prophet.

Allah's words: ﴿O Zakariyya﴾. There is an omission in the speech, meaning: so Allah answered his supplication and said: "O Zakariyya, We give you good news of a boy whose name is Yahya." This good news comprised three things: first, the answering of his supplication, which is an honour. Second, the giving of a son, which is strength. Third, that he be singled out by his naming; the meaning of his naming Yahya has already been mentioned in "Al 'Imran" (see vol. 4, p. 75 onward). Muqatil said: He named him Yahya because he was made to live (hayiya) between an aged father and an old mother. This is questionable, given what has preceded, that his wife was barren and could not bear. And Allah knows best.

Allah's words: ﴿We have not made for him before, any namesake﴾, that is, We have not named anyone before Yahya with this name. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, Qatadah, Ibn Aslam and al-Suddi. He was blessed by Allah, Exalted, in that his naming was not left to his parents. Mujahid and others said: "samiyyan" means a like and an equal, and it is like His saying, Exalted: ﴿Do you know anyone of similar name to Him?﴾ [Maryam: 65], meaning a like and equal. It is as if it derives from "musamah" and "sumuw" (height). This is far-fetched, because he is not preferred over Ibrahim and Musa, except in specific matters such as nobility and chastity, as has already been explained in "Al 'Imran" (vol. 4, pp. 74 and 79). Ibn 'Abbas also said: the meaning is that barren women did not bear a son like him. It has been said: Allah, Exalted, stipulated "before," because He intended to create after him one more excellent than him, who is Muhammad ﷺ. In this verse there is evidence and proof that beautiful names (al-asami al-sung) are worthy of preference, and it was for these that the Arabs aimed in naming, because they are more distinguished and more free from reproach (nabz), until a poet said:
"Beautiful names, wearing red garments
That touch the ground with their fringes."
Ru'bah said to the genealogist al-Bakri, when he asked him about his lineage: "I am the son of al-'Ajjaj." He said: "You have fallen short and made yourself known."

Allah's words: ﴿He said: My Lord, how can I have a boy when my wife is barren and I have reached extreme old age?﴾ 40. This is not in the sense of denying what Allah, Exalted, has informed of, but in the manner of wonder at the power of Allah, Exalted, to bring forth a child from a barren woman and an aged old man. It has been said: other than this, which has been explained earlier in "Al 'Imran" (vol. 4, pp. 74 and 79).

(And I have indeed reached extreme old age) meaning the utmost in old age, dryness and desiccation. Similar to it is "al-'usiyy." Al-Asma'i said: "'asa al-shay'" (the thing) dries and hardens, "'asa'" (with extended vowel) means it dried and became hard, and "qad 'asa al-shaykh ya'su 'usiyyan" means the old man became decrepit and aged, like "ata." It is said: "'ata al-shaykh ya'tu 'utuwwan wa 'itiyyan" means the old man aged and became decrepit, and "'atawta ya fulan ta'tu 'utuwwan wa 'itiyyan." The original form is "'utuww," since it is from the roots with waw, so they changed the waw into ya', because it is its cognate and lighter than it, and the verses are on ya' endings. Whoever says "'itiyyan" dislikes the damma with the kasra and the ya'. The poet said:
"Only the youth is excused, and not
he who was in the time 'itiyyan."
Ibn 'Abbas read "'usiyyan," and it is so in the codex of Ubayy. Yahya ibn Wathhab, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Hafs read "'itiyyan" with a kasra on the 'ayn, and likewise "jithiyyan" and "siliyyan" wherever they occur. Hafs alone read "bukiyyan" with a damma, and the rest read all of them with a damma; both are dialects. It has been said: "'itiyyan" means "qasiyyan" (hard), as one says: "malik 'at" (a tyrannical king) when he is hard-hearted.

Allah's words: ﴿He said: Thus [it is]; your Lord says: It is easy for Me﴾. That is, the angel said to him: "Thus your Lord says," and the kaf is in the place of nominative, meaning: the matter is thus, as it was said to you: "It is easy for Me." Al-Farra' said: His creating him is easy for Me.

(And I created you before, when you were nothing) meaning: before Yahya. This is the reading of the people of Madinah, Basra and 'Asim. The rest of the Kufans read "wa qad khalaqnahu" with nun and alif in the plural form of majesty. The first reading is more consistent with the written text (al-sawad).

(And you were not a thing) meaning: just as Allah created you after non-existence, when you were not a thing existing, so He is capable of creating Yahya and bringing him into being.

Allah's words: ﴿He said: My Lord, make for me a sign﴾. He asked for a sign, to be carried by her (fi jamlih) after the angels' good news to him, and after Allah's words: "And I created you before, when you were nothing," as added reassurance, meaning: complete the favour by making for me a sign, and let that sign be an increase in favour and honour. It has also been said: he asked for a sign that would show him the good news of Yahya came from Him and not from Satan, because Satan had cast that thought into him. This was said by al-Dahhak, and it is the meaning of al-Suddi's view. This is questionable, given Allah's report that the angels called out to him, as has preceded in "Al 'Imran" (vol. 4, p. 80 onward).

(He said: Your sign is that you will not speak to people for three nights while being sound) 10. Its explanation has preceded in "Al 'Imran" (vol. 4, p. 80 onward), so there is no point in repeating it.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 19, verses 1–15 (part 4 of 4):**

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿So he came out to his people from the prayer niche (mihrab), and signaled to them to glorify [Allah] morning and evening﴾. In this there are five issues.

**The first issue:** His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So he came out to his people from the prayer niche﴾, meaning he appeared before them from the place of prayer (al-musalla). The *mihrab* (prayer niche) is the highest place and the most honorable seat, and they used to make *mihrabs* in what was raised from the ground. The evidence for this is the *mihrab* of Dawud, peace be upon him, as will come. People differed about its derivation. One group said: it is derived from *al-harb* (war), as if its occupant wages war (yuharib) against Satan and desires. Another group said: it is derived from *al-harab* (with a fatha on the ra'), as if its occupant encounters from it war (harab), weariness and fatigue.

**The second issue:** This verse indicates that it was legislated among them in their prayer for the imam to be raised above the congregation. The jurists of the cities differed on this matter. Imam Ahmad [ibn Hanbal [[from manuscripts J and K.]]] and others permitted it, holding to the story of the pulpit (minbar). Malik prohibited it when the elevation is great, but not when it is slight, and his companions justified the prohibition by fear of arrogance on the part of the imam. I say: this is open to scrutiny. The best that has been said on this is what Abu Dawud related from Hammam: that Hudhayfa led the people in prayer at al-Mada'in standing on a raised platform (dukkan), and Abu Mas'ud took hold of his garment and pulled him, and when he had finished his prayer he said: "Did you not know that they used to forbid this?" Or: "they used to forbid that!" He said: "Yes, I remembered when you pulled me." It is also related from Adi ibn Thabit al-Ansari, who said: A man related to me that he was with Ammar ibn Yasir at al-Mada'in, and the prayer was established, and Ammar ibn Yasir went forward and stood on a raised platform to pray while the people were below him. Hudhayfa came forward and took hold of his hands, and Ammar followed him until Hudhayfa brought him down. When Ammar had finished his prayer, Hudhayfa said to him: "Did you not hear the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say: 'When a man leads the people in prayer, he should not stand in a place higher than their station,' or words to that effect?" Ammar said: "For that I followed you when you took hold of my hands." I say: these are three of the Companions who reported the prohibition of this, and none of them argued against the other with the hadith of the pulpit. This indicates that it has been abrogated (mansukh). Among what indicates its abrogation is that it involves an additional action in the prayer, namely descending and ascending, so it was abrogated just as speech and greeting (during prayer) were abrogated. This is better than what our companions have offered as an excuse, that the Prophet ﷺ was protected from arrogance, because many imams are found to have no arrogance in them, and some of them justified it by saying that the elevation of the pulpit was slight. And Allah knows best.

**The third issue:** His saying, the Exalted: ﴿and He revealed to them that they should glorify [Him] morning and evening﴾. Al-Kalbi, Qatada and Ibn Munabbih said: *awha* means he signaled (ashara). Al-Qutabi said: he gestured (awma'a) [in manuscripts J and K: he instructed (awsa)]. Mujahid said: he wrote on the ground. Ikrima said: he wrote in a book. Revelation (al-wahy) in the speech of the Arabs means writing, and from it is the saying of Dhu al-Rummah:

*Except the four dark-colored ones, as if they were*
*A remnant of revelation in the bellies of the pages.*

And Antara said:

*Like the writing of pages from the era of Kisra,*
*Which he sent as a gift to a non-Arab, mumbling (tamtami).* [[al-tamtami: the non-Arab who does not speak clearly.]]

"Morning and evening" (bukratan wa 'ashiyyan) are two adverbs of time. Al-Farra' claimed that *al-ashi* is feminine, but it may be masculinized when left indefinite. He said: *al-'ashi* may also be the plural of *'ashiyya*.

**The fourth issue:** The ruling on signaling has already been mentioned in Al 'Imran [[see vol. 4, p. 81.]]. Our scholars differed regarding one who swears not to speak to a person and then writes to him a letter, or sends a messenger to him. Malik said: he breaks his oath, unless he intends to speak to him face to face. Then he retracted and said: he is not believed regarding the letter, and he breaks the oath unless he retrieves the letter before it reaches him. Ibn al-Qasim said: if he reads the letter he breaks the oath, and likewise if the one who swore reads the letter of the one sworn against. Ashhab said: he does not break the oath if he reads it, and this is clear, because he has not spoken to him nor initiated speech with him, unless he intends that he should not know the meaning of his speech, in which case he breaks it; and Ibn al-Qasim's view is to be understood in this way. If he swears that he will certainly speak to him, he is not fulfilling it except by speaking to him face to face. Ibn al-Majishun said: if he swears "if I come to know of such-and-such, I will certainly inform him or report it to him," and then he writes to him or sends a messenger to him, he fulfills the oath; but if they both come to know it together, he does not fulfill it until he informs him, because their knowledge differs.

**The fifth issue:** Malik, al-Shafi'i and the Kufans agreed that if a mute person writes a divorce with his own hand, it is binding upon him. The Kufans said: except if a man has been silenced for days and then writes, in which case nothing of that is valid. Al-Tahawi said: muteness (al-kharas) differs from temporary silence, just as inability to have intercourse that is caused by illness or the like for a day or so differs from the permanent impotence that one despairs of, such as insanity, in the chapter on the wife's option regarding separation.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿O Yahya, take the Scripture with determination﴾. There is an ellipsis in the speech, the meaning being: a child was born to him, and Allah the Exalted said to the newborn: "O Yahya, take the Scripture with determination." This is an abbreviation that the context indicates. "The Scripture" is the Torah, without disagreement. "With determination" means with earnestness and diligence, as Mujahid said. It was also said: [it means] knowing it, memorizing it, and acting upon it, which is adherence to its commands and refraining from its prohibitions; Zayd ibn Aslam said this. It has already been discussed in al-Baqarah [[see vol. 1, p. 437.]].

[His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And We gave him judgment while still a child﴾ [[from manuscripts J and K.]]: It was said: judgment means legal rulings and knowledge of them. Ma'mar related that the children said to Yahya: "Come, let us go and play," and he said: "I was not created for play." So Allah the Exalted revealed: "And We gave him judgment while still a child." Qatada said: he was two or three years old. Muqatil said: he was three years old. "Sabiyyan" (as a child) is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (hal). Ibn 'Abbas said: whoever recites the Qur'an before reaching puberty is among those who were given judgment as children. It is related in the explanation of this verse, by way of 'Abdullah ibn 'Umar, from the Prophet ﷺ, that he said: "Every son of Adam will come on the Day of Resurrection carrying a sin, except Yahya ibn Zakariyya." Qatada said: Yahya, peace be upon him, never disobeyed Allah [[from manuscript K.]] the Exalted, neither in a minor sin nor a major one, and he never even desired a woman. Mujahid said: the food of Yahya, peace be upon him, was grass, and there were permanent channels of tears on his cheeks.]

The discussion of the meaning of His saying: ﴿and a leader and chaste﴾ [Al 'Imran: 39] has already passed in Al 'Imran [[see vol. 4, p. 86.]].

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿and compassion from Us﴾. "Hananan" (compassion) is conjoined with "al-hukm" (judgment). It is related from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "By Allah, I do not know what 'al-hanan' is." The majority of the exegetes said: al-hanan is tenderness, mercy and love, and it is one of the actions of the soul. Al-Nahhas said: regarding the meaning of al-hanan from Ibn 'Abbas there are two statements. The first: he said: Allah the Mighty and Majestic showed him tenderness with mercy. The second statement is what was given to him of the mercy of people, to the extent that he delivered them from disbelief and polytheism [[in manuscript J: "the evil."]]. Its origin is from the yearning (haniin) of the she-camel for her offspring. It is said: *hanaanaka* and *hanaaniyka*; it was said these are two dialects with the same meaning, and it was said *hanaaniyka* is the dual of *al-hanan*. Abu 'Ubayda said: the Arabs say: "Hanaanaka, O Lord" and "Hanaaniyka, O Lord" with the same meaning, meaning Your mercy. Imru' al-Qays said:

*And the sons of Shamaji ibn Jarm grant them*
*Their goats, [saying] "Your mercy, O Merciful One" (hanaanaka dha al-hanan).* [[Hanaanaka dha al-hanan means: Your mercy, O Merciful. The narration in Lisan: "yamna'uha" (withhold).]]

Tarafa said:

*O father of Mundhir, you have destroyed us, so spare some of us,*
*Have mercy (hanaaniyka), for some evil is less harmful than some other evil.*

Al-Zamakhshari said: "hananan" means mercy toward his parents and others, tenderness and compassion. Sibawayh recited:

*She said: "Hanan, what brought you here?*
*Are you of lineage, or are you one who knows the tribe?"*

Ibn al-A'rabi said: al-Hanan (with a shadda), as an attribute of Allah the Exalted, means the Compassionate; al-Hanan (without shadda) means tenderness and mercy, and al-hanan also means provision and blessing. Ibn 'Atiyya said: al-hanan in the speech of the Arabs also means what is great among matters concerning the Essence of Allah the Exalted, and from it is the saying of Zayd ibn 'Amr ibn Nufayl in the hadith of Bilal: "By Allah, if you kill this servant, I will certainly take his grave as a hanan (sanctuary)." Al-Harawi related this report and said: in the hadith of Bilal, when Waraqa ibn Nawfal passed by him while he was being tortured, he said: "By Allah, if you kill him, I will certainly take him as a hanan," meaning: I will certainly not stop touching him (la amsahanna bihi). Al-Azhari said: it means: I will certainly not show tenderness toward him nor have mercy upon him, because he is among the people of Paradise. I say: so al-hanan is tenderness, and Mujahid also said this. "Hananan" means tenderness from Us toward him, or from him toward creation. Al-Hutay'a said:

*Show me compassion (tahannan), may the King guide you,*
*For every station has its speech.*

Ikrima said: it means love. And the wife of a man is called *hunna* because of their mutual affection. The poet said:

*She said: "Hanan, what brought you here?*
*Are you of lineage, or are you one who knows the tribe?"*

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿and purity﴾. "Zakat" means purification, blessing, and growth in all forms of goodness and righteousness; that is, We made him blessed for the people, guiding them. It was also said: the meaning is that We purified him by giving him good praise, as witnesses commend a person. It was also said: "zakatan" means charity given on his behalf to his parents, said by Ibn Qutayba.

(And he was pious) meaning obedient to Allah the Exalted; for this reason he did not commit a sin and did not approach one.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿and dutiful to his parents﴾. "Barr" is in the sense of "barr" (dutiful), which is one who is abundantly dutiful. And ﴿tyrannical﴾ means arrogant. This is a description of Yahya, peace be upon him, in gentleness of manner and lowering of the wing (humility).

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And peace be upon him the day he was born﴾. Al-Tabari and others said: its meaning is safety (aman). Ibn 'Atiyya said: in my view the more evident meaning is the customary greeting, which is more honorable and more striking than safety, because safety is attained for him through the absence of disobedience from him, and that is the least of his ranks; rather, the honor lies in that Allah the Exalted greeted him with peace and saluted him in the situations in which a person is in utmost weakness, need, lack of resources, and poverty before Allah the Exalted, [and in manuscripts J and K: and the magnitude of the terror] before the Mighty Power.

I say: this is a good statement. We have already mentioned its meaning from Sufyan ibn 'Uyayna in the chapter of Subhan [[see vol. 10, p. 220.]] [al-Isra': 1], regarding the killing of Yahya. Al-Tabari related from al-Hasan that 'Isa and Yahya met, and they were cousins through their mothers. Yahya said to 'Isa: "Pray to Allah for me, for you are better than me." 'Isa said to him: "Rather, you pray to Allah for me, for you are better than me. Allah greeted you with peace, and I greeted myself with peace." Some scholars derived from this verse concerning the greeting that 'Isa is superior, saying: his greeting upon himself indicates his rank with Allah the Exalted, which required that, when he is established in the Mighty Book, he is greater in station than to be greeted upon. Ibn 'Atiyya said: each has its own perspective.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 19, verse 16–26 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And mention in the Book Mary﴾
[He means] the story to its end. This is the beginning of a story that is not part of the first one. The address is to Muhammad (ﷺ), i.e., inform them of her story so that they may know the completeness of Our power.

(﻿When she withdrew) means she withdrew and distanced herself. Al-nabdh (rejection, casting away) is throwing and casting off. God, may He be exalted, says: ﴿So they cast it behind their backs﴾[[See vol. 2 p. 40 and vol. 4 p. 305.]] [Al Imran: 187].

(from her family)
i.e., from those who were with her. "Idh" (when) is a substitute for "Maryam," a substitute of inclusion, because times include what is in them. Al-intibadh (withdrawal) is seclusion and isolation. People differed about why she withdrew. Al-Suddi said: she withdrew to purify herself from menstruation or post-natal bleeding. Others said: to worship God, and this is good. That is because Maryam, peace be upon her, was dedicated to the service of the sanctuary (sidana), its service and worship within it, so she withdrew from people for that reason, and entered the mosque beside the mihrab on its eastern side to be alone for worship, and Gabriel, peace be upon him, came in to her. So His saying: (a place toward the east) means a place on the eastern side. Al-sharq (with a sukun on the ra') is the place where the sun rises, and al-sharaq (with a fatha on the ra') is the sun. The place was singled out as eastern because they used to honour the direction of the east, from where the lights rise, and the eastern directions of everything were considered better than others; this is related by al-Tabari. It is reported from Ibn Abbas that he said: I know best of people why the Christians took the east as a qibla, based on God's saying, Mighty and Majestic: "When she withdrew from her family to a place toward the east," so they took the birth of Jesus, peace be upon him, as a qibla, and said: If any place on earth were better than the east, Mary would have placed Jesus there. People differed about the prophethood of Maryam. It was said: she was a prophetess by this sending and conversation with the angel. It was also said: she was not a prophetess, but a human-like figure spoke to her, and her seeing the angel was like Gabriel's appearance in the form of Dihya al-Kalbi when he asked about faith and Islam. The first view is more apparent. The discussion of this matter has been fully covered in "Al Imran" [[See vol. 4 p. 83 and following.]] and praise be to God.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So We sent to her Our Spirit﴾
It was said: it is the spirit of Jesus, peace be upon him, because God created the spirits before the bodies, so He placed the spirit in the body of Jesus, peace be upon him, which He had created in her womb. It was also said: it is Gabriel, and the spirit was attributed to God, may He be exalted, as a specification and honour. The apparent meaning is that it is Gabriel, peace be upon him, because of His saying: (and he appeared to her) i.e., the angel appeared to her.

(as a man)
is an explanation or a circumstantial clause.

(in every way) [[sawiyyan]]
i.e., of complete form, because she could not bear to look at Gabriel in his true form. When she saw a man of good appearance in human form who had broken through the veil for her, she thought he intended her harm, so she said: ﴿I seek refuge in the Most Merciful from you, if you are God-fearing﴾, i.e., among those who fear God. Al-Bakali said: Gabriel, peace be upon him, recoiled in alarm at the mention of the Most Merciful, blessed and exalted is He. Al-Tha'labi said: he was a righteous man, so she sought refuge in him out of amazement. It was also said: taqiyy is an fa'il in the sense of a maf'ul, i.e., you were one from whom one guards oneself. In al-Bukhari, Abu Wa'il said: Maryam knew that the God-fearing person has restraint when she said: "if you are God-fearing." It was also said: taqiyy is the name of a well-known wicked man at that time, said by Wahb ibn Munabbih, related by Makki and others; Ibn Atiyya said: this is weak and goes with conjecture. Then Gabriel, peace be upon him, said to her: ﴿I am only the messenger of your Lord, to give you a pure son﴾.

He made the giving come from Himself since the announcement of it came from Him. Warsh, from Nafi', read "li-yahaba laki" (that He may give you), meaning God sent me so that He may give you. It was also said: the meaning of "li-ahaba" with hamza is taken according to meaning, i.e., he said: I was sent to give you. "Li-yahaba" without hamza may carry the meaning of the hamzated form, with the hamza then softened.

When Maryam heard that from his words, she asked about the manner of it, so she said: ﴿How can I have a son when no man has touched me﴾ [20], i.e., by marriage.

(and I have not been unchaste) [20], i.e., an adulteress. She mentioned this for emphasis, because her saying "no man has touched me" includes both lawful and unlawful. It was also said: she did not consider anything of God's power unlikely, but she wanted to know how this child would come about: from a husband in the future, or would God create him from the beginning? It is narrated that when Gabriel, peace be upon him, said this to her, he blew into the opening of her garment and sleeve; this is said by Ibn Jurayj. Ibn Abbas said: Gabriel, peace be upon him, took the cuff of her shirt with his finger and blew into it, and she conceived Jesus at that very moment. Al-Tabari said: the Christians claim that Maryam conceived Jesus when she was thirteen years old, that Jesus lived until he was raised at thirty-two years and some days, and that Maryam remained six years after his raising, so the whole of her life was over fifty-some years.

His saying: (and so that We may make him) is connected to an omitted element, i.e., and We create him so that We may make him: (a sign) [10], a proof of Our wondrous power, (and a mercy) [i.e. [[from K.]]] for whoever believes in him.

(And it was a matter decreed) i.e., determined, written in the Preserved Tablet.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So she withdrew with him to a remote place﴾, i.e., she withdrew with the pregnancy to a distant place. Ibn Abbas said: to the farthest part of the valley, which is the valley of Bethlehem, four miles between it and Iliya. She went far away only to flee from her people's reproach for bearing a child without a husband. Ibn Abbas said: it was only that she conceived, then gave birth immediately, and this is the apparent meaning, because God mentioned the withdrawal right after the conception. It was also said otherwise, as will come: His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And the pains of childbirth drove her to the trunk of a palm tree﴾. "Ajaaha" [in the sense of [[from J. and K.]]] compelled her; it is the causative of "jaa'a" with a hamza. One says: jaa'ahu bihi and ajaahu ila mawdi' kadha, as one says dhahaba bihi and adhhabahu. Shubayl read, and it is related from Asim: "fa-ajaaha" from al-mufaja'a (suddenness). In the codex of Ubayy: "falamma ajaahaha al-makhadu" (when the pains came upon her). Zuhayr said:

A neighbour who came walking toward us, / fear and hope brought him (ajaathu al-makhafatu wa'l-rajau)

The majority read "al-makhadu" with a fatha on the mim, and Ibn Kathir, according to what is related from him, read it with a kasra. It means the labour pangs and the severity of childbirth and its pains. The woman "makhidat tamkhadu makhadan wa-mikhadan." A she-camel is "makhid," meaning her delivery is near. (to the trunk of a palm tree) as though she sought something to lean on and cling to, as a pregnant woman clings from the severity of labour pains. The "jidh" is the dry trunk of a palm tree in the desert which has no fronds or branches on it, and for this reason He did not say "to the palm tree."

(She said: Would that I had died before this) Maryam, peace be upon her, wished for death for religious reasons, for two reasons: first, she feared that evil would be assumed of her in her religion and she would be blamed, and that would trouble her. Second, lest people fall into slander and accuse her of fornication, and that is destructive. On this basis, wishing for death is permissible, and this meaning has been explained in Surat Yusuf [[See vol. 9 p. 269.]], peace be upon him, and praise be to God. I say: I have heard that Maryam, peace be upon her, heard the call of someone saying: "Come out, O you who are worshipped besides God," so she grieved over that, and (she said: Would that I had died before this and been a forgotten, forgotten thing). Al-nisy in the speech of the Arabs is a worthless thing which is likely to be forgotten and whose loss causes no pain, like a peg or a rope for the traveller and the like.

It is related from the Arabs that when they wished to leave a dwelling they said: "Guard your al-ansa'" (the trifles); al-ansa' is the plural of nisy, which is a worthless thing that is overlooked and forgotten. From it is the saying of al-Kumayt, may God be pleased with him:

"Will you make us a bridge for the dog of Qudaa'a, / while I am no nisy among Ma'add nor Dakhal?"

Al-Farra said: al-nisy is what a woman discards of her menstrual rags, so Maryam's saying "nasyan mansiyyan" means a discarded menstrual rag. It is read "nasyan" with a fatha on the nun, and both are dialectal variants, like al-hijr and al-hajar, al-widr and al-wadr. Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi read it with hamza: "nisya" with a kasra on the nun. Nawf al-Bakali read "nasya" with a fatha on the nun, from "nasa'a Allahu fi ajalihi," i.e., He delayed it. Abu al-Fath and al-Dani related it from Muhammad ibn Ka'b. Bakr ibn Habib read "nassan" with a shadda on the sin and a fatha on the nun without hamza.

Al-Tabari has related in her story that when she conceived Jesus, peace be upon him, her sister also conceived Yahya, so her sister came visiting and said: "Maryam, did you know that I have conceived?" She replied: "I find that what is in my belly prostrates to what is in your belly." This is because it is narrated that she felt her unborn child bow its head toward the side of Maryam's belly. Al-Suddi said: this is His saying: ﴿confirming a word from God, and a lord and chaste, and a prophet from the righteous﴾ [[See vol. 4 p. 74.]] [Al Imran: 39]. It is also mentioned in her story that she went out fleeing with a man from the Children of Israel called Yusuf the carpenter, who had served with her in the mosque, and this was prolonged. Al-Kalbi said: it was said to Yusuf, and it had been reported to him, that she had conceived from fornication: "Now the king will kill her." So he fled with her, and on the way he intended to kill her, but Gabriel, peace be upon him, came to him and said: "She is of the Holy Spirit." Ibn Atiyya said: all of this is weak. This story implies that she conceived and remained pregnant according to the custom of women, and the reports agree that she gave birth to him after eight months. Ikrima said this, and for that reason it was said: a child of eight months does not live, as a special sign for Jesus. It was also said: she bore him after nine months, and it was said: after six months. What we have related from Ibn Abbas is more correct and more apparent. And God knows best.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Then he called to her from beneath her﴾. It is read with a fatha and with a kasra on the mim. Ibn Abbas said: the meaning of "from beneath her" is Gabriel, and Jesus did not speak until she brought him to her people. This is also said by Alqama, al-Dahhak and Qatada. In this there is a sign for her and an indication that this is one of the matters that breaks habit, which God, may He be exalted, intends for a great purpose. His saying: (Do not grieve) explains the call, and "an" is explanatory in the sense of "i.e.": the meaning is: do not grieve over your delivery.

(Your Lord has placed beneath you a stream) meaning Jesus. Al-sariyy among men is the noble of qualities, the lord. Al-Hasan said: by God, he was a noble man among men. It is said: so-and-so was "sariyy" over so-and-so, i.e., he was generous; and so-and-so is a sariyy from a people of nobles. The majority said: he pointed for her to the small stream that was near the trunk of the palm tree. Ibn Abbas said: it was a river whose water had dried up, and God caused it to flow for Maryam. The river is called "sariyy" because water flows in it. The poet said:

"A bucket... you see the drawing-bucket from it turning, / when it gushes into the sariyy, making a splashing sound."

And Labid said:

"They passed through the middle of the stream and split... the spring full, its reeds close together."

And it was said: Isa called to her (ﷺ)... [Note: this is the reading of one who reads "min" with a fatha, meaning "from below her."] This would have been a miracle, a sign, and a comfort to her heart. The first view is more apparent. Ibn Abbas read: ﴿Then a angel called to her from below her﴾. They said: Jibril (peace be upon him) was in a place on the ground lower than the place where she was.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And shake toward yourself the trunk of the palm tree; it will drop upon you fresh ripe dates. So eat and drink and be cool of eye﴾. In it are four issues.

The first: His saying, ﴿And shake﴾. He commanded her to shake the dry trunk so that she would see another sign in the revival of the dead trunk. The *ba'* in "bi-jidh'" is superfluous and emphatic, as one says: "Take hold of the rein," and "Give with your hand." God said: ﴿let him stretch a rope to the sky﴾, meaning, let him stretch a rope. It was also said that the meaning is: "Shake toward yourself ripe dates upon the trunk of the palm tree." "Tusaqit" means "tatasaqat," so the *ta'* was assimilated into the *sin*. Hamzah read "tasaqat" with a light pronunciation, omitting the one that the others assimilated. Asim, in the transmission of Hafs, read "tusaqit" with a *damma* on the *ta'*, lightly pronounced, and a *kasra* on the *qaf*. It was also read: "tatasaqat" with both *ta'*s pronounced, and "yassaqat" with a *ya'* and assimilation of the *ta'*, "tusqit," "yusqit," "tasquts," and "yasquts," with *ta'* referring to the palm tree and *ya'* referring to the trunk. These are nine readings, as al-Zamakhshari, may Allah have mercy on him, mentioned. "Ruṭaban" is in the accusative governed by the shaking: that is, when you shake the trunk, by its shaking you cause "ruṭaban janiyyan" [fresh ripe dates] to fall. Overall, the accusative of "ruṭaban" varies according to the meanings of the readings: at times the verb is attributed to the trunk, at times to the shaking, and at times to the palm tree.

"Janiyyan" means that they have ripened and become fit for picking, and it derives from "janaytu al-thamarah" (I picked the fruit). It is transmitted from Ibn Mas'ud, though this is not authentic, that he read: "tusaqit 'alayki ruṭaban janiyyan barniyyan." [Barni: a kind of yellow, round date, the best of dates; its singular is barniyyah.] Mujahid said of "ruṭaban janiyyan": it was ajwah [a type of date]. Abbas ibn al-Fadl said: I asked Abu Amr ibn al-'Ala' about His saying "ruṭaban janiyyan," and he said: "It had not withered." He said: Its explanation is that it had not dried out or become desiccated, and had not moved far from the hands of the one picking it. This is the correct view. Al-Farra' said: "al-janiyy" and "al-mujnay" are the same; he holds that they are like "al-qatil" and "al-maqtul," and "al-jarih" and "al-majruh." Other than al-Farra' said: "al-janiyy" is what is cut from a single palm tree and taken from the place where it grew. They recited:

*The goodness of fruits in a fertile garden, and branches of trees picked near at hand.*

He means by "al-jana" what is picked from them, that is, cut and taken.

Ibn Abbas said: the trunk was dry and bare. When she shook it, she looked up at the top of the trunk and saw that the fronds had sprouted; then she looked at the spathe emerging from between the fronds; then it turned green and became unripe dates, then reddened and became ripe-colored dates, then fully ripe dates, all within the twinkling of an eye. The dates began to fall before her, and none of them were crushed.

The second: Some people derived from this verse that although provision is decreed, God has entrusted the son of Adam to strive for what is in it, because He commanded Maryam to shake the palm trunk so that she would see a sign, and the sign would have been by not shaking it.

The third: The command to undertake earning one's provision is God's practice among His servants, and this does not detract from reliance upon God, contrary to what the ignorant ascetics say. This meaning and the disagreement about it have already been discussed. Before that, her provision used to come to her without any effort, as He said: ﴿Whenever Zakariya entered upon her in the sanctuary, he found provision with her﴾ [Ali Imran: 37], up to the end of the verse. When she gave birth, she was commanded to shake the trunk. Our scholars said: When her heart was free, God freed her limbs from exertion. When she gave birth to Isa and her heart became attached to his love, and her inner self became preoccupied with his matter and affair, He entrusted her to her own earning and returned her to the usual course of attachment to means among His servants.

Al-Tabari related from Ibn Zayd that Isa (peace be upon him) said to her: "Do not grieve." She said to him: "How should I not grieve, when you are with me? I am neither a wife nor a slave! What excuse will I have before the people?!" ﴿Would that I had died before this and had become a thing forgotten﴾. Then Isa said to her: "I will suffice you in speech."

The fourth: Al-Rabi' ibn Khaythum said: For the woman in postpartum bleeding, I hold nothing better than fresh dates, because of this verse. Had God known of anything better than fresh dates for a woman in postpartum bleeding, He would have fed it to Maryam. For this reason they said: dates are customary for a woman in postpartum bleeding from that time on, and likewise the *tahnik* (rubbing the newborn's palate with date). It was also said: if her delivery is difficult, there is nothing better for her than fresh dates, and nothing better for the sick than honey. Al-Zamakhshari mentioned this. Ibn Wahb said: Malik said: God said ﴿fresh ripe dates﴾; "janiyy" among dates is that which has ripened without being scored or spoiled. "Naqsh" is when one scores the bottom of the unripe date until it softens; this is disliked. Malik means that this is hastening a thing before its time, so no one should do it. If someone does it, that does not make it permissible to sell it, nor is it a judgment that it is good. This view has already passed in *al-An'am* [see vol. 7, p. 50 and what follows]. Praise be to God.

It is transmitted from Talhah ibn Sulayman that he read "janiyyan" with a *kasra* on the *jim*, for harmony (*al-ittba'*). That is, we made for you in the stream and the ripe dates two benefits: one is eating and drinking, and the second is consolation of the heart, because both are miracles. This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿So eat and drink and be cool of eye﴾, that is: eat from the ripe dates, drink from the stream, and "be cool of eye" by seeing your child, the prophet. It was read with a *fatha* on the *qaf*, which is the reading of the majority. Al-Tabari related the reading "wa qirri" with a *kasra* on the *qaf*, which is the dialect of Najd. It is said: "qarra 'aynan yaqurru wa yaqirru" with a *damma* or *kasra* on the *qaf*, and "aqarra Allahu 'aynahu fa-qarrat" (God cooled his eye, so it became cool). It derives from "al-qurr" and "al-qurrah," which are coolness. The tear of joy is cool, and the tear of sorrow is hot. A group weakened this view and said: all tears are hot; so the meaning of "aqarra Allahu 'aynahu" is that God calmed his eye by looking at the one he loves until it becomes cool and still, and "so-and-so is the coolness of my eye" means my soul is at rest by his nearness. Al-Shaybani said: "wa qirri 'aynan" means "sleep": he urged her to eat, drink, and sleep. Abu Amr said: "aqarra Allahu 'aynahu" means God made his eye sleep and removed his wakefulness. "'Aynan" is in the accusative as a specification (*tamyiz*), like your saying "tibb nafsan" (be content in soul). In reality the verb belongs to the eye, so it was transferred to the possessor of the eye, and what was in reality the subject is put in the accusative as explanation. Similar to this are "tibtu nafsan" (I was content in soul), "tafa'a'tu shahman" (I burst with fat), and "tasabbabtu 'arqan" (I poured out sweat), and there are many such.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if you see any human, say: I have vowed to the Most Merciful a fast﴾. In it are three issues.

The first: His saying, ﴿And if you see﴾. The original form of "tarayinna" is "tar'ayina" [before emphasis and the entry of the jussive particle, it is of the pattern "tamna'in"]. The hamzah was dropped as it was dropped from "tara," and its vowel was moved to the *ra'*, so it became "tarayina." Then the first *ya'* was changed to an *alif* because it was vowelled and what preceded it was open. So two unvowelled letters met: the *alif* converted from *ya'* and the feminine *ya'*. The *alif* was dropped to avoid the meeting of two unvowelled letters, so it became "tarayna." Then the *nun* was dropped as the sign of the jussive, because "in" is a conditional particle and "ma" is an added element, so "tarai" remained. Then the emphatic *nun*, which is doubled, entered; the feminine *ya'* was given a *kasra* to avoid meeting two unvowelled letters, because the doubled *nun* is like two *nun*s, the first being unvowelled, so it became "tarayinna." On this pattern is the saying of Ibn Duraid:

*If you see my head, its color has imitated [the color of white],*
*[Its completion: "I flew at dawn beneath the trailing skirts of the darkness."]*

And the saying of al-Afwah:

*If you see my head, time has worn it down...*
*[Its completion: "The time of the one with reverses, the disappointed, has swayed."]*

The *nun* entered here only because of the preparatory *ma*, just as the oath particle *lam* also prepares for its entry. Talhah, Abu Ja'far, and Shaybah read "tarayna" with the *ya'* unvowelled and the *nun* light with a *fatha*. Abu al-Fath said: this is anomalous.

The second: His saying, ﴿So say: I have vowed﴾. This is the response of the conditional, and in it is an implied element, that is: if he asks you about your child, then say: "I have vowed to the Most Merciful a fast," that is, silence. This was said by Ibn Abbas and Anas ibn Malik. In the reading of Ubayy ibn Ka'b: "I have vowed to the Most Merciful a fast, a silence (*sawman samtan*)." It is also transmitted from Anas: "wa samtan" with a *waw*. The difference between the two wordings shows that the word was mentioned as an explanation, not as Qur'an. When the *waw* accompanies it, it is possible that it refers to something other than fasting. What has been consistently transmitted from the people of hadith and the transmitters of language is that *sawm* is *samt*, because *sawm* is abstention and *samt* is abstention from speech. It was also said: it is fasting in the ordinary sense, and they were required to be silent on the day of fasting except by gesture. On this basis Anas's reading "wa samtan" with a *waw* is understood: silence was among them in fasting, bound by the vow, just as whoever vows from us to walk to the House requires that one enter into *ihram* for Hajj or *'umrah*.

The meaning of this verse is that God commanded her, through the tongue of Jibril (peace be upon him), or through her son according to the earlier disagreement, to refrain from addressing humans, and to refer the matter to her son, so that her embarrassment would be lifted and the verse would be manifest, and her excuse would stand. The apparent meaning of the verse is that she was permitted to say these words that are in the verse, and this is the view of the majority. A group said: the meaning of "qouli" (say) is by gesture, not by speech. Al-Zamakhshari said: In it is that silence before a fool is obligatory, and among the most humiliated people is a fool who finds no one to reply to him.

The third: Whoever binds himself by a vow not to speak with any of the sons of Adam, it may be said that it is an act of worship, and so it becomes binding by vow; and it may be said that this is not permissible in our law, because it involves constriction and self-torment, like vowing to stand in the sun and the like. On this basis, the vow of silence was in that law, not in ours, as already mentioned. Ibn Mas'ud ordered one who did this to speak. This is the correct view, based on the hadith of Abu Isra'il, which al-Bukhari transmitted from Ibn Abbas: [The hadith as in al-Bukhari, from Ibn Abbas, who said: While the Prophet (ﷺ) was delivering a sermon, he saw a man standing, and he asked about him. They said: "Abu Isra'il vowed to stand and not sit, to not seek shade, to not speak, and to fast." The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Tell him to speak, to seek shade, to sit, and to complete his fast."] Ibn Zayd and al-Suddi said: The custom of fasting among them was abstaining from food and speech. I say: Among our own practices in fasting is abstaining from foul speech. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "When one of you is fasting, let him not utter obscenity or act ignorantly. If someone fights him or insults him, let him say: 'I am fasting.'" He (ﷺ) also said: "Whoever does not give up false speech and acting upon it, God has no need that he give up his food and drink."

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 19, verse 16–26 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And mention in the Book Mary﴾
[He means] the story to its end. This is the beginning of a story that is not part of the first one. The address is to Muhammad (ﷺ), i.e., inform them of her story so that they may know the completeness of Our power.

(﻿When she withdrew) means she withdrew and distanced herself. Al-nabdh (rejection, casting away) is throwing and casting off. God, may He be exalted, says: ﴿So they cast it behind their backs﴾[[See vol. 2 p. 40 and vol. 4 p. 305.]] [Al Imran: 187].

(from her family)
i.e., from those who were with her. "Idh" (when) is a substitute for "Maryam," a substitute of inclusion, because times include what is in them. Al-intibadh (withdrawal) is seclusion and isolation. People differed about why she withdrew. Al-Suddi said: she withdrew to purify herself from menstruation or post-natal bleeding. Others said: to worship God, and this is good. That is because Maryam, peace be upon her, was dedicated to the service of the sanctuary (sidana), its service and worship within it, so she withdrew from people for that reason, and entered the mosque beside the mihrab on its eastern side to be alone for worship, and Gabriel, peace be upon him, came in to her. So His saying: (a place toward the east) means a place on the eastern side. Al-sharq (with a sukun on the ra') is the place where the sun rises, and al-sharaq (with a fatha on the ra') is the sun. The place was singled out as eastern because they used to honour the direction of the east, from where the lights rise, and the eastern directions of everything were considered better than others; this is related by al-Tabari. It is reported from Ibn Abbas that he said: I know best of people why the Christians took the east as a qibla, based on God's saying, Mighty and Majestic: "When she withdrew from her family to a place toward the east," so they took the birth of Jesus, peace be upon him, as a qibla, and said: If any place on earth were better than the east, Mary would have placed Jesus there. People differed about the prophethood of Maryam. It was said: she was a prophetess by this sending and conversation with the angel. It was also said: she was not a prophetess, but a human-like figure spoke to her, and her seeing the angel was like Gabriel's appearance in the form of Dihya al-Kalbi when he asked about faith and Islam. The first view is more apparent. The discussion of this matter has been fully covered in "Al Imran" [[See vol. 4 p. 83 and following.]] and praise be to God.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So We sent to her Our Spirit﴾
It was said: it is the spirit of Jesus, peace be upon him, because God created the spirits before the bodies, so He placed the spirit in the body of Jesus, peace be upon him, which He had created in her womb. It was also said: it is Gabriel, and the spirit was attributed to God, may He be exalted, as a specification and honour. The apparent meaning is that it is Gabriel, peace be upon him, because of His saying: (and he appeared to her) i.e., the angel appeared to her.

(as a man)
is an explanation or a circumstantial clause.

(in every way) [[sawiyyan]]
i.e., of complete form, because she could not bear to look at Gabriel in his true form. When she saw a man of good appearance in human form who had broken through the veil for her, she thought he intended her harm, so she said: ﴿I seek refuge in the Most Merciful from you, if you are God-fearing﴾, i.e., among those who fear God. Al-Bakali said: Gabriel, peace be upon him, recoiled in alarm at the mention of the Most Merciful, blessed and exalted is He. Al-Tha'labi said: he was a righteous man, so she sought refuge in him out of amazement. It was also said: taqiyy is an fa'il in the sense of a maf'ul, i.e., you were one from whom one guards oneself. In al-Bukhari, Abu Wa'il said: Maryam knew that the God-fearing person has restraint when she said: "if you are God-fearing." It was also said: taqiyy is the name of a well-known wicked man at that time, said by Wahb ibn Munabbih, related by Makki and others; Ibn Atiyya said: this is weak and goes with conjecture. Then Gabriel, peace be upon him, said to her: ﴿I am only the messenger of your Lord, to give you a pure son﴾.

He made the giving come from Himself since the announcement of it came from Him. Warsh, from Nafi', read "li-yahaba laki" (that He may give you), meaning God sent me so that He may give you. It was also said: the meaning of "li-ahaba" with hamza is taken according to meaning, i.e., he said: I was sent to give you. "Li-yahaba" without hamza may carry the meaning of the hamzated form, with the hamza then softened.

When Maryam heard that from his words, she asked about the manner of it, so she said: ﴿How can I have a son when no man has touched me﴾ [20], i.e., by marriage.

(and I have not been unchaste) [20], i.e., an adulteress. She mentioned this for emphasis, because her saying "no man has touched me" includes both lawful and unlawful. It was also said: she did not consider anything of God's power unlikely, but she wanted to know how this child would come about: from a husband in the future, or would God create him from the beginning? It is narrated that when Gabriel, peace be upon him, said this to her, he blew into the opening of her garment and sleeve; this is said by Ibn Jurayj. Ibn Abbas said: Gabriel, peace be upon him, took the cuff of her shirt with his finger and blew into it, and she conceived Jesus at that very moment. Al-Tabari said: the Christians claim that Maryam conceived Jesus when she was thirteen years old, that Jesus lived until he was raised at thirty-two years and some days, and that Maryam remained six years after his raising, so the whole of her life was over fifty-some years.

His saying: (and so that We may make him) is connected to an omitted element, i.e., and We create him so that We may make him: (a sign) [10], a proof of Our wondrous power, (and a mercy) [i.e. [[from K.]]] for whoever believes in him.

(And it was a matter decreed) i.e., determined, written in the Preserved Tablet.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So she withdrew with him to a remote place﴾, i.e., she withdrew with the pregnancy to a distant place. Ibn Abbas said: to the farthest part of the valley, which is the valley of Bethlehem, four miles between it and Iliya. She went far away only to flee from her people's reproach for bearing a child without a husband. Ibn Abbas said: it was only that she conceived, then gave birth immediately, and this is the apparent meaning, because God mentioned the withdrawal right after the conception. It was also said otherwise, as will come: His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And the pains of childbirth drove her to the trunk of a palm tree﴾. "Ajaaha" [in the sense of [[from J. and K.]]] compelled her; it is the causative of "jaa'a" with a hamza. One says: jaa'ahu bihi and ajaahu ila mawdi' kadha, as one says dhahaba bihi and adhhabahu. Shubayl read, and it is related from Asim: "fa-ajaaha" from al-mufaja'a (suddenness). In the codex of Ubayy: "falamma ajaahaha al-makhadu" (when the pains came upon her). Zuhayr said:

A neighbour who came walking toward us, / fear and hope brought him (ajaathu al-makhafatu wa'l-rajau)

The majority read "al-makhadu" with a fatha on the mim, and Ibn Kathir, according to what is related from him, read it with a kasra. It means the labour pangs and the severity of childbirth and its pains. The woman "makhidat tamkhadu makhadan wa-mikhadan." A she-camel is "makhid," meaning her delivery is near. (to the trunk of a palm tree) as though she sought something to lean on and cling to, as a pregnant woman clings from the severity of labour pains. The "jidh" is the dry trunk of a palm tree in the desert which has no fronds or branches on it, and for this reason He did not say "to the palm tree."

(She said: Would that I had died before this) Maryam, peace be upon her, wished for death for religious reasons, for two reasons: first, she feared that evil would be assumed of her in her religion and she would be blamed, and that would trouble her. Second, lest people fall into slander and accuse her of fornication, and that is destructive. On this basis, wishing for death is permissible, and this meaning has been explained in Surat Yusuf [[See vol. 9 p. 269.]], peace be upon him, and praise be to God. I say: I have heard that Maryam, peace be upon her, heard the call of someone saying: "Come out, O you who are worshipped besides God," so she grieved over that, and (she said: Would that I had died before this and been a forgotten, forgotten thing). Al-nisy in the speech of the Arabs is a worthless thing which is likely to be forgotten and whose loss causes no pain, like a peg or a rope for the traveller and the like.

It is related from the Arabs that when they wished to leave a dwelling they said: "Guard your al-ansa'" (the trifles); al-ansa' is the plural of nisy, which is a worthless thing that is overlooked and forgotten. From it is the saying of al-Kumayt, may God be pleased with him:

"Will you make us a bridge for the dog of Qudaa'a, / while I am no nisy among Ma'add nor Dakhal?"

Al-Farra said: al-nisy is what a woman discards of her menstrual rags, so Maryam's saying "nasyan mansiyyan" means a discarded menstrual rag. It is read "nasyan" with a fatha on the nun, and both are dialectal variants, like al-hijr and al-hajar, al-widr and al-wadr. Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi read it with hamza: "nisya" with a kasra on the nun. Nawf al-Bakali read "nasya" with a fatha on the nun, from "nasa'a Allahu fi ajalihi," i.e., He delayed it. Abu al-Fath and al-Dani related it from Muhammad ibn Ka'b. Bakr ibn Habib read "nassan" with a shadda on the sin and a fatha on the nun without hamza.

Al-Tabari has related in her story that when she conceived Jesus, peace be upon him, her sister also conceived Yahya, so her sister came visiting and said: "Maryam, did you know that I have conceived?" She replied: "I find that what is in my belly prostrates to what is in your belly." This is because it is narrated that she felt her unborn child bow its head toward the side of Maryam's belly. Al-Suddi said: this is His saying: ﴿confirming a word from God, and a lord and chaste, and a prophet from the righteous﴾ [[See vol. 4 p. 74.]] [Al Imran: 39]. It is also mentioned in her story that she went out fleeing with a man from the Children of Israel called Yusuf the carpenter, who had served with her in the mosque, and this was prolonged. Al-Kalbi said: it was said to Yusuf, and it had been reported to him, that she had conceived from fornication: "Now the king will kill her." So he fled with her, and on the way he intended to kill her, but Gabriel, peace be upon him, came to him and said: "She is of the Holy Spirit." Ibn Atiyya said: all of this is weak. This story implies that she conceived and remained pregnant according to the custom of women, and the reports agree that she gave birth to him after eight months. Ikrima said this, and for that reason it was said: a child of eight months does not live, as a special sign for Jesus. It was also said: she bore him after nine months, and it was said: after six months. What we have related from Ibn Abbas is more correct and more apparent. And God knows best.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Then he called to her from beneath her﴾. It is read with a fatha and with a kasra on the mim. Ibn Abbas said: the meaning of "from beneath her" is Gabriel, and Jesus did not speak until she brought him to her people. This is also said by Alqama, al-Dahhak and Qatada. In this there is a sign for her and an indication that this is one of the matters that breaks habit, which God, may He be exalted, intends for a great purpose. His saying: (Do not grieve) explains the call, and "an" is explanatory in the sense of "i.e.": the meaning is: do not grieve over your delivery.

(Your Lord has placed beneath you a stream) meaning Jesus. Al-sariyy among men is the noble of qualities, the lord. Al-Hasan said: by God, he was a noble man among men. It is said: so-and-so was "sariyy" over so-and-so, i.e., he was generous; and so-and-so is a sariyy from a people of nobles. The majority said: he pointed for her to the small stream that was near the trunk of the palm tree. Ibn Abbas said: it was a river whose water had dried up, and God caused it to flow for Maryam. The river is called "sariyy" because water flows in it. The poet said:

"A bucket... you see the drawing-bucket from it turning, / when it gushes into the sariyy, making a splashing sound."

And Labid said:

"They passed through the middle of the stream and split... the spring full, its reeds close together."

And it was said: Isa called to her (ﷺ)... [Note: this is the reading of one who reads "min" with a fatha, meaning "from below her."] This would have been a miracle, a sign, and a comfort to her heart. The first view is more apparent. Ibn Abbas read: ﴿Then a angel called to her from below her﴾. They said: Jibril (peace be upon him) was in a place on the ground lower than the place where she was.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And shake toward yourself the trunk of the palm tree; it will drop upon you fresh ripe dates. So eat and drink and be cool of eye﴾. In it are four issues.

The first: His saying, ﴿And shake﴾. He commanded her to shake the dry trunk so that she would see another sign in the revival of the dead trunk. The *ba'* in "bi-jidh'" is superfluous and emphatic, as one says: "Take hold of the rein," and "Give with your hand." God said: ﴿let him stretch a rope to the sky﴾, meaning, let him stretch a rope. It was also said that the meaning is: "Shake toward yourself ripe dates upon the trunk of the palm tree." "Tusaqit" means "tatasaqat," so the *ta'* was assimilated into the *sin*. Hamzah read "tasaqat" with a light pronunciation, omitting the one that the others assimilated. Asim, in the transmission of Hafs, read "tusaqit" with a *damma* on the *ta'*, lightly pronounced, and a *kasra* on the *qaf*. It was also read: "tatasaqat" with both *ta'*s pronounced, and "yassaqat" with a *ya'* and assimilation of the *ta'*, "tusqit," "yusqit," "tasquts," and "yasquts," with *ta'* referring to the palm tree and *ya'* referring to the trunk. These are nine readings, as al-Zamakhshari, may Allah have mercy on him, mentioned. "Ruṭaban" is in the accusative governed by the shaking: that is, when you shake the trunk, by its shaking you cause "ruṭaban janiyyan" [fresh ripe dates] to fall. Overall, the accusative of "ruṭaban" varies according to the meanings of the readings: at times the verb is attributed to the trunk, at times to the shaking, and at times to the palm tree.

"Janiyyan" means that they have ripened and become fit for picking, and it derives from "janaytu al-thamarah" (I picked the fruit). It is transmitted from Ibn Mas'ud, though this is not authentic, that he read: "tusaqit 'alayki ruṭaban janiyyan barniyyan." [Barni: a kind of yellow, round date, the best of dates; its singular is barniyyah.] Mujahid said of "ruṭaban janiyyan": it was ajwah [a type of date]. Abbas ibn al-Fadl said: I asked Abu Amr ibn al-'Ala' about His saying "ruṭaban janiyyan," and he said: "It had not withered." He said: Its explanation is that it had not dried out or become desiccated, and had not moved far from the hands of the one picking it. This is the correct view. Al-Farra' said: "al-janiyy" and "al-mujnay" are the same; he holds that they are like "al-qatil" and "al-maqtul," and "al-jarih" and "al-majruh." Other than al-Farra' said: "al-janiyy" is what is cut from a single palm tree and taken from the place where it grew. They recited:

*The goodness of fruits in a fertile garden, and branches of trees picked near at hand.*

He means by "al-jana" what is picked from them, that is, cut and taken.

Ibn Abbas said: the trunk was dry and bare. When she shook it, she looked up at the top of the trunk and saw that the fronds had sprouted; then she looked at the spathe emerging from between the fronds; then it turned green and became unripe dates, then reddened and became ripe-colored dates, then fully ripe dates, all within the twinkling of an eye. The dates began to fall before her, and none of them were crushed.

The second: Some people derived from this verse that although provision is decreed, God has entrusted the son of Adam to strive for what is in it, because He commanded Maryam to shake the palm trunk so that she would see a sign, and the sign would have been by not shaking it.

The third: The command to undertake earning one's provision is God's practice among His servants, and this does not detract from reliance upon God, contrary to what the ignorant ascetics say. This meaning and the disagreement about it have already been discussed. Before that, her provision used to come to her without any effort, as He said: ﴿Whenever Zakariya entered upon her in the sanctuary, he found provision with her﴾ [Ali Imran: 37], up to the end of the verse. When she gave birth, she was commanded to shake the trunk. Our scholars said: When her heart was free, God freed her limbs from exertion. When she gave birth to Isa and her heart became attached to his love, and her inner self became preoccupied with his matter and affair, He entrusted her to her own earning and returned her to the usual course of attachment to means among His servants.

Al-Tabari related from Ibn Zayd that Isa (peace be upon him) said to her: "Do not grieve." She said to him: "How should I not grieve, when you are with me? I am neither a wife nor a slave! What excuse will I have before the people?!" ﴿Would that I had died before this and had become a thing forgotten﴾. Then Isa said to her: "I will suffice you in speech."

The fourth: Al-Rabi' ibn Khaythum said: For the woman in postpartum bleeding, I hold nothing better than fresh dates, because of this verse. Had God known of anything better than fresh dates for a woman in postpartum bleeding, He would have fed it to Maryam. For this reason they said: dates are customary for a woman in postpartum bleeding from that time on, and likewise the *tahnik* (rubbing the newborn's palate with date). It was also said: if her delivery is difficult, there is nothing better for her than fresh dates, and nothing better for the sick than honey. Al-Zamakhshari mentioned this. Ibn Wahb said: Malik said: God said ﴿fresh ripe dates﴾; "janiyy" among dates is that which has ripened without being scored or spoiled. "Naqsh" is when one scores the bottom of the unripe date until it softens; this is disliked. Malik means that this is hastening a thing before its time, so no one should do it. If someone does it, that does not make it permissible to sell it, nor is it a judgment that it is good. This view has already passed in *al-An'am* [see vol. 7, p. 50 and what follows]. Praise be to God.

It is transmitted from Talhah ibn Sulayman that he read "janiyyan" with a *kasra* on the *jim*, for harmony (*al-ittba'*). That is, we made for you in the stream and the ripe dates two benefits: one is eating and drinking, and the second is consolation of the heart, because both are miracles. This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿So eat and drink and be cool of eye﴾, that is: eat from the ripe dates, drink from the stream, and "be cool of eye" by seeing your child, the prophet. It was read with a *fatha* on the *qaf*, which is the reading of the majority. Al-Tabari related the reading "wa qirri" with a *kasra* on the *qaf*, which is the dialect of Najd. It is said: "qarra 'aynan yaqurru wa yaqirru" with a *damma* or *kasra* on the *qaf*, and "aqarra Allahu 'aynahu fa-qarrat" (God cooled his eye, so it became cool). It derives from "al-qurr" and "al-qurrah," which are coolness. The tear of joy is cool, and the tear of sorrow is hot. A group weakened this view and said: all tears are hot; so the meaning of "aqarra Allahu 'aynahu" is that God calmed his eye by looking at the one he loves until it becomes cool and still, and "so-and-so is the coolness of my eye" means my soul is at rest by his nearness. Al-Shaybani said: "wa qirri 'aynan" means "sleep": he urged her to eat, drink, and sleep. Abu Amr said: "aqarra Allahu 'aynahu" means God made his eye sleep and removed his wakefulness. "'Aynan" is in the accusative as a specification (*tamyiz*), like your saying "tibb nafsan" (be content in soul). In reality the verb belongs to the eye, so it was transferred to the possessor of the eye, and what was in reality the subject is put in the accusative as explanation. Similar to this are "tibtu nafsan" (I was content in soul), "tafa'a'tu shahman" (I burst with fat), and "tasabbabtu 'arqan" (I poured out sweat), and there are many such.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if you see any human, say: I have vowed to the Most Merciful a fast﴾. In it are three issues.

The first: His saying, ﴿And if you see﴾. The original form of "tarayinna" is "tar'ayina" [before emphasis and the entry of the jussive particle, it is of the pattern "tamna'in"]. The hamzah was dropped as it was dropped from "tara," and its vowel was moved to the *ra'*, so it became "tarayina." Then the first *ya'* was changed to an *alif* because it was vowelled and what preceded it was open. So two unvowelled letters met: the *alif* converted from *ya'* and the feminine *ya'*. The *alif* was dropped to avoid the meeting of two unvowelled letters, so it became "tarayna." Then the *nun* was dropped as the sign of the jussive, because "in" is a conditional particle and "ma" is an added element, so "tarai" remained. Then the emphatic *nun*, which is doubled, entered; the feminine *ya'* was given a *kasra* to avoid meeting two unvowelled letters, because the doubled *nun* is like two *nun*s, the first being unvowelled, so it became "tarayinna." On this pattern is the saying of Ibn Duraid:

*If you see my head, its color has imitated [the color of white],*
*[Its completion: "I flew at dawn beneath the trailing skirts of the darkness."]*

And the saying of al-Afwah:

*If you see my head, time has worn it down...*
*[Its completion: "The time of the one with reverses, the disappointed, has swayed."]*

The *nun* entered here only because of the preparatory *ma*, just as the oath particle *lam* also prepares for its entry. Talhah, Abu Ja'far, and Shaybah read "tarayna" with the *ya'* unvowelled and the *nun* light with a *fatha*. Abu al-Fath said: this is anomalous.

The second: His saying, ﴿So say: I have vowed﴾. This is the response of the conditional, and in it is an implied element, that is: if he asks you about your child, then say: "I have vowed to the Most Merciful a fast," that is, silence. This was said by Ibn Abbas and Anas ibn Malik. In the reading of Ubayy ibn Ka'b: "I have vowed to the Most Merciful a fast, a silence (*sawman samtan*)." It is also transmitted from Anas: "wa samtan" with a *waw*. The difference between the two wordings shows that the word was mentioned as an explanation, not as Qur'an. When the *waw* accompanies it, it is possible that it refers to something other than fasting. What has been consistently transmitted from the people of hadith and the transmitters of language is that *sawm* is *samt*, because *sawm* is abstention and *samt* is abstention from speech. It was also said: it is fasting in the ordinary sense, and they were required to be silent on the day of fasting except by gesture. On this basis Anas's reading "wa samtan" with a *waw* is understood: silence was among them in fasting, bound by the vow, just as whoever vows from us to walk to the House requires that one enter into *ihram* for Hajj or *'umrah*.

The meaning of this verse is that God commanded her, through the tongue of Jibril (peace be upon him), or through her son according to the earlier disagreement, to refrain from addressing humans, and to refer the matter to her son, so that her embarrassment would be lifted and the verse would be manifest, and her excuse would stand. The apparent meaning of the verse is that she was permitted to say these words that are in the verse, and this is the view of the majority. A group said: the meaning of "qouli" (say) is by gesture, not by speech. Al-Zamakhshari said: In it is that silence before a fool is obligatory, and among the most humiliated people is a fool who finds no one to reply to him.

The third: Whoever binds himself by a vow not to speak with any of the sons of Adam, it may be said that it is an act of worship, and so it becomes binding by vow; and it may be said that this is not permissible in our law, because it involves constriction and self-torment, like vowing to stand in the sun and the like. On this basis, the vow of silence was in that law, not in ours, as already mentioned. Ibn Mas'ud ordered one who did this to speak. This is the correct view, based on the hadith of Abu Isra'il, which al-Bukhari transmitted from Ibn Abbas: [The hadith as in al-Bukhari, from Ibn Abbas, who said: While the Prophet (ﷺ) was delivering a sermon, he saw a man standing, and he asked about him. They said: "Abu Isra'il vowed to stand and not sit, to not seek shade, to not speak, and to fast." The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Tell him to speak, to seek shade, to sit, and to complete his fast."] Ibn Zayd and al-Suddi said: The custom of fasting among them was abstaining from food and speech. I say: Among our own practices in fasting is abstaining from foul speech. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "When one of you is fasting, let him not utter obscenity or act ignorantly. If someone fights him or insults him, let him say: 'I am fasting.'" He (ﷺ) also said: "Whoever does not give up false speech and acting upon it, God has no need that he give up his food and drink."

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 19, verse 16–26 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And mention in the Book Mary﴾
[He means] the story to its end. This is the beginning of a story that is not part of the first one. The address is to Muhammad (ﷺ), i.e., inform them of her story so that they may know the completeness of Our power.

(﻿When she withdrew) means she withdrew and distanced herself. Al-nabdh (rejection, casting away) is throwing and casting off. God, may He be exalted, says: ﴿So they cast it behind their backs﴾[[See vol. 2 p. 40 and vol. 4 p. 305.]] [Al Imran: 187].

(from her family)
i.e., from those who were with her. "Idh" (when) is a substitute for "Maryam," a substitute of inclusion, because times include what is in them. Al-intibadh (withdrawal) is seclusion and isolation. People differed about why she withdrew. Al-Suddi said: she withdrew to purify herself from menstruation or post-natal bleeding. Others said: to worship God, and this is good. That is because Maryam, peace be upon her, was dedicated to the service of the sanctuary (sidana), its service and worship within it, so she withdrew from people for that reason, and entered the mosque beside the mihrab on its eastern side to be alone for worship, and Gabriel, peace be upon him, came in to her. So His saying: (a place toward the east) means a place on the eastern side. Al-sharq (with a sukun on the ra') is the place where the sun rises, and al-sharaq (with a fatha on the ra') is the sun. The place was singled out as eastern because they used to honour the direction of the east, from where the lights rise, and the eastern directions of everything were considered better than others; this is related by al-Tabari. It is reported from Ibn Abbas that he said: I know best of people why the Christians took the east as a qibla, based on God's saying, Mighty and Majestic: "When she withdrew from her family to a place toward the east," so they took the birth of Jesus, peace be upon him, as a qibla, and said: If any place on earth were better than the east, Mary would have placed Jesus there. People differed about the prophethood of Maryam. It was said: she was a prophetess by this sending and conversation with the angel. It was also said: she was not a prophetess, but a human-like figure spoke to her, and her seeing the angel was like Gabriel's appearance in the form of Dihya al-Kalbi when he asked about faith and Islam.
