And this is the first view. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: A group said rather that in that time there was a wicked man named Harun, and they ascribed her to him by way of reproach and rebuke; al-Tabari mentioned it but did not name its speaker. I say: al-Ghaznawi mentioned it from Sa'id ibn Jubayr that he was a notorious sinner, a proverb for debauchery, so she was ascribed to him. The meaning: neither your father nor your mother was fit for this deed, so how did you come with it?! This is a form of insinuation (ta'ridh) that takes the place of explicit statement. And that, in our view, necessitates the hadd punishment, and its discussion will come in surah "al-Nur," God willing [[See vol. 12, p. 159 and following.]]. This last view is refuted by the sound hadith, which is an explicit text, so no one has any argument against it, and there is no dust upon it. And praise be to God. 'Umar ibn Laja' al-Taymi read: (Ma kana abaki imru' [[He said in al-Bahr: he makes the predicate definite and the subject indefinite, and this is good although rare, since it has a justification for beginning with an indefinite, which is the idafah.]] su').

There are five issues in this passage.

**The first issue:** His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So she pointed to him. They said, "How can we speak to one who is in the cradle, a child?"﴾ Maryam, peace be upon her, kept to what she had been commanded, which was to abstain from speech. This verse does not report that she spoke the words, "Indeed, I have vowed to the Most Merciful a fast," but only that she pointed. This strengthens the view of those who said that her command to "say" (*qulī*) meant only a gesture. It is related that when she pointed to the child, they said: "Her treating us lightly is harder on us than her fornication." Then they said to her, by way of rebuke and reproach: "How can we speak to one who is in the cradle, a child?" Here *kāna* (was) is not meant in the past tense, because each of them had once been a child in the cradle. Rather, it has the sense of "is now" (*huwa al-āna*) [the addition is from the books of tafsir (exegesis)]. Abu 'Ubayda said: *kāna* here is superfluous (*laghw*), as in the line of the poet al-Farazdaq, whose first half is: "So how, when you see the abodes of a people / and our neighbours who were noble," [ ..... ].

It was also said that *kāna* means existence and occurrence, as in His saying: ﴿And if the debtor is in hardship﴾ (2:280), which has already been discussed. Ibn al-Anbari said: It is not permissible to call it superfluous, since it governs the accusative *ṣabiyyan* (a child), nor to say that *kāna* means "occurred" (*ḥadatha*), because if it meant occurrence and happening, it would be complete without a predicate. You say *kāna al-ḥarr* ("the heat occurred") and you suffice with it. The correct view is that *man* (whoever) has the sense of a conditional, and *kāna* means *yakun* (will be), so the sense is: "Whoever will be in the cradle, a child, how can we speak to him?" Just as you say: "How can I give to whoever was not accepting a gift," meaning whoever is not accepting. The past tense may be used with the meaning of the future in a conditional, as in His saying: ﴿Blessed is He who, if He wills, will give you better than that: gardens beneath which rivers flow﴾ (25:10), meaning: if He wills, He will give. And you say: "Whoever has done me a kindness, I will do the same to him," meaning: whoever will do a kindness to me, will receive the same from me.

Regarding *al-mahd* (the cradle): It was said that it was a bed like a cradle. It was also said that *al-mahd* here means the mother's lap. It was also said that the meaning is: "How can we speak to one whose custom is to be laid to sleep in the cradle because of his youth?" When 'Isa, peace be upon him, heard their speech, he said to them from his resting place: ﴿Indeed, I am the servant of Allah﴾ (19:30).

**The second issue:** It was said that 'Isa, peace be upon him, was nursing. When he heard their speech, he left off nursing and turned his face towards them, leaned on his left side, pointed at them with his right index finger, and said: ﴿Indeed, I am the servant of Allah﴾. So the first thing he uttered was the acknowledgment of his servitude to Allah and of His lordship, in refutation of those who exaggerated about him after him. As for "the Book," which is the Injil (Gospel): it was said that He gave him the Book in that state, gave him understanding and taught him, and gave him prophethood, just as He taught Adam all the names. He used to fast and pray. This view is extremely weak, as we will explain in the next issue. It was said that the meaning is: He decreed for me the giving of the Book and prophethood in eternity, even if the Book was not revealed at present. This is more correct.

﴿And made me blessed﴾: that is, one possessing blessings and benefits in religion and in calling to it, and a teacher of it. Al-Tustari [in manuscript K: al-Qushayri] said: "And made me one who enjoins good and forbids evil, guides the one who has gone astray, supports the oppressed, and relieves the one who is distressed."

﴿And enjoined upon me prayer and zakat﴾: that is, to perform them when I reach the age of obligation and am able to perform them, according to the last and correct view.

﴿As long as I am alive﴾: *mā* is in the accusative position as an adverbial of time, meaning: for the duration of my life.

﴿And dutiful to my mother﴾: Ibn 'Abbas said: When he said "dutiful to my mother" and did not say "to my parents," it was known that this was from Allah, exalted.

﴿And not made me arrogant﴾: that is, one who magnifies himself and is proud, who kills and strikes in anger. It was also said: *al-jabbār* is the one who does not recognize any right of anyone over him at all.

﴿Wretched﴾: that is, deprived of good. Ibn 'Abbas said: disobedient to his parents. It was also said: disobedient to his Lord. And it was said: "He did not make me one who abandons His command, so that I would be wretched as Iblis was wretched when he abandoned His command."

**The third issue:** Malik ibn Anas, may Allah have mercy on him, said about this verse: "How severe it is upon the people of *qadar* (those who deny divine predestination)! He informed 'Isa, peace be upon him, of what had been decreed concerning him, and of what would happen to him until he died." It is related in the narratives about this verse, from Ibn Zayd and others, that when they heard the speech of 'Isa, they submitted and said: "Indeed, this is a great matter." It is also related that 'Isa, peace be upon him, spoke in his infancy with this verse, then returned to the state of infants, until he walked in the manner of humans until he reached the stage of boys. So his speech was a manifestation of his mother's innocence, not that he was someone who understood in that state. This is like how Allah makes the limbs speak on the Day of Resurrection. It is not reported that his speech continued, nor that he prayed while he was a day or a month old. Had his speech, glorification, admonition and prayer continued from the time of his birth in his childhood, it would have been something that could not be concealed. All of this indicates the falsehood of the first view and clearly exposes the ignorance of its proponent. It also indicates that he spoke in the cradle, contrary to the Jews and Christians. The evidence for this is the consensus of the sects that she was not subjected to the legal penalty (*ḥadd*). Her innocence from fornication was established only by his speech in the cradle.

This verse also indicates that prayer, zakat and kindness to parents were obligatory upon earlier nations and ancient generations. Thus this is a ruling that remains established and was not abrogated (*naskh*) in the law of his community. 'Isa, peace be upon him, was in the utmost humility: he ate from trees, wore wool, sat on the dust, and took shelter wherever the night overtook him, having no dwelling. (ﷺ).

**The fourth issue:** A gesture has the same status as speech and conveys what speech conveys. How could it not, when Allah, exalted, has told us about Maryam: "So she pointed to him," and the people understood her intention and purpose and said: "How can we speak...?" This has been discussed in full in *Āl ʿImrān* [see vol. 4, pp. 81 and 68].

**The fifth issue:** The Kufans said: The slander (*qadhf*) of a mute person is not valid, nor is his *li'an* (mutual oath of condemnation). The same was related from al-Sha'bi, and al-Awza'i, Ahmad and Ishaq also said so. According to them, slander is valid only with explicit mention of fornication, not with its meaning, and this cannot come from a mute person by necessity. So he is not a slanderer, and a gesture cannot distinguish accusation of fornication from lawful intercourse or intercourse under a mistaken belief. They said: Our *li'an* consists of testimonies, and the testimony of a mute person is not accepted by consensus.

Ibn al-Qassar said: Their claim that slander is valid only with explicit words is false in all languages other than Arabic; likewise, the gesture of a mute person. Their claim of consensus regarding the testimony of a mute person is an error. Malik explicitly stated that his testimony is accepted if his gesture is understood, and that it takes the place of verbal testimony; but when he is able to speak, it is valid only with words.

Ibn al-Mundhir said: Those who disagree require the mute person to bear the consequences of divorce, sales, and all other rulings, so slander should be similar to these.

Al-Muhallab said: In many areas of jurisprudence a gesture may be stronger than speech, such as his peace and blessings be upon him saying: "I have been sent as the Hour is, like these two" (ﷺ), and we know the closeness between them by the amount by which the middle finger exceeds the index finger. The consensus of minds that direct observation is stronger than report is evidence that a gesture may in some situations be stronger than speech.

﴿And peace be upon me﴾: that is, security from Allah, exalted, upon me. Al-Zajjaj said: "Peace" was mentioned before this without the definite article *alif-lām*, so mentioning it with *alif-lām* in the second instance is good.

His saying: ﴿The day I was born﴾ means in this world. It was also said: that is, safety from the prodding of Satan, as was discussed earlier in *Āl ʿImrān*.

﴿The day I die﴾: that is, in the grave. ﴿And the day I am raised alive﴾: that is, in the Hereafter, because he has three states: in this world alive, in the grave dead, and in the Hereafter resurrected. So he was given peace in all his states, and this is the meaning of al-Kalbi's statement.

Then his speech in the cradle ceased until he reached the age of boys. Qatada said: It was mentioned to us that a woman saw 'Isa, peace be upon him, bringing the dead to life and healing the blind and the leper, among his other signs in his time, and she said: "Blessed is the womb that bore you and the breast that nursed you!" 'Isa, peace be upon him, said to her: "Blessed is the one who recites the Book of Allah, exalted, follows what is in it, and acts upon it."

**Tafsir al-Qurtubi, *al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Qur'an*, on Surah Maryam (19), verses 34–40**

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿That is Jesus, son of Mary﴾. That is, the one we have mentioned is Jesus son of Mary, so believe in him as such. Do not believe as the Jews say, that he was born outside lawful marriage and was the son of Yusuf the carpenter, nor as the Christians say, that he is God or the son of God.

(﴿A word of truth﴾) Al-Kisa'i said: "A word of truth" is a qualifier (na't) of Jesus. That is, "That is Jesus, son of Mary, [a word of truth]" [an addition required by the context]. He is called "a word of truth" just as he is called "the Word of Allah," and the Truth is Allah, Mighty and Majestic. Abu Hatim said: the meaning is "it is the word of truth." It was also said: the implied sense is "this statement is a word of truth." Ibn 'Abbas said: (he means this is the speech of Jesus, son of Mary [from manuscripts J and K] — ﷺ — "a word of truth, not falsehood"). The word is attributed to truth just as Allah says: ﴿the promise of truth which they were promised﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 16], meaning "the promise and the truth." And He says: ﴿and the Hereafter abode is better﴾ [al-An'am: 32], meaning "and the Hereafter abode." 'Asim and Ibn 'Amir read "qawla al-haqq" in the accusative (nasb) as a circumstantial accusative (hal), meaning "I say a true word." The governing element is the sense of pointing in (dhalika, "that"). Al-Zajjaj said: it is a verbal noun (masdar), meaning "I say the word of truth," because what precedes it indicates it. It was also said that it is praise, and that it is an incitement (idghra'). 'Abdullah read "qala al-haqq." Al-Hasan read "qulu al-haqq" with a dammah on the qaf, and likewise in al-An'am "qawla al-haqq." "Al-qawl," "al-qal" and "al-qul" have the same meaning, like "al-rahb," "al-rahab" and "al-ruhb."

(﴿of which﴾) is a qualifier of Jesus.

(﴿about which they dispute﴾) That is, they doubt. That is, that Jesus son of Mary, about whom they dispute, is the word of truth. It was also said that "yamtarun" means "they differ." 'Abd al-Razzaq reported, saying: Ma'mar informed us, on the authority of Qatada, regarding Allah's words ﴿That is Jesus son of Mary, a word of truth about which they dispute﴾: He said: The Children of Israel gathered and chose four men from among them, each group bringing out its scholar. They disputed about Jesus when he was raised. One of them said: "He is God; he descended to earth, gave life to whom he gave life, and caused to die whom he caused to die, then ascended to heaven." These are the Ya'qubiyya. The other three said: "You have lied." Then two of them said to the third: "Say what you say about him." He said: "He is the son of God." These are the Nusturiyya. The two said: "You have lied." Then one of the two said to the other: "Say what you say about him." He said: "He is the third of three: God is a god, he is a god, and his mother is a god." These are the Israeliyya, the kings of the Christians. The fourth said: "You have lied. Rather, he is the servant of God, His messenger, His spirit and His word." These are the Muslims. Each man then had followers, as he said, and they fought, and the Muslims were overcome. That is the meaning of Allah's words: ﴿and they kill those who enjoin justice among mankind﴾ [Al 'Imran: 21]. Qatada said: "They are those about whom Allah the Exalted said: ﴿so the factions differed among themselves﴾." They differed concerning him and became factions. This is the meaning of His words ﴿about which you dispute﴾, with a ta' with a dot above, which is the reading of Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami and others. Ibn 'Abbas said: Mary's cousin passed by with her and her son to Egypt, and they remained there for twelve years until the king they feared died. This was mentioned by al-Mawardi. I say: it is recorded in the history of Egypt, as far as I have seen, and it appears in the Gospel that when the Lord Messiah was born in Bethlehem, Herod was king at that time, and that Allah revealed to Yusuf the carpenter in a dream, saying to him: "Arise, take the child and his mother, go to Egypt and remain there until I tell you, for Herod is about to seek Jesus to destroy him." He rose from his sleep, obeyed the command of his Lord, took the Lord Messiah and Mary his mother, and came to Egypt. On his way to Egypt he stopped at the Balsam Well, which is on the outskirts of Cairo [in the Matariyya suburb], and washed his clothes at that well. Balsam grows and sprouts only in that land, and from it comes the oil mixed with the olive oil with which the Christians are baptized. For this reason, a single flask from the days of the Egyptians had great value, and it was highly prized in the hearts of Christian kings, such as the king of Constantinople, the king of Sicily, the king of Abyssinia, the king of Nubia, the king of the Franks and others, when the kings of Egypt sent it to them as a gift, and it was more beloved to them than any gift of value. On that journey the Lord Messiah reached the city of al-Ushmunayn [al-Ushmunayn: one of the villages of the Mallawi district] and Qaskam [Qaskam: now al-Qusiyya, one of the villages of the Manfalut district], known today as al-Muharraqa [al-Muharraqa: today known as the Burning Monastery in the Manfalut district]. For this reason the Christians still venerate it to this day, and they come to it from everywhere for the Feast of Easter, because it was the furthest point he reached in the land of Egypt, and from there he returned to al-Sham. And it is as He said: ﴿And who would turn away from the religion of Abraham except one who makes a fool of himself?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 130].

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿When he said to his father﴾. He is Āzar, and this has already been discussed (see vol. 7, p. 22).

(﴿O my father﴾): the discussion of this has already been given in "Yusuf" (see vol. 9, p. 121).

(﴿Why do you worship﴾), meaning: what is it that you worship? (﴿that which neither hears nor sees, and does not avail you anything﴾), meaning the idols.

(﴿O my father, indeed there has come to me of knowledge what has not come to you﴾), meaning: of certainty and knowledge of Allah, and of what happens after death, and that whoever worships other than Allah will be punished. (﴿So follow me; I will guide you to a straight path﴾), meaning: I will guide you to a upright religion in which there is salvation.

(﴿O my father, do not worship Satan﴾), meaning: do not obey him in what he commands you of disbelief. Whoever obeys anyone in disobedience to Allah has worshipped him.

(﴿Indeed, Satan has ever been disobedient to the Most Merciful﴾). Here "kāna" is a ṣila zā'ida (a redundant or extra particle, a term used in grammar for a word that adds no meaning). It was also said that kāna means ṣāra (became). It was said that it means the present state, i.e., he is (disobedient) to the Most Merciful. ʿAṣiyyan and ʿāṣin have the same meaning, as al-Kisa'i said.

(﴿O my father, indeed I fear that a punishment from the Most Merciful will touch you﴾), meaning: if you die in the state you are in. "Akhāfu" (I fear) may mean "a'lamu" (I know). It is also permissible for "akhāfu" to retain its own meaning, so the meaning would be: I fear that you will die in your disbelief and the punishment will touch you. (﴿and you will be a companion of Satan﴾), meaning: a partner in the Fire.

(He said: "Do you turn away from my gods, O Abraham?"), meaning: do you turn away from them to other than them?

(﴿If you do not desist, I will surely stone you﴾). Al-Hasan said: meaning with stones. al-Dahhak said: with words, meaning "I will surely revile you." Ibn ʿAbbas said: "I will surely strike you." It was also said: "I will surely expose your matter."

(﴿And leave me for a long time﴾). Ibn ʿAbbas said: meaning, keep away from me while your honour is safe, so that no harm from me touches you. al-Tabari chose this view, so according to it, "malīyyan" is a state (ḥāl) of Abraham. *So the solid mountains split apart at his death,*
*and the widowed women wept for him for a long time.*

It was said to Ibn ʿUyayna: Is it permissible to greet a disbeliever? He said: Yes. Abu Hurayrah narrated that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Do not begin the Jews and the Christians with salām. When you meet one of them on the road, force him to its narrowest part." It was recorded by al-Bukhari and Muslim. In the two Sahihs, on the authority of Usamah ibn Zayd, that the Prophet ﷺ rode a donkey with a pack-saddle beneath which was a Fadakī woollen cloth, and he had Usamah ibn Zayd riding behind him. He was visiting Saʿd ibn ʿUbadah in the Banu al-Harith ibn al-Khazraj, and that was before the Battle of Badr. Among them was ʿAbdullah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul, and in the gathering was ʿAbdullah ibn Rawahah. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Indeed, He has ever been gracious to me (ḥafiyyan)﴾. Al-ḥafiyy is one who exceeds in kindness and gentleness. It is said: "ḥafiya bihi" and "tahaffā" when he is kind to him. al-Kisa'i said: it is said "ḥafiya bī ḥifāwatan wa ḥifwatan." al-Farra' said: "innahu kāna bī ḥafiyyan" means a knowing, gentle one who answers me when I call upon him.

(﴿And We gave him, out of Our mercy, his brother Aaron as a prophet﴾) This was when he asked, saying: "And appoint for me a minister from my family, Aaron, my brother" [[See p. 191 and following of this part.]].

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 19, verses 54–55:**

There are six issues concerning this.

**The first issue:** God's words, ﴿And mention in the Book Ismail﴾. Scholars differed about him. It was said: he is Ismail son of Hizqil, whom God sent to his people, and they flayed the skin of his head. God gave him the choice regarding what punishment of theirs he wished, and he asked Him to pardon them and was content with His reward, and he entrusted their affair to Him, whether to forgive them or punish them. But the majority hold that he is Ismail the sacrificed one, father of the Arabs, son of Ibrahim. It has also been said that the one sacrificed was Ishaq (Isaac). The first view is more evident, as has preceded and as will come in "As-Saffat" [[See vol. 15, p. 98 onward.]], God willing. God singled him out for truthfulness in promise, although it exists in other prophets as well, as an honour and a mark of distinction for him, like being given titles such as *al-Halim* (the Forbearing), *al-Awwah* (the Compassionate), and *al-Siddiq* (the Truthful). It is also because it was the most famous and most consistently associated of his qualities [[Thus in ج، وا، وح، وك. In ى: "al-mutarahif", and the correct reading is "al-mutarasif", meaning "well-arranged/aligned".]].

**The second issue:** Truthfulness in promise is praiseworthy; it is a trait of the prophets and messengers. Its opposite, breaking promises (*al-khulf*), is blameworthy, and it is a trait of the depraved and the hypocrites, as its explanation has preceded in "Bara'ah" [[See vol. 8, p. 212 onward.]]. God praised His prophet Ismail and described him with truthfulness in promise. Concerning this there is a difference of opinion. It was said: he promised himself to endure the slaughter, and he endured until he was ransomed. This is according to the view of those who hold that he was the one sacrificed. It was also said: he promised a man to meet him at a certain place. Ismail came and waited for the man for his whole day and night. On the next day the man came and said to him, "I have been here waiting for you since yesterday." It was said he waited for him three days. Our Prophet ﷺ did the same before his mission; al-Naqqash mentioned it, and al-Tirmidhi and others transmitted it from Abdullah ibn Abi al-Hamsa', who said: "I made a transaction with the Prophet ﷺ before he was sent (as a prophet), and a remainder of it was still due to him. I promised him that I would bring it to him at his place, but I forgot. Then I remembered after three days, and I came, and he was in his place. He said: 'O young man, you have put me to hardship. I have been here for three days waiting for you.'" This is the wording of Abu Dawud. Yazid al-Raqashi said: Ismail waited for him twenty-two days; al-Mawardi mentioned it. In the book of Ibn Salam, it is that he waited for him a year. Al-Zamakhshari mentioned from Ibn Abbas that he promised a companion of his that he would wait for him at a place, and he waited a year. Al-Qushayri mentioned: "He did not leave his place for a year until Jibril (peace be upon him) came to him and said: 'The merchant who asked you to sit for him until he returns is Iblis, so do not sit, and there is no honour for him.'" This is far-fetched and not sound. It has also been said: Ismail never promised anything without fulfilling it. This is a sound view, and it is what the apparent meaning of the verse requires, and God knows best.

**The third issue:** From this category is his ﷺ saying, "The promise is a debt." In a report also: "The *wa'y* (promise) of the believer is obligatory" [[*al-wa'y*: the promise.]], meaning among the traits of believers. We have said that this is not obligatory as a religious duty (*fard*), by the consensus of the scholars, as Abu Umar (Ibn Abd al-Barr) related: whoever promises someone money, it is not incumbent upon him to pay it with the creditors. Therefore we say that fulfilling it is good by way of manliness (*al-muruwwah*), but it is not enforced by judgment. The Arabs praise fulfilment of promise and blame breaking promises and treachery, and so do all nations. The poet has indeed said well:

*Whenever a free man says to one with a need, "Yes, I will fulfil it,"*
*the free man is a guarantor for his promise.*

There is no disagreement that the one who fulfils a promise deserves praise and thanks, and the one who breaks it deserves blame. God, blessed and exalted, has praised the one who is truthful in his promise and fulfils his vow, and this suffices as praise and commendation, and what opposes it as blame.

**The fourth issue:** Malik said: If a man asks another to grant him a gift, and he says "Yes," then it appears to him not to do it, I do not see it as binding on him. Malik said: And if it concerned paying a debt, so that he asked him to pay it on his behalf, and he said "Yes," and there were men present who witnessed it, then it is more fitting that he be bound by it if two witnessed against him. Abu Hanifa and his companions, al-Awza'i, al-Shafi'i, and all the jurists said: A promise does not create any obligation, because it concerns benefits that have not been received in the case of a loan (*al-ariyah*), since it is incidental; and in other than a loan, they are persons and specific objects that have been given as gifts but have not been taken possession of, so the giver has the right to retract them. In al-Bukhari: "And mention in the Book Ismail; indeed he was truthful in promise" [[Qur'an 19:54.]]. Ibn Ashwa' judged by the promise, and this is related from Samura ibn Jundub. Al-Bukhari said [[He said this in *al-Tarikh al-Awsat*, as in *Tahdhib al-Tahdhib*.]]: "I saw Ishaq ibn Ibrahim citing the hadith of Ibn Ashwa' as evidence."

**The fifth issue:** ﴿And he was a messenger, a prophet﴾ [[Qur'an 19:54.]]. It was said: Ismail was sent to Jurhum. All the prophets, when they promised, were truthful, and Ismail was singled out for mention as an honour to him. And God knows best.

**The sixth issue:** ﴿And he used to enjoin his family﴾ [[Qur'an 19:55.]]. Al-Hasan said: "That is, his nation." In the reading of Ibn Mas'ud: "And he used to enjoin his family, Jurhum, and his offspring, to pray and to give zakah."

﴿And he was with his Lord well-pleasing﴾ [[Qur'an 19:55.]], meaning: *radiyyan* (pleased), pure, righteous. Al-Kisa'i and al-Farra' said: Whoever says *mardiyy* (well-pleasing) derives it from *radiytu* (I was pleased). They said: The people of the Hijaz say *marduww*. Al-Kisa'i and al-Farra' also said: Among the Arabs are those who say *ridwan* and *ridyan* in the dual of *ridan* (satisfaction); so *ridwan* is on the pattern of *marduww*, and *ridyan* on the pattern of *mardiyy*. The Basrans do not permit anything but *ridwan* and *ribawan*. Abu Ja'far al-Nahhas said: I heard Abu Ishaq al-Zajjaj say: "They err in the writing, writing *riba* with a *ya*, and then they err in what is even worse than this, saying *ribayan*, whereas only *ribawan* and *ridwan* are permissible." God, the Exalted, said: ﴿And whatever you give in riba (usury) to increase within the wealth of people﴾ [[See vol. 13, p. 36.]] [[Qur'an 30:39.]].

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 19, verses 56–57:

His words, may He be exalted: ﴿And mention in the Book Idris. Indeed, he was a man of truth and a prophet.﴾ Idris, peace be upon him, was the first to write with the pen, the first to sew garments and to wear sewn clothing, and the first to study the science of the stars, their computation and their courses. Idris was named Idris because of his frequent study (dars) of the Book of God, the Exalted. God the Exalted revealed to him thirty scrolls (suhuf), as is related in the hadith (prophetic report) of Abu Dharr.

Al-Zamakhshari said: It has also been said that Idris was named Idris because of his frequent study of the Book of God, the Exalted, and that his name was Akhnukh. This is not correct, because if it were an ifʿīl form derived from dars (study), it would have only one cause preventing it from taking tanwin, namely being a proper noun, and it would be declinable (munsarif). Its failure to take tanwin is therefore evidence of its being foreign (ʿujma, non-Arabic). Likewise, Iblis is foreign and is not from iblas (despair), as they claim, nor is Yaʿqub from ʿaqab (heel), nor is Israʾil from Isral, as Ibn al-Sikkit claimed. Whoever does not verify and is not trained in the discipline (ṣinaʿa) will commit many errors of this kind. It is possible that the meaning of Idris, peace be upon him, in that language was close to this, so the narrator assumed it was derived from dars.

Al-Tha'labi, al-Ghaznawi and others said: He was the grandfather of Nuh (Noah). This is an error. Its explanation has already been given in "al-Aʿraf" [[See vol. 7, p. 232 onward.]]. Likewise, it occurs in the biography (sirah) that Nuh, peace be upon him, was the son of Lamak, son of Mattushalakh, son of Akhnukh, who is Idris the prophet, according to what they claim. And God knows best.

He was the first of the sons of Adam to be given prophethood [[This should be considered alongside the established prophethood of Adam and Shith.]], and he wrote with the pen. He was the son of Yard, son of Mahalaʾil, son of Qaynan, son of Yanash, son of Shith, son of Adam (ﷺ). [So God knows best [[From ja, wa, and ya.]]].

His words, may He be exalted: ﴿And We raised him to a lofty place.﴾ Anas ibn Malik, Abu Saʿid al-Khudri and others said: It means the fourth heaven. This was related from the Prophet (ﷺ), and Kaʿb al-Ahbar also said it. Ibn ʿAbbas and al-Dahhak said: It means the sixth heaven, as mentioned by al-Mahdawi.

I say: In al-Bukhari, from a noble hadith [[In ja: from a noble hadith.]], on the authority of Shurayk ibn ʿAbd Allah ibn Abi Namir, who said: I heard Anas ibn Malik say: On the night when the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was taken on the night journey from the Masjid al-Haram, the hadith continues, and in it: Every heaven contained prophets, whom he named, and among them Idris was in the second. This is an error. The correct version is that he was in the fourth heaven, as Thabit al-Bunani related it from Anas ibn Malik, from the Prophet (ﷺ), and Muslim recorded it in his Sahih. Malik ibn Saʿsaʿa also related that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "When I was taken up to the heaven, I came upon Idris in the fourth heaven." Muslim also transmitted this.

The cause of his being raised, according to what Ibn ʿAbbas, Kaʿb and others said, was that he once walked on an errand and was struck by the heat of the sun. He said: "O Lord, I walked one day, so how will one who carries it for five hundred years in a single day fare? O God, lighten its weight from him," meaning the angel appointed over the sun's sphere. Idris said: "O God, lighten its weight from him and bear its heat for him." When the angel awoke, he found a lightness from the sun and shade that he did not recognize, and said: "O Lord, You created me to carry the sun. What have You decreed concerning this?" God the Exalted said: "Indeed, My servant Idris asked Me to lighten its burden and heat for you, and I granted his request." The angel said: "O Lord, bring me together with him, and make between me and him a close friendship." God permitted him, and he came to Idris, and Idris used to ask him. He said: "I have been told that you are the most honored of the angels and the most esteemed with the Angel of Death. So intercede for me with him, that he may delay my term, so that I may increase in gratitude and worship." The angel said: "God does not delay a soul when its term has come." Idris said to the angel: "I know that, but it is more comforting to my soul." He said: "Yes." Then the sun's angel carried him on his wing, lifted him to the heaven, and placed him at the rising place of the sun. Then he said to the Angel of Death: "I have a friend among the sons of Adam who has asked me to intercede with you that you delay his term." He said: "That is not up to me, but if you wish to know it, I will inform him when he will die." He said: "Yes." Then he looked into his register and said: "You are asking me about a man whom I do not see dying ever." He said: "How?" He said: "I do not find him dying except at the rising place of the sun." He said: "I came to you and left him there." He said: "Go, for I do not think you will find him except that he has died." By God, there remained of Idris's term nothing. The angel returned and found him dead.

Al-Suddi said: He slept one day, and the heat of the sun intensified upon him, so he got up while distressed by it and said: "O God, lighten the heat of the sun for the sun's angel, and help him with its weight, for he handles a scorching fire." The sun's angel awoke to find a chair of light set up for him, with seventy thousand angels on his right and the same number on his left, serving him and managing his affairs and work under his command. The sun's angel said: "O Lord, from where is this for me?" He said: "A man from the sons of Adam called Idris prayed for you," and then he related something similar to the account of Kaʿb. He said: The sun's angel said to him: "Do you want a need fulfilled?" He said: "Yes, I wish I could see Paradise."

He said: So he lifted him on his wing and flew with him. While he was in the fourth heaven, he met the Angel of Death, who was looking into the heaven, looking right and left. The sun's angel greeted him and said: "O Idris, this is the Angel of Death, so greet him." The Angel of Death said: "Glory be to God! For what purpose did you raise him here?" He said: "I raised him so that he might see Paradise." He said: "God the Exalted has commanded me to take the soul of Idris in the fourth heaven. I said: O Lord, where is Idris in relation to the fourth heaven? So I descended, and behold, he was with You." Then he took his soul, lifted it to Paradise, and the angels buried his body in the fourth heaven. That is His words: ﴿And We raised him to a lofty place.﴾

Wahb ibn Munabbih said: Each day, the worship of Idris was raised up equal to what was raised for the people of the earth in his time. The angels marveled at him, and the Angel of Death longed for him. He asked his Lord for permission to visit him, and He permitted him. He came to him in the form of a human being. Idris, peace be upon him, used to fast by day, so when it was time for his breaking of the fast, he invited him to his food, but he refused to eat. He did this for three nights, and Idris disapproved of him and said: "Who are you?" He said: "I am the Angel of Death. I asked my Lord for permission to accompany you, and He granted it to me." He said: "I have a need of you." He said: "What is it?" He said: "That you take my soul." So God the Exalted revealed to him that he should take his soul; he took it, and God returned it to him after an hour. The Angel of Death said to him: "What is the benefit of taking your soul?" He said: "So that I may taste the agonies of death, and so I may be better prepared for it." Then, after an hour, Idris said to him: "I have another need of you." He said: "What is it?" He said: "That you lift me up to the heaven so that I may look upon Paradise and the Fire." God the Exalted permitted him to be lifted up through the heavens. He saw the Fire and swooned. When he recovered, he said: "Show me Paradise," and he brought him into Paradise. Then the Angel of Death said to him: "Come out, so that you may return to your abode." He clung to a tree and said: "I will not come out of it." So God the Exalted sent between them an angel as arbiter. He said: "Why will you not come out?" He said: "Because God the Exalted said: ﴿Every soul shall taste death﴾ [Al ʿImran: 185], and I have tasted it. He said: ﴿And there is none of you but will pass over it﴾ [Maryam: 71], and I have passed over it. He said: ﴿And they will not be removed from it﴾ [al-Hijr: 48], so how shall I come out?" God the Exalted, Blessed and Exalted, said to the Angel of Death: "By My permission he entered Paradise, and by My command he will come out." So he is alive there, and that is His words: ﴿And We raised him to a lofty place.﴾

Al-Nahhas said: Idris's saying, "And they will not be removed from it," may be something God informed Idris of, and then the Qur'an was revealed with it. Wahb ibn Munabbih said: Idris sometimes frolics in Paradise, and at other times worships God the Exalted with the angels in the heaven.

Idris said: "O God, lighten its weight from him and bear its heat for him." When the angel awoke, he found a lightness from the sun and shade that he did not recognize, and said: "O Lord, You created me to carry the sun. What have You decreed concerning this?" God the Exalted said: "Indeed, My servant Idris asked Me to lighten its burden and heat for you, and I granted his request." The angel said: "O Lord, bring me together with him, and make between me and him a close friendship." God permitted him, and he came to Idris, and Idris used to ask him. He said: "I have been told that you are the most honored of the angels and the most esteemed with the Angel of Death. So intercede for me with him, that he may delay my term, so that I may increase in gratitude and worship." The angel said: "God does not delay a soul when its term has come." Idris said to the angel: "I know that, but it is more comforting to my soul." He said: "Yes." Then the sun's angel carried him on his wing, lifted him to the heaven, and placed him at the rising place of the sun. Then he said to the Angel of Death: "I have a friend among the sons of Adam who has asked me to intercede with you that you delay his term." He said: "That is not up to me, but if you wish to know it, I will inform him when he will die." He said: "Yes." Then he looked into his register and said: "You are asking me about a man whom I do not see dying ever." He said: "How?" He said: "I do not find him dying except at the rising place of the sun." He said: "I came to you and left him there." He said: "Go, for I do not think you will find him except that he has died." By God, there remained of Idris's term nothing. The angel returned and found him dead.

Al-Suddi said: He slept one day, and the heat of the sun intensified upon him, so he got up while distressed by it and said: "O God, lighten the heat of the sun for the sun's angel, and help him with its weight, for he handles a scorching fire." The sun's angel awoke to find a chair of light set up for him, with seventy thousand angels on his right and the same number on his left, serving him and managing his affairs and work under his command. The sun's angel said: "O Lord, from where is this for me?" He said: "A man from the sons of Adam called Idris prayed for you," and then he related something similar to the account of Kaʿb. He said: The sun's angel said to him: "Do you want a need fulfilled?" He said: "Yes, I wish I could see Paradise."

He said: So he lifted him on his wing and flew with him. While he was in the fourth heaven, he met the Angel of Death, who was looking into the heaven, looking right and left. The sun's angel greeted him and said: "O Idris, this is the Angel of Death, so greet him." The Angel of Death said: "Glory be to God! For what purpose did you raise him here?" He said: "I raised him so that he might see Paradise." He said: "God the Exalted has commanded me to take the soul of Idris in the fourth heaven. I said: O Lord, where is Idris in relation to the fourth heaven? So I descended, and behold, he was with You." Then he took his soul, lifted it to Paradise, and the angels buried his body in the fourth heaven. That is His words: ﴿And We raised him to a lofty place.﴾

Wahb ibn Munabbih said: Each day, the worship of Idris was raised up equal to what was raised for the people of the earth in his time. The angels marveled at him, and the Angel of Death longed for him. He asked his Lord for permission to visit him, and He permitted him. He came to him in the form of a human being. Idris, peace be upon him, used to fast by day, so when it was time for his breaking of the fast, he invited him to his food, but he refused to eat. He did this for three nights, and Idris disapproved of him and said: "Who are you?" He said: "I am the Angel of Death. I asked my Lord for permission to accompany you, and He granted it to me." He said: "I have a need of you." He said: "What is it?" He said: "That you take my soul." So God the Exalted revealed to him that he should take his soul; he took it, and God returned it to him after an hour. The Angel of Death said to him: "What is the benefit of taking your soul?" He said: "So that I may taste the agonies of death, and so I may be better prepared for it." Then, after an hour, Idris said to him: "I have another need of you." He said: "What is it?" He said: "That you lift me up to the heaven so that I may look upon Paradise and the Fire." God the Exalted permitted him to be lifted up through the heavens. He saw the Fire and swooned. When he recovered, he said: "Show me Paradise," and he brought him into Paradise. Then the Angel of Death said to him: "Come out, so that you may return to your abode." He clung to a tree and said: "I will not come out of it." So God the Exalted sent between them an angel as arbiter. He said: "Why will you not come out?" He said: "Because God the Exalted said: ﴿Every soul shall taste death﴾ [Al ʿImran: 185], and I have tasted it. He said: ﴿And there is none of you but will pass over it﴾ [Maryam: 71], and I have passed over it. He said: ﴿And they will not be removed from it﴾ [al-Hijr: 48], so how shall I come out?" God the Exalted, Blessed and Exalted, said to the Angel of Death: "By My permission he entered Paradise, and by My command he will come out." So he is alive there, and that is His words: ﴿And We raised him to a lofty place.﴾

Al-Nahhas said: Idris's saying, "And they will not be removed from it," may be something God informed Idris of, and then the Qur'an was revealed with it. Wahb ibn Munabbih said: Idris sometimes frolics in Paradise, and at other times worships God the Exalted with the angels in the heaven.

**Question 1:** Concerning this verse there are four issues.

The first is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Those are they upon whom Allah bestowed favor among the prophets, of the descendants of Adam﴾. He means Idris alone.

(And of those We carried with Noah) means Ibrahim alone. (And of the descendants of Ibrahim) means Isma'il, Ishaq and Ya'qub.

(And of) the descendants of (Isra'il) means Musa, Harun, Zakariyya, Yahya and Isa. Idris and Nuh thus had the honor of being close to Adam, Ibrahim had the honor of being close to Nuh, and Isma'il, Ishaq and Ya'qub had the honor of being close to Ibrahim.

(And of those whom We guided) means to Islam, (and chose) by faith.

(When the verses of the Most Merciful are recited to them.) Shibl ibn 'Abbad al-Makki read *yutlā* with the masculine form, because the feminine here is not real (*ta'nīth ghayr ḥaqīqī*) and there is an intervening separator.

(They fell down prostrating and weeping.) He described them with humility before Allah and with weeping. This has already been discussed in *Sūrat Subḥān* [[See vol. 10, p. 341 onward.]] [al-Isra': 1]. It is said *bakā yabkī bukā'an* and *bukan* and *bukiyyan*. However, al-Khalil said: when you shorten *al-bukā'* it is like *al-ḥuzn* (grief), meaning there is no accompanying sound, as the poet said: [[This is ʿAbdullāh ibn Rawāḥa weeping for Ḥamza ibn ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib, may Allah have mercy on him. Abū Zayd recited it, attributing to Kaʿb ibn Mālik in several verses.]]

*My eye wept, and its weeping is rightly due,*
*but weeping and wailing avail nothing.*

*Sujjadan* is in the accusative as a circumstantial accusative (*ḥāl*), and *wa-bukiyyan* is coordinated with it (*'aṭf*).

The second issue: this verse indicates that the verses of the Most Merciful have an effect on the hearts. Al-Hasan said: (When the verses of the Most Merciful are recited to them, they fell down prostrating and weeping) refers to the prayer. Al-Asamm said: what is meant by the verses of the Most Merciful is the books containing His Oneness and His proofs, and that they used to prostrate when reciting them and weep when mentioning them. What is related from Ibn 'Abbas is that what is meant is the Qur'an specifically, and that they used to prostrate and weep when reciting it. Al-Kiya said: from His saying in this [verse [[from k.]]] there is an indication that the Qur'an is what was recited to all the prophets. Were that so, the Messenger, may the prayers and peace of Allah be upon him, would not have been specially chosen for its revelation.

The third issue: Abu Bakr al-Razi (al-Jassas) used this verse as evidence for the obligation of the prostration of recitation upon the listener and the reciter. Al-Kiya said: this is far-fetched, for this description encompasses all the signs of Allah, exalted is He. He combined prostration with weeping, and by this he made clear the way of the prophets, peace be upon them, in glorifying Allah and His signs. There is no indication in it of an obligation to do this at a specific verse.

The fourth issue: the scholars said: whoever recites a prostration verse should supplicate in it with what suits its verses. If he recites the prostration of *Sūrat al-Sajda* ("Alif-Lam-Mim, the revelation"), he says: "O Allah, make me among those who prostrate to Your Face, who glorify You with Your praise, and I seek refuge in You from being among those who are arrogant toward Your command." If he recites the prostration of *Sūrat Subḥān* [[10]], he says: "O Allah, make me among those who weep to You, who are humble before You." If he recites this (verse), he says: "O Allah, make me among Your servants upon whom You have bestowed favor, those who are guided, who prostrate to You, who weep at the recitation of Your verses."

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 19, verses 59–63 (part 1 of 2):

There are four issues here.

The first concerns His saying, ﴿Then there succeeded them a later generation﴾. That is, bad offspring. Abu 'Ubayda said: Hajjaj narrated to us from Ibn Juraij, from Mujahid, who said: "That is at the coming of the Hour, and the passing away of the righteous of this nation, the nation of Muhammad (ﷺ). They will leap upon one another in the alleys like fornication (zina)." The discussion of "khalf" (succession) at "al-A'raf" has already passed [[See vol. 7, p. 310 onward.]], so there is no point in repeating it.

The second issue concerns His saying, ﴿they neglected the prayer﴾. 'Abd Allah (Ibn Mas'ud) and al-Hasan read "adaa' al-salawat" (they neglected the prayers) in the plural. This is a condemnation and a clear text that neglecting the prayer is among the major sins (al-kaba'ir) by which its neglecter is destroyed, and there is no disagreement on this. 'Umar said: "Whoever neglects it, for other than it he is more neglectful."

The scholars differed about who is meant by this verse. Mujahid said: "The Christians, who came after the Jews." Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi, Mujahid also, and 'Ata' said: "They are a people from the nation of Muhammad (ﷺ) at the end of time." That is, there will be in this nation people with this description, not that they are the ones intended by this verse.

They also differed about the meaning of neglecting it. al-Qurazi said: "It is neglect through disbelief and denial of it." al-Qasim ibn Mukhaymira and 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud said: "It is neglecting its times and not fulfilling its rights," and this is the correct view. And if it is prayed without its proper conditions, it is not valid and does not suffice, because of the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying to the man who prayed and came and greeted him: "Go back and pray, for you have not prayed," three times. (Related by Muslim.)

Hudhayfa said to a man who was praying and performing it carelessly (fa-taffafa) [[That is, he reduced it, and tatfif can mean both increase and reduction.]]: "How long have you been praying this prayer?" He said: "For forty years." He said: "You have not prayed. And if you died while praying this prayer, you would die upon other than the fitrah (natural disposition) of Muhammad (ﷺ)." Then he said: "A man may make the prayer light, and complete it and do it well." (Related by al-Bukhari, and the wording is that of al-Nasa'i.)

In al-Tirmidhi, from Abu Mas'ud al-Ansari, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "A prayer is not valid in which a man does not straighten his spine (sulb)," meaning in bowing and prostration. He said: "It is a hasan sahih hadith, and the practice among the people of knowledge from the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ) and those after them is that a man should straighten his spine in bowing and prostration." al-Shafi'i, Ahmad and Ishaq said: "Whoever does not straighten his spine in bowing and prostration, his prayer is invalid." The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "That is the prayer of the hypocrite: he sits watching the sun until, when it is between the two horns of the Shaytan, he stands and pecks it four times, not remembering Allah in it except a little." This is a condemnation of whoever does that.

Farwa ibn Khalid ibn Sinan said: The companions of al-Dahhak once delayed an emir in the 'Asr prayer until the sun almost set. Al-Dahhak recited this verse, then said: "By Allah, to leave it would be dearer to me than to neglect it."

The summary of this chapter: whoever does not preserve the perfection of its ablution, its bowing and its prostration, is not preserving it. Whoever does not preserve it has neglected it. Whoever neglects it, for other than it he is more neglectful. Just as whoever preserves it, Allah preserves his religion for him, and there is no religion for one who has no prayer.

al-Hasan said: "They left the mosques idle and occupied themselves with crafts and means of livelihood." ﴿and followed their desires﴾: that is, pleasures and sins.

The third issue: al-Tirmidhi and Abu Dawud narrated from Anas ibn Hakim al-Dabbi that he came to Madina and met Abu Hurayra, who said to him: "O young man, shall I not narrate to you a hadith that Allah may benefit you by?" I said: "Yes." He said: The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The first thing people will be reckoned by on the Day of Resurrection of their deeds is the prayer. Allah, blessed and exalted, will say to His angels, and He knows best: 'Look at the prayer of My servant: did he complete it or diminish it?' If it was complete, it will be recorded complete for him. If he fell short in some of it, He will say: 'Look, does My servant have any voluntary (tatawwu') prayer?' If he has voluntary prayer, He will say: 'Complete for My servant his obligatory prayer from his voluntary prayer.' Then the deeds will be taken according to that."

Yunus said: "And I think it is from the Prophet (ﷺ)," and this is the wording of Abu Dawud. He said: Musa ibn Isma'il narrated to us, Hammad narrated to us, Dawud ibn Abi Hind narrated to us, from Zurara ibn Awfa, from Tamim al-Dari, from the Prophet (ﷺ), with this meaning. He said: "Then zakat is similar to that," and "then the deeds will be taken according to that proportion."

al-Nasa'i also narrated it from Hammam, from al-Hasan, from Hurayth ibn Qabisa, from Abu Hurayra, who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "The first thing a servant will be reckoned by on the Day of Resurrection is his prayer. If it is sound, he has succeeded and prospered. If it is corrupt, he has failed and lost." Hammam said: "I do not know whether this is from the words of Qatada or from the narration." "If he falls short in his obligatory prayer, He will say: 'Look, does My servant have voluntary prayer, by which what he lacked of the obligatory prayer may be completed?' Then all the rest of his deeds will be on that pattern."

Abu al-'Awwam opposed him: he narrated it from Qatada, from al-Hasan, from Abu Rafi', from Abu Hurayra, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The first thing a servant will be reckoned by on the Day of Resurrection is his prayer. If it is found complete, it is recorded complete. If he fell short in some of it, He will say: 'Look, do you find for him any voluntary prayer by which he may complete what he neglected of his obligatory prayer?' Then the rest of the deeds run according to that."

al-Nasa'i said: Ishaq ibn Ibrahim informed us, he said: al-Nadr ibn Shumayl narrated to us, he said: Hammad ibn Salama informed us, from al-Azraq ibn Qays, from Yahya ibn Ya'mar, from Abu Hurayra, from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), who said: "The first thing a servant will be reckoned by on the Day of Resurrection is his prayer. If he completed it, well; otherwise Allah, mighty and majestic, says: 'Look for My servant any voluntary prayer.' If he has voluntary prayer, He says: 'Complete the obligatory prayer with it.'"

Abu 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-Barr said in his book "al-Tamhid": "As for completing the obligatory prayer from the voluntary, it happens, and Allah knows best, only with one who forgot an obligatory prayer and did not perform it, or did not do well its bowing and prostration and did not know the measure of that. As for one who abandoned it, or forgot and then remembered and did not perform it, deliberately, and busied himself with voluntary prayer instead of performing its obligation while he remembered it, then an obligatory prayer is not completed for him from his voluntary prayer. And Allah knows best."

A hadith has been narrated from the Syrians on this subject, a munkar hadith, narrated by Muhammad ibn Himyar from 'Amr ibn Qays al-Sakuni, from 'Abd Allah ibn Qurt, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Whoever prays a prayer in which he does not complete his bowing and prostration, it will be increased for him with glorifications until it is complete." Abu 'Umar said: "This is not known from the Prophet (ﷺ) except by this route, and it is not strong. And even if it is sound, its meaning is that he came out of a prayer which he had completed in his own estimation, and it was not complete in ruling." [And Allah knows best.] [[From B, J, T, Z, K.]]

I say: a person should perform well his obligatory and voluntary prayers, so that he has a voluntary prayer that he finds beyond his obligatory prayer, which brings him near to his Lord, as He, glorified and exalted, said: "My servant continues to draw near to Me by voluntary works until I love him," and the hadith continues. As for when the voluntary prayer is what completes the obligatory, its ruling in meaning is the ruling of the obligatory. And whoever does not perform the obligatory prayer well, it is more fitting and more appropriate that he does not perform the voluntary prayer well. Indeed, people's voluntary prayers are in the worst state of deficiency and defect, because of its lightness in their eyes and their negligence of it, to the point that it is as if it were not counted.

By the life of Allah, there is seen in existence one who is pointed out and is thought to have knowledge, whose voluntary prayer is like that. Rather his obligatory prayer, as he pecks at it like a rooster's pecking, because of his lack of knowledge of the hadith. How then with the ignorant who do not know?

The scholars said: No bowing, no prostration, no standing after bowing, and no sitting between the two prostrations is valid until one is upright while bowing, standing, prostrating and sitting. This is the sound view in the reports, and the majority of scholars and the people of reasoning hold it. This is the narration of Ibn Wahb and Abu Mus'ab from Malik. This meaning has already passed in "al-Baqara" [[See vol. 1, p. 190 onward.]]. If this is so, how can what was lacking from this obligatory prayer be completed by that voluntary prayer, when it was lacking through ignorance and forgetfulness?! Rather all of that is not correct and not accepted, because it fell on other than what was required. And Allah knows best.

[The fourth issue] [[From B, J, Z, T, K.]]: His saying, ﴿and followed their desires﴾. 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, said regarding His saying, "and followed their desires," that it is the one who builds the "mushayyad" (lofty) and rides the "manzur" (the noble one), and not the "mashhur" (the famous). [[In the text: "from bana al-shadid" (the strong). The printed "al-mushayyad" is in the reading of Ruh al-Ma'ani, which is correct; the other sources read "man bana al-shadid." In Ya: "wa rakiba al-maqtur" (the cut-off one), which is likelier.]]

I say: "shahawat" (desires) is an expression for what agrees with a person, what he craves, what suits him, and what he does not guard against. In the Sahih: "Paradise is surrounded by hardships, and the Fire is surrounded by desires." What was reported from 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, is a part of this.

His saying, ﴿Then they will meet error (ghayy)﴾. Ibn Zayd said: "Evil, or misguidance, or failure." He said [[The line is by al-Muraqqish, as in Lisan al-'Arab.]]:

"Whoever meets good, people will praise his affair,
and whoever goes astray will not lack a blamer for his error."

Ibn Mas'ud said: "It is a valley in Hell." The grammatical reading among the people of the language is: "they will meet this ghayy," as His exalted mention said: ﴿And whoever does that will meet a penalty﴾ [al-Furqan: 68]. [[See vol. 13, p. 76.]] The more apparent view is that ghayy is a name for the valley, named so because those who go astray arrive at it. Ka'b said: "There will appear at the end of time a people with whips in their hands like the tails of cows," and then he recited the verse: "So they will meet ghayy," that is, destruction and misguidance in Hell.

Also from him: "Ghayy is a valley in Hell, the deepest of it in depth and the most intense in heat. In it is a well called al-Bahim. Whenever Hell subsides, Allah opens that well and Hell is kindled by it."

Ibn 'Abbas said: "Ghayy is a valley in Hell, and the valleys of Hell seek refuge from its heat. Allah has prepared that valley for the fornicator who persists in fornication, for the drinker of wine who is addicted to it, for the consumer of usury who does not desist from it, for the disobedient to parents, for the false witness, and for a woman who brought into her husband's family a child that is not his."

His saying, ﴿except one who repents﴾ [60]: that is, from neglecting the prayer and following desires, so he returns to obedience to his Lord.

(﴿and believes﴾ [[Reading: "in Him."]] ﴿and does righteous work, those will enter Paradise﴾ [60].) Abu Ja'far, Shayba, Ibn Kathir, Ibn Muhaysin, Abu 'Amr, Ya'qub and Abu Bakr read "yudkhalun" (they are made to enter) with a fatha on the kha'. The rest read the ya' with a fatha (yadkhulun).

﴿and they will not be wronged in the least﴾ [60]: that is, nothing will be diminished from their righteous deeds, except that for each good deed ten up to seven hundred will be recorded for them.

﴿Gardens of Eden﴾ is in apposition to "Paradise," so it is in the accusative. Abu Ishaq al-Zajjaj said: "It is also permissible that 'Gardens of Eden' be in the nominative as a new beginning." Abu Hatim said: "Were it not for the script, it would be 'Jannati 'Adn' (genitive), because before it is 'they enter Paradise.'"

(الَّتِي وَعَدَ الرَّحْمنُ عِبادَهُ بِالْغَيْبِ) That is, [the Garden] which the Most Merciful promised to His servants unseen. It is said: the meaning is that they believed in Paradise without having seen it, and they kept His covenant in the unseen.

﴿إِنَّهُ كَانَ وَعْدُهُ مَأْتِيًّا﴾ "Ma'tiyyan" (coming, reached) is a passive participle from "al-ityan" (coming to, arriving). Whatever reaches you, you have reached it. You say: "Sixty years have come upon me" (ataat 'alayya sittuna sanah), and "I have come upon sixty years" (ataytu 'ala sittina sanah). And good reached me from so-and-so, and I reached good from him. Al-Qutabi said: "ma'tiyyan" means "ati" (coming), so it is a passive form with the meaning of an active one. "Ma'tiyyan" has a hamza, because it derives from "ata ya'ti." Whoever softens the hamza makes it an alif. Al-Tabari said: "al-wa'd" here means the promised thing, which is Paradise; that is, His friends will come to it.

(لَا يَسْمَعُونَ فِيها لَغْواً) That is, in Paradise. Al-laghw (idle talk, vain speech) means falsehood in speech, and foul speech from it, and superfluity, and whatever is of no benefit. From it comes the hadith: "If you say to your companion on Friday, 'Be silent,' while the imam is delivering the sermon, you have done idle talk (laghawta)." It is also narrated as "laghaita," which is the dialect of Abu Hurayrah, as the poet said:

"And the Lord of herds of pilgrims, restrained
from idle talk and obscene speech."

[Footnote: This is by Ru'bah; Ibn Bari attributed it to al-'Ajjaj. (Lisan al-'Arab).]

Ibn 'Abbas said: al-laghw is everything in which there is no mention of Allah the Exalted. That is, their speech in Paradise is praise of Allah and His glorification.

(إِلَّا سَلاماً) That is, but they hear "salam" (peace). This is an exception of the type called al-istithna' al-munqati' (discontinuous exception, where what is excepted is not of the same kind as what precedes it). It means the greeting of some of them to others, and the greeting of the King to them. This was said by Muqatil and others. Al-salam is a comprehensive name for all good. The meaning is that they hear in it only what they love.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿وَلَهُمْ رِزْقُهُمْ فِيها بُكْرَةً وَعَشِيًّا﴾ "And for them is their provision in it, morning and evening." That is, for them is whatever they desire of food and drink, morning and evening; that is, in the measure of those two times, since there is no morning or evening there, as in His saying, the Exalted: "Its morning journey is a month and its evening journey is a month" (i.e., the measure of a month). This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Jurayj and others. It is also said: it informs them of the moderate condition of the people of Paradise. Among the Arabs, the most pleasant blessing was being provided with food and drink morning and evening. Yahya ibn Abi Kathir and Qatadah said: In their time among the Arabs, whoever found both lunch and dinner was considered prosperous, so this verse was revealed. It is also said: their provision in it is not cut off, as He said: "neither cut off nor forbidden" (see vol. 17, p. 210). It is like when you say: "I begin the morning and end the evening in Your remembrance," meaning my remembrance of You is constant. It is also possible that the morning refers to the time before they occupy themselves with their pleasures, and the evening to the time after they finish their pleasures, because between them there are intervals of transition from one state to another. This returns to the first view.

Al-Zubayr ibn Bakkar narrated from Isma'il ibn Abi Uways, who said: Malik ibn Anas said: "The food of the believers is twice a day," and he recited the saying of Allah, Mighty and Majestic: "And for them is their provision in it, morning and evening." Then he said: Allah, Mighty and Majestic, compensated the believers in fasting with the suhur (pre-dawn meal) in place of lunch, so that they may be strengthened by it for the worship of their Lord.

It is also said: this was mentioned because the description and form of lunch differ from the description and form of dinner, and this is known only to kings. Likewise in Paradise, the provision of lunch is different from the provision of dinner, so the blessings vary for them, that they may increase in enjoyment and delight.

Al-Tirmidhi al-Hakim recorded in (Nawadir al-Usul), from the hadith of Aban, from al-Hasan and Abu Qilabah, who said: A man said: "O Messenger of Allah, is there night in Paradise?" He said: "What prompted you to this?" He said: "I heard Allah, the Exalted, mention in the Book: 'And for them is their provision in it, morning and evening,' and I said: 'The night is between the morning and the evening.'" The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "There is no night there; there is only light and radiance, which returns the morning to the evening and the evening to the morning, and gifts from Allah, the Exalted, come to them at the appointed times of the prayers they used to pray at in the world, and the angels greet them." This is in the utmost clarity regarding the meaning of the verse, and we have mentioned it in the book (al-Tadhkirah).

The scholars said: There is no night or day in Paradise; rather, they are always in light. They know the measure of night from day by lowering the veils and closing the doors, and they know the measure of day by raising the veils and opening the doors. This was mentioned by Abu al-Faraj al-Jawzi, al-Mahdawi and others.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿تِلْكَ الْجَنَّةُ الَّتِي﴾ "That is the Garden which," that is, this Garden whose people's conditions we have described. (Nuthi) is read with light emphasis (tukhfif).
