Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 19, verse 77–80:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Have you seen the one who disbelieved in Our verses and said, "I will surely be given wealth and children"?﴾ The Imams narrated, and the wording is that of Muslim, from Khabbab, who said: I had a debt owed to me by al-'As ibn Wa'il, so I came to him seeking repayment. He said to me: "I will not pay you until you disbelieve in Muhammad." I said to him: "I will not disbelieve in him until you die and are resurrected." He said: "And will I truly be resurrected after death? Then I will pay you when I return to wealth and children." Waki' said: "This is what al-A'mash said." So this verse was revealed: "Have you seen the one who disbelieved in Our verses and said, 'I will surely be given wealth and children'?" up to His saying: "and he will come to Us alone" (19:80). In another narration he said: I was a qayn [[al-qayn: the blacksmith and the goldsmith.]] in the Jahiliyyah, and I did work for al-'As ibn Wa'il, so I came to him seeking repayment. Al-Bukhari also transmitted it. Al-Kalbi and Muqatil said: Khabbab was a qayn, and he fashioned jewelry for al-'As, then demanded his wage from him. Al-'As said: "I do not have anything to pay you with today." Khabbab said: "I will not leave you until you pay me." Al-'As said: "O Khabbab, what is wrong with you? You were not like this, and indeed you were good at seeking [payment]." Khabbab said: "I was upon your religion, but today I am upon the religion of Islam, separated from your religion." He said: "Do you not claim that in Paradise there is gold, silver and silk?" Khabbab said: "Yes." He said: "Then delay me until I pay you in Paradise," in mockery. "By God, if what you say is true, I will indeed pay you there. By God, you, O Khabbab, and your companions will not have any more right to it than I do." So God the Exalted revealed: "Have you seen the one who disbelieved in Our verses," meaning al-'As ibn Wa'il, the verses. "Has he gained knowledge of the Unseen?" Ibn 'Abbas said: "Has he looked into the Preserved Tablet?" Mujahid said: "Has he known the Unseen, so that he knows whether he will be in Paradise or not?" "Or has he taken a covenant with the Most Merciful?" Qatadah and al-Thawri said: that is, a righteous deed. It was also said: it is monotheism. It was also said: it is from the promise. Al-Kalbi said: he made a covenant with God the Exalted that He would admit him to Paradise. "Nay" is a rejection of him, meaning: that did not happen; he did not gain knowledge of the Unseen, and he did not take a covenant with the Most Merciful. The speech is complete at His saying: "Nay." Al-Hasan said: the verses were revealed concerning al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah. The first view is more sound because it is recorded in the authentic collections.

Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read: "wuldan" with a damma on the waw, and the rest read it with a fatha. The difference in damma and fatha is explained in two ways. The first: they are two dialects with the same meaning, as one says walad and wuld, just as one says 'adam and 'udm. Al-Harith ibn Hilliza said:

"Indeed I have seen people who multiplied wealth and wuld (children)."

Another said:

"Would that so-and-so had been in his mother's womb, and would that so-and-so had been the wuld (offspring) of a donkey."

The second: the Qays tribe makes wuld with a damma a plural and walad with a fatha singular. Al-Mawardi said: In His saying, "I will surely be given wealth and children," there are two interpretations. The first: he meant in the Hereafter, in mockery of what God promised for obedience and worship; this was said by al-Kalbi. The second: he meant in this world, and this is the view of the majority, and it has two possible meanings. The first: "If you remain upon the religion of my fathers and the worship of my gods, I will surely be given wealth and children." The second: "Even if I were upon falsehood, I would not have been given wealth and children." I say: al-Kalbi's view is more consistent with the apparent meaning of the hadiths; rather, their text indicates it. Masruq said: I heard Khabbab ibn al-Aratt say: I came to al-'As ibn Wa'il al-Sahmi seeking a right I had with him. He said: "I will not give it to you until you disbelieve in Muhammad." I said: "No, not until you die and are resurrected." He said: "Will I truly die and then be resurrected?" I said: "Yes." He said: "Indeed, there I will have wealth and children, and I will pay you." So the verse was revealed: "Have you seen the one who disbelieved in Our verses..." to the end. Al-Tirmidhi said: this is a hadith that is hasan sahih.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Has he gained knowledge of the Unseen?﴾ Its alif is the alif of interrogation, because "am" comes after it, and its meaning is rebuke. Its origin is "a-ttala'a," and the second alif was dropped because it is an alif of connection. If it is asked: why did they not put a madda after the alif, saying "a-ttala'a," as they said "lillahi khayr" [[see vol. 13 p. 219 and following.]] and "a-dhdhakarayni harrama" [[see vol. 7 p. 113.]]? It is answered: the original in these was "a-Allahu" and "a-dhdhakarayni," and they replaced the second alif with a madda in order to distinguish the interrogative from the declarative. For if they had said "Allahu khayr" without a madda, the interrogative would be confused with the declarative. They did not need this madda in His saying "attala'a," because the interrogative alif is fatha and the declarative alif is kasra. You say in the interrogative: "a-ttala'a?" "a-fatara?" "a-stafa?" "a-staghfarta?" with a fatha on the alif, and you say in the declarative: "ittala'a," "iftara," "istafa," "istaghfarta lahum" with a kasra. They made the distinction by fatha and kasra and did not need another distinction.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Nay﴾ There is no mention of "kalla" in the first half [[i.e., of the Qur'an. Al-Alusi said: (This is the first place in it of the Qur'an, and it is repeated in the last half, occurring in thirty-three places).]]; its mention came only in the second half. It has two meanings: one is "in truth," and the other is "no." When it means "in truth," it is permissible to stop on what precedes it and then begin with "kalla," meaning "truly." When it means "no," stopping on "kalla" is permissible, as in this verse, because the meaning is: "No, the matter is not as such." It is also permissible to stop on His saying "covenant (ahdan) [19:80]" and begin with "kalla," meaning "truly": "We will record what he says." Likewise His saying, the Exalted: ﴿That I may do righteousness in what I have left behind. No!﴾ [23:100] — it is permissible to stop on "kalla" and on "taraktu." And His saying: "And they have a charge against me, so I fear they will kill me. He said: Never [kalla]" [[see vol. 13 p. 91.]] — stopping on "kalla" is correct because the meaning is "no, and the matter is not as you suppose; so go" — and there is no place for "in truth" in this meaning. Al-Farra' said: "kalla" is in the position of "sawfa," because it is a particle of connection and a particle of refusal, so it is like "na'am" and "la" in being sufficient by itself. He said: If you make it a connection to what follows it, you do not stop on it, as in your saying: "Kalla, by the Lord of the Ka'bah," you do not stop on "kalla," because it is in the position of "i, by the Lord of the Ka'bah." God the Exalted said: ﴿Nay, by the moon﴾ [74:32], so stopping on "kalla" is ugly because it is a connection to the oath. Abu Ja'far Muhammad ibn Sa'dan used to say about "kalla" the same as al-Farra' said. Al-Akhfash said: the meaning of "kalla" is restraint and rebuke. Abu Bakr ibn al-Anbari said: I heard Abu al-'Abbas say: one does not stop on "kalla" throughout the Qur'an, because it is a response and the benefit falls in what follows it. The first view is the view of the people of tafsir.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿We will record what he says﴾ means: We will preserve his statement against him and recompense him for it in the Hereafter.

(And We will extend for him the extension of punishment) means: We will increase his punishment above punishment.

(And We will inherit from him what he says) [19:80]: means: We will strip him of what We gave him in this world of wealth and children. Ibn 'Abbas and others said: that is, We will inherit from him the wealth and children after We destroy him. It was also said: We will deprive him of what he wished for in the Hereafter of wealth and children, and We will give it to another of the Muslims.

(And he will come to Us alone) [19:80]: meaning, singular, having no wealth, no children, and no kin to support him.

Al-'As said: "I do not have anything to pay you with today." Khabbab said: "I will not leave you until you pay me." Al-'As said: "O Khabbab, what is wrong with you? Al-Kalbi said: he made a covenant with God the Exalted that He would admit him to Paradise. Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 19, verses 81–82:

God, exalted is He, says: ﴿And they have taken gods besides God, that they may be for them a source of might﴾. That means the idolaters of Quraysh. "Izz" (might) means helpers and protection, that is, children. Al-'izz also means abundant rain (al-matar al-jud [[al-matar al-jud: the heavy, abundant rain.]]), as al-Harawi said. The apparent meaning of the speech is that "izz" refers back to the gods they worshipped besides God. It is in the singular because it is used as a verbal noun (masdar), meaning that they would gain might through them and be protected by them from the punishment of God. God, exalted is He, then says: ﴿No!﴾ That is, the matter is not as they supposed and imagined. Rather, ﴿they will deny their worship﴾, that is, they will deny that they worshipped the idols; or the gods will reject the worship of the idolaters, as He says: ﴿"We disown You; they never used to worship us."﴾ [al-Qasas: 63] [[In k: "they said".]] [[See vol. 13, p. 303 onward.]] This is because idols are inanimate objects that do not know that they are being worshipped. ﴿And they will be opposed to them﴾, that is, helpers against them in their dispute and their denial. This is related from Mujahid and al-Dahhak: they will be enemies to them. Ibn Zayd said: they will be a trial against them. Their gods will be gathered, given intellect, and they will speak and say: "O Lord, punish those who worshipped us besides You."

The word "kalla" here may mean "no" (la), and it may mean "truly" (haqqan), that is, truly "they will deny their worship." Abu Nuhayk recited "kallan sayakfurun" with tanwin (nunation). It is also related from him, in addition, that the kaf was read with both damma and fatha.

Al-Mahdawi said: "kalla" is a rebuke, a warning, an alert, and a rejection of a preceding statement. It may also occur to confirm what follows and to draw attention to it, as in His words: ﴿No! Indeed, man transgresses﴾ [al-'Alaq: 6]. It is therefore not stopped upon (waqf) in this sense, but it is stopped upon in the first sense. If both meanings are suitable, it is permissible to pause on it (waqf) and to begin with it (ibtida').

As for the one who gives tanwin to "kalla" in "kallan sayakfurun bi-'ibadatihim" with a fatha on the kaf, it is a verbal noun of kalla, and its accusative case is governed by a hidden verb. The meaning is: this opinion and belief is weakened (kalla), a weakening, namely their taking of the gods. ﴿That they may be for them a source of might﴾. So a pause is made here on "izz" and on "kalla." The same applies to the recitation of the majority, because it is suitable as a rejection of what precedes it and as an affirmation of what follows it. Whoever related the kaf with damma and tanwin, it is also accusative, governed by a hidden verb, as if he had said: "They will deny." "Kallan sayakfurun bi-'ibadatihim" means "the gods."

I say: four meanings are thus established for "kalla": affirmation, meaning "truly" (haqqan); negation; warning and alert; and a connector to an oath. A pause is made upon it only in the first sense.

Al-Kisa'i said: "la" only negates, whereas "kalla" negates one thing and affirms another. So when one says, "I ate dates," one replies: "Kalla, I ate honey, not dates." In this word there is negation of what precedes it and affirmation of what follows it.

The word "diddun" (opposite, enemy) may be singular or plural, as in "al-'aduw" (enemy) and "al-rasul" (messenger). It is also said: "diddun" stands in the place of a verbal noun, that is, "they will be a support against them." For this reason it is not made plural. This corresponds to His words: "that they may be for them a source of might," and "'izz" is a verbal noun, so what stands opposite it is likewise.

Then it is said: the verse refers to the worshippers of idols, and the idols are treated as if they had intellect, following the assumption of the disbelievers. It is also said: it refers to those who worshipped Christ, or the angels, or the jinn, or the devils. And God knows best.

Whoever loved riding ships, then upon ships of [emerald and [[from B, J, Z, T, K, Y.]]] ruby, having felt safe from drowning and safe from terrors. I have seen kings and their delegations, and I have not seen a delegation except riding." meaning the wurrad, those who desire the water.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿They will not possess intercession﴾. That is, these disbelievers will not possess intercession for anyone, (except one who has taken a covenant with the Most Merciful), and these are the Muslims, who will possess intercession. So "man" (whoever) is in the accusative position on this view. It was also said that it is in the nominative position, as a substitute (badal) for the waw in "yamlikun" (they possess). That is, no one possesses intercession with God, except whoever has taken a covenant with the Most Merciful, for he possesses it. On this view the exception is connected (istithna' muttasil). And "the criminals" in His saying, "And We drive the criminals to Hell as a thirsty herd," includes both disbelievers and disobedient sinners. Then He informs that they do not possess intercession, except the disobedient believers, for they possess it by being interceded for. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "I will not cease to intercede until I say, 'O Lord, grant me intercession for whoever said, there is no god but Allah, Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah,' and He will say, 'O Muhammad, it is not for you, but it is for Me.'" Muslim recorded it with this meaning, and it has already been mentioned. The reports are consistent that the people of virtue, knowledge and righteousness will intercede, and they will be granted intercession. On the first view, the speech is connected to His saying: ﴿And they have taken other gods besides Allah that they may be for them a source of might﴾. So on the Day of Judgment the intercession of idol-worshippers will not be accepted for anyone, nor will the idols' intercession be accepted for anyone, and they will not possess the intercession of anyone for them. That is, no intercession will benefit them, as He said: ﴿So the intercession of the interceders will not benefit them﴾ [[See vol. 19, p. 82.]]. It was also said: That is, We will gather the righteous and the criminals, and no one will possess intercession, "except whoever has taken a covenant with the Most Merciful," that is, when Allah permits him to intercede, as He said: ﴿Who is it that can intercede with Him except by His permission?﴾ [[See vol. 3, p. 268 onward.]] [Al-Baqarah: 255]. And this covenant is what He referred to in: "Or has he taken a covenant with the Most Merciful?" It is a comprehensive term for faith and all the righteous deeds by which their doer reaches the sphere of those who intercede. Ibn Abbas said: the covenant is "There is no god but Allah." Muqatil and Ibn Abbas also said: No one intercedes except one who testifies that there is no god but Allah, disavows his own power and strength before Allah, and hopes for nothing but Allah, the Exalted. Ibn Mas'ud said: I heard the Messenger of God (ﷺ) say to his companions: "Is one of you incapable of taking a covenant with Allah every morning and evening?" It was asked, "O Messenger of God, what is that?" He said: "He says every morning and evening: 'O Allah, Originator of the heavens and the earth, Knower of the unseen and the witnessed, I make a covenant with You in this life, that I bear witness that there is no god but You alone, without partner, and that Muhammad is Your servant and Messenger. [So do not leave me to myself,] for if You leave me to myself, You will distance me from good and bring me near to evil, and I trust only in Your mercy. So make for me with You a covenant that You will fulfil for me on the Day of Resurrection, for You do not break Your promise.'" When he says that, Allah sets a seal upon it and places it beneath the Throne. Then on the Day of Resurrection a caller will call out: "Where are those who have a covenant with Allah?" Then he will stand up and enter Paradise.

meaning the wurrad, those who desire the water.

It was also said: "Wirdan" means the coming (al-wurud), like your saying: "I came to you in honour of you," meaning for your honour; that is, We drive them to the arrival at the Fire.

I say: There is no contradiction between these sayings, so they are driven thirsty, barefoot, on foot, in separate groups [[In A: in groups.]]. Ibn 'Arafa said: "Al-wird" is the people who come to water, so the thirsty are called "wird" because they seek to come to water, just as you say "qawm sawm," meaning fasting people, and "qawm zawr," meaning visitors; it is a noun in the form of a verbal noun, and its singular is "warid." Al-wird also means the group that comes to water, of birds and camels. Al-wird also means the water that is brought. This is of the nature of pointing to one thing by another. Al-wird also means the portion [of the Qur'an [[Addition from (Lisan al-'Arab).]]]; one says: "I recited my wird." Al-wird also means the day of fever when it seizes its sufferer for a time. Its apparent meaning is a shared term. A poet, describing a well [[al-qalib: the well.]], said:

It fills up when the wird crowds around it [[Its first half: "They came in the morning to a well of Washha, narrow"; Washha: name of a well; al-sakk: narrow. Al-takk al-wird: crowded and struck one another. Tamat al-bi'r tatmu tamwan and tatma tamyan: it filled up.]]

meaning the wurrad, those who desire the water.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿They will not possess intercession﴾. That is, these disbelievers will not possess intercession for anyone, (except one who has taken a covenant with the Most Merciful), and these are the Muslims, who will possess intercession. This is an exception of a thing from what is not of its kind. That is, "but whoever has taken a covenant with the Most Merciful" will intercede. So "man" (whoever) is in the accusative position on this view. It was also said that it is in the nominative position, as a substitute (badal) for the waw in "yamlikun" (they possess). That is, no one possesses intercession with God, except whoever has taken a covenant with the Most Merciful, for he possesses it. On this view the exception is connected (istithna' muttasil). And "the criminals" in His saying, "And We drive the criminals to Hell as a thirsty herd," includes both disbelievers and disobedient sinners. Then He informs that they do not possess intercession, except the disobedient believers, for they possess it by being interceded for. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "I will not cease to intercede until I say, 'O Lord, grant me intercession for whoever said, there is no god but Allah, Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah,' and He will say, 'O Muhammad, it is not for you, but it is for Me.'" Muslim recorded it with this meaning, and it has already been mentioned. The reports are consistent that the people of virtue, knowledge and righteousness will intercede, and they will be granted intercession. On the first view, the speech is connected to His saying: ﴿And they have taken other gods besides Allah that they may be for them a source of might﴾. So on the Day of Judgment the intercession of idol-worshippers will not be accepted for anyone, nor will the idols' intercession be accepted for anyone, and they will not possess the intercession of anyone for them. That is, no intercession will benefit them, as He said: ﴿So the intercession of the interceders will not benefit them﴾ [[See vol. 19, p. 82.]]. It was also said: That is, We will gather the righteous and the criminals, and no one will possess intercession, "except whoever has taken a covenant with the Most Merciful," that is, when Allah permits him to intercede, as He said: ﴿Who is it that can intercede with Him except by His permission?﴾ [[See vol. 3, p. 268 onward.]] [Al-Baqarah: 255]. And this covenant is what He referred to in: "Or has he taken a covenant with the Most Merciful?" It is a comprehensive term for faith and all the righteous deeds by which their doer reaches the sphere of those who intercede. Ibn Abbas said: the covenant is "There is no god but Allah." Muqatil and Ibn Abbas also said: No one intercedes except one who testifies that there is no god but Allah, disavows his own power and strength before Allah, and hopes for nothing but Allah, the Exalted. Ibn Mas'ud said: I heard the Messenger of God (ﷺ) say to his companions: "Is one of you incapable of taking a covenant with Allah every morning and evening?" It was asked, "O Messenger of God, what is that?" He said: "He says every morning and evening: 'O Allah, Originator of the heavens and the earth, Knower of the unseen and the witnessed, I make a covenant with You in this life, that I bear witness that there is no god but You alone, without partner, and that Muhammad is Your servant and Messenger. [So do not leave me to myself,] for if You leave me to myself, You will distance me from good and bring me near to evil, and I trust only in Your mercy. So make for me with You a covenant that You will fulfil for me on the Day of Resurrection, for You do not break Your promise.'" When he says that, Allah sets a seal upon it and places it beneath the Throne. Then on the Day of Resurrection a caller will call out: "Where are those who have a covenant with Allah?" Then he will stand up and enter Paradise.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 19, verses 83–87 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Do you not see that We have sent the devils upon the disbelievers?﴾ That is, We have empowered them over them through seduction, and that was when He said to Iblis: ﴿And incite whomever you can among them with your voice﴾ [al-Isra' 17:64]. [[See vol. 10, p. 288.]] It was also said that "arsalna" means "We left them free," as one says: "arsaltu al-ba'ir," meaning "I left the camel loose." That is, We left the devils and them, and We did not protect them from accepting from them. Al-Zajjaj said: "We appointed them (qayyadna)."

﴿Inciting them with incitement﴾ (ta'uzzuhum azzan). Ibn 'Abbas said: "They agitate them with agitation from obedience to disobedience." And from him: "They urge them with urging to evil: go on, go on in this matter, until they cast them into the Fire." Al-Tha'labi related the first, and al-Mawardi the second, and the meaning is one. Al-Dahhak said: "They lead them astray with misguidance." Mujahid said: "They incite them with incitement." Its root meaning is movement and boiling, and from it is the report that the Prophet (ﷺ) "stood up for the prayer and there was a sound in his chest like the sound of a cauldron from weeping." And "a'tazzati al-qidr i'tizazan" means the pot boiled vehemently. Al-azz means agitation and incitement. Allah, may He be exalted, said: "Do you not see that We have sent the devils upon the disbelievers, inciting them with incitement?", meaning They urge them on to sins. Al-azz also means mixing. And "azaztu al-shay'a a'uzzuhu azzan" means I gathered parts of it together, as al-Jawhari said.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So do not be hasty against them﴾, that is, do not seek punishment for them.

﴿Indeed, We are counting for them a count﴾ (innama na'uddu lahum 'addan). Al-Kalbi said: "Their terms, meaning the days, nights, months and years, until the end of the term of punishment." Al-Dahhak said: "The breaths." Ibn 'Abbas said: "That is, We count their breaths in this world just as We count their years." It was also said: "The steps." It was said: "The pleasures." It was said: "The glances." It was said: "The hours." Qutrub said: "We count their deeds with a count." It was also said: Do not be hasty against them, for We are only delaying them so that they may increase in sin.

It is related that al-Ma'mun recited this surah and passed over this verse while a group of jurists was with him. He gestured with his head to Ibn al-Simak to admonish him, and he said: "If breaths are by number and have no replenishment, how quickly they will be exhausted." And concerning this meaning it has been said:
Your life is breaths that are counted; whenever
a breath passes from you, you lose a part by it.
What gives you life also brings you death every night,
and a driver drives you, intending by it mockery.

It is said that the breaths of the son of Adam between the day and the night are twenty-four thousand breaths: twelve thousand breaths in the day and twelve thousand in the night — and Allah knows best. They are counted and enumerated with an enumeration, and they have a known number, and they have no replenishment, so how quickly they will be exhausted.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿The Day We gather the God-fearing to the All-Merciful as a delegation﴾. There is an ellipsis in the speech, meaning to the Garden of the All-Merciful and the abode of His honour, like His saying: ﴿Indeed I am going to my Lord; He will guide me﴾ [al-Saffat 37:99], and as in the report: "Whoever's emigration was to Allah and His Messenger, his emigration is to Allah and His Messenger." "Wafd" is a noun for those who come as delegates, as one says "sawm" and "fitr" and "zawr"; it is the plural of "al-wafid," like "rakb" and "rakib," and "sahb" and "sahib." It comes from "wafada, yafidu, wafdan, wufudan, wifadatan," when one goes out to a king for a conquest or a momentous matter. Al-Jawhari said: One says "Fulan wafada 'ala al-amir," meaning he came as an envoy, so he is "wafid," and the plural is "wafd," like "sahib" and "sahb"; the plural of "wafd" is "wifad" and "wufud," and the noun is "wifada." "Awfadtuhu ana ila al-amir" means I sent him to the ruler. In the tafsir: "Wafdan" means riders upon the swift camels of their obedience. This is because the one who comes as a delegate is usually a rider, and "wafd" means riders; it is singular in form because it is a verbal noun. Ibn Jurayj said: "Wafdan upon the swift camels." 'Amr ibn Qays al-Mala'i said: When the believer comes out of his grave, his deed meets him in the best form and the sweetest scent, and says: "Do you know me?" He says: "No, except that Allah has made your scent sweet and your form beautiful." It says: "Thus you were in the world; I am your righteous deed. You have ridden me many times in the world; ride me today." And he recited: "The Day We gather the God-fearing to the All-Merciful as a delegation." And the disbeliever's deed meets him in the ugliest form and the foulest scent, and says: "Do you know me?" He says: "No, except that Allah has made your form ugly and your scent foul." It says: "Thus you were in the world; I am your evil deed. You rode me in the world, and today I ride you." And he recited: ﴿And they will bear their burdens upon their backs﴾ [al-An'am 6:31]. [[See vol. 6, p. 423.]] This report is not sound in its chain of transmission, as Ibn al-'Arabi said in "Siraj al-Muridin." Abu Nasr 'Abd al-Rahim ibn 'Abd al-Karim al-Qushayri mentioned this report in his tafsir from Ibn 'Abbas with its wording and meaning. He also said, from Ibn 'Abbas: Whoever loved riding horses comes as a delegation to Allah, the Exalted, upon horses that do not dung nor urinate, whose bridles are of red ruby, green emerald and white pearl, and whose saddles are of silk brocade and thick silk. Whoever loved riding camels, then upon swift camels that do not dung, whose bridles are of ruby and emerald. Whoever loved riding ships, then upon ships of [emerald and [[from B, J, Z, T, K, Y.]]] ruby, having felt safe from drowning and safe from terrors. He also said, from 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him: When this verse was revealed, 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "O Messenger of Allah! I have seen kings and their delegations, and I have not seen a delegation except riding." "So what is the delegation of Allah?" The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed they will not be gathered on their feet, nor driven as driven herds, but they will be brought mounts of the she-camels of Paradise, which no creatures have looked upon the like of, their saddles of gold and their reins of emerald, and they will ride them until they knock at the gate of Paradise." Al-Tha'labi's wording of this report from 'Ali is clearer. 'Ali said: When this verse was revealed, I said: "O Messenger of Allah! I have seen kings and their delegations, and I have not seen a delegation except riding." He said: "O 'Ali, when the departure from before Allah, the Exalted, takes place, the angels will meet the believers with white she-camels, their saddles and reins of gold, and on every mount a robe that the world cannot equal, and every believer will wear a robe; then their mounts will carry them, and the she-camels will bring them swiftly until they reach Paradise, and the angels will receive them: ﴿Peace be upon you; you are good, so enter it, abiding forever﴾ [al-Zumar 39:73]." [[See vol. 15, p. 284 onward.]]

I say: This report explicitly states that they do not ride nor wear anything except from the place of standing, but when they come out of the graves they are walking, barefoot, naked, uncircumcised (ghurl) [[Al-ghurl (plural of aghral): the uncircumcised.]] to the place of standing, according to the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) stood among us with an exhortation and said: "O people, indeed you will be gathered to Allah, the Exalted, barefoot, naked, uncircumcised..." the hadith. Al-Bukhari and Muslim recorded it, and it will come in full in surah "al-Mu'minun," Allah willing. It has preceded in "Al 'Imran" [[See vol. 4, p. 273.]] from the hadith of 'Abd Allah ibn Unays with a similar meaning, and praise be to Allah, the Exalted. It is not far-fetched that both states may occur for the blessed, so the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas would be specific. And Allah knows best. Abu Hurayra said: "Wafdan" means upon camels. Ibn 'Abbas said: Riders; they will be brought she-camels from Paradise, upon which are saddles of gold, and their saddles and reins are of emerald, and they will be gathered upon them. 'Ali said: By Allah, they will not be gathered on their feet, but upon she-camels whose saddles are of gold and noble mounts whose saddles are hyacinths; if they wish to go, they go, and if they urge them, they fly. It was also said: They come as delegations upon what they love of camels, horses or ships, according to what has preceded from Ibn 'Abbas. And Allah knows best. It was also said: He said "wafdan" because it is the custom of delegations among the Arabs to come bearing good news and to await rewards; so the God-fearing await the gift and the reward.

﴿And We drive the criminals to Hell as thirsty herds﴾ (wirdan). Driving (sawq) is urging to walk. "Wirdan" means thirsty, as said by Ibn 'Abbas, Abu Hurayra and al-Hasan, may Allah be pleased with them. Al-Akhfash, al-Farra' and Ibn al-A'rabi said: barefoot, on foot. It was also said: in separate groups [[In A: in groups.]]. Al-Azhari said: that is, on foot and thirsty, like camels that come to water, so it is said: "The wird of the sons of so-and-so has come." Al-Qushayri said: His saying "wirdan" indicates thirst, because water is generally brought to the thirsty. In the tafsir: on foot and thirsty, their necks cut off from thirst. And if the driving of the criminals is to the Fire, then the gathering of the God-fearing is to the Garden. It was also said: "Wirdan" means the coming (al-wurud), like your saying: "I came to you in honour of you," meaning for your honour; that is, We drive them to the arrival at the Fire.

Al-wird also means the group that comes to water, of birds and camels. Al-wird also means the water that is brought. This is of the nature of pointing to one thing by another. Al-wird also means the portion [of the Qur'an [[Addition from (Lisan al-'Arab).]]]; one says: "I recited my wird." Al-wird also means the day of fever when it seizes its sufferer for a time. Its apparent meaning is a shared term. A poet, describing a well [[al-qalib: the well.]], said:

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 19, verses 88–95 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And they say, "The Most Merciful has taken to Himself a son."﴾ He means the Jews and the Christians, and whoever claims that the angels are the daughters of Allah.

Yahya, al-A'mash, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, 'Asim and Khalaf read "wuldan" (وُلْدًا) with a damma on the waw and sukun on the lam, in four places: in this surah, His saying, ﴿"Have I seen the Unseen, or have I taken a covenant with the Most Merciful?" ... "I will surely be given wealth and children (walad)."﴾ [Maryam: 77], which has already been discussed; His saying, "that they ascribe a son (walad) to the Most Merciful. And it is not befitting for the Most Merciful to take a son (walad)"; and in Surah Nuh, ﴿"his wealth and his children (waladuhu)"﴾ [Nuh: 21]. Ibn Kathir, Mujahid, Humayd, Abu 'Amr and Ya'qub agreed with them in "Nuh" specifically. The rest read all of them with a fatha on the waw and the lam. Both forms are dialectal variants, like "al-'arab" and "al-'urb" and "al-'ajam" and "al-'ujm." The poet said:

"And indeed I have seen people who have multiplied wealth and offspring (wuldan)."

Another said:

"Would that So-and-so had been in his mother's belly, would that So-and-so had been the offspring (wuld) of a donkey."

And al-Nabigha said, in the same sense:

"Gently! May all the people be ransomed for you, and may I not have accumulated wealth and offspring (walad)."

So he used the fatha. The Qays tribe use "wuld" with a damma as the plural and "walad" with a fatha as the singular. Al-Jawhari said: "Walad may be singular or plural, and likewise wuld with a damma." From the proverbs of the Banu Asad: "Your offspring is the one who bled your heels" [meaning: the one you bore in childbirth, whose afterbirth bled your heels, is your child]. Wuld may also be the plural of walad, like usd and asad. Al-Wild with a kasra is a dialect form of walad. Al-Nahhas said: Abu 'Ubayda distinguished between them, claiming that walad applies to the family and to offspring collectively. Abu Ja'far said: This is a rejected opinion that none of the lexicographers recognises. Walad and wuld refer only to a man's child and his child's child, except that walad is more common in the speech of the Arabs, as in the verse:

"Gently! May all the people be ransomed for you, and may I not have accumulated wealth and offspring (walad)."

Abu Ja'far said: I heard Muhammad ibn al-Walid say: It is permissible for wuld to be the plural of walad, as one says wathan and wuthn, and asad and usd. And it is permissible for walad and wuld to have one meaning, as one says 'ajam and 'ujm, and 'arab and 'urb, as mentioned earlier.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed you have brought forth a thing that is idd (monstrous)﴾, that is, a grave evil, according to Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and others. Al-Jawhari said: Al-idd and al-iddah mean a calamity and a dreadful matter, and from it is His saying: ﴿Indeed you have brought forth a thing that is idd.﴾ Likewise al-add, on the pattern of fa'il. The plural of iddah is idad. "A calamity afflicted So-and-so (addahu), so that it weighed heavily upon him" (adda, with a fatha). Al-add also means hardship. [Al-add: domination and strength. In the originals: al-idd is strength and hardness; the plural al-idd is also strength. The correct form, as in Lisan al-Arab, is: al-idd with a kasra is hardship, and al-add with a fatha is domination and strength.] The reciter said:

"They stripped from me hardship and weight, after I had been firm and sturdy."

End of his words. Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami read "addan" (أَدًّا) with a fatha on the hamza. Al-Nahhas said: One says adda yauddu adda, so he is addun, and the noun is idd, when he brings a great, monstrous thing. The reciter said:

"The rivals have met from me a horror, a calamity, a great and dreadful thing."

Al-Nahhas' statement, from al-Tha'labi: There are three forms. "Iddan" with a kasra is the reading of the common people. "Addan" with a fatha is the reading of al-Sulami. "Addun" on the pattern of madd is a dialect of some Arabs, transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas and Abu al-'Aliyah, and it seems to be derived from weight. One says: "al-himl a'dahu, ya'uduhu, awdan," meaning the load made him heavy.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿The heavens are almost rent (takadu)﴾. The common reading here and in "al-Shura" [see vol. 16, p. 4] is with the taa'. The reading of Nafi', Yahya and al-Kisa'i is "yakadu" with the yaa', because the verb comes first.

(yatafattarna minhu) [verse 90], that is, they split apart. Nafi', Ibn Kathir, Hafs and others read it with a taa' after the yaa' and with a shadda on the taa' from tafattur, here and in "al-Shura." Hamzah and Ibn 'Amir agreed with them in "al-Shura." Here they read "yanfatirna" from infitar. Abu 'Amr, Abu Bakr and al-Mufaddal read it in both surahs in this way too. This is the preference of Abu 'Ubayd, because of His saying: ﴿When the heaven is split asunder (infatarat)﴾ [al-Infitar: 1] and His saying: ﴿The heaven will be split asunder (munfatirun) by it﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 18].

His saying: (And the earth is split open (tanshaqqu)) [verse 90], that is, it cracks open.

(And the mountains fall down in ruins (hadda)) [verse 90]. Ibn 'Abbas said: Demolished, that is, they fall with a loud noise. In a hadith: "O Allah, I seek refuge in You from hadd and hadda." Shamir said: Ahmad ibn Ghiyath al-Marwazi said: al-hadd is demolition and al-hadda is subsidence. Al-Layth said: It is a severe collapse, like a wall that is brought down all at once. One says: "The matter hadda me, and hadda my pillar," meaning it broke me and reached me, as reported by al-Harawi. Al-Jawhari said: "Hadda al-bina' yahudduhu hadda" means he broke it and shattered it. "The calamity hadda him," meaning it weakened his support. "The mountain inhadda," meaning it broke. Al-Asma'i said: Al-hadd is a weak man. A man says to another, when threatening him: "I am not a weakling (hadd)," meaning I am not weak. Ibn al-A'rabi said: Al-hadd among men is the generous and noble one, while the cowardly and weak one is hid (with a kasra). He recited the line of al-'Abbas ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib, may Allah be pleased with him, [the lines mean: "They are not weak (yahudduna) in wars when the belts (nutuq) are tied above the hips (harqafat)."]:

"They are not weak in wars, when the belts are tied above the hips."

Al-hadda is the sound of a wall or the like falling. One says from it: "hadda yahiddu" (with a kasra) hadidan. Al-hadd is a sound heard by the people of the coast, coming to them from the sea, which has a resonance in the earth; sometimes an earthquake comes from it, and its resonance is its hadid. Al-Nahhas: "Hadda" [verse 90] is a verbal noun, because the meaning of "takharru" [verse 90] is "tuhaddu" (is demolished). Others said: it is a state (hal), that is, demolished.

(That they ascribe a son to the Most Merciful) [verse 91]. "An" (that) is in the accusative position according to al-Farra', because of "an da'aw" (that they ascribed), and from "an da'aw" the position of "an" is accusative by the removal of the preposition. Al-Farra' claimed that al-Kisa'i said: it is in the genitive position by the implied preposition.

Ibn al-Mubarak mentioned: Misar related to us from Wasil, from 'Awn ibn 'Abd Allah, who said: 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud said: "The mountain says to the mountain: 'O So-and-so, did anyone who remembers Allah pass by you today?' If he says yes, it rejoices." Then 'Abd Allah recited: ﴿And they say, "The Most Merciful has taken to Himself a son."﴾ and said: [that is, 'Awn said, as in al-Durr al-Manthur and elsewhere]: "Do you think they hear falsehood and do not hear good?"

He said: Awf related to me from Ghalib ibn 'Ajrad [so it is in the originals; probably Ghalib ibn Hujrah, and the text here is corrupted], who said: A man from the people of Syria related to me in the mosque of Mina: When Allah created the earth and created what is in it of trees, there was no tree on the earth to which the children of Adam came without obtaining some benefit from it, and they had benefit from it. The earth and the trees remained so until the wicked among the children of Adam uttered that great word: their saying "The Most Merciful has taken to Himself a son." When they said it, the earth shuddered and the trees bristled.

Ibn 'Abbas said: The mountains shuddered, and what is in them of trees, seas, and fish. From that came the thorns on the fish and the thorns on the trees. Ibn 'Abbas and Ka'b also said: The heavens, the earth, the mountains and all creatures, except the two weighty ones [humans and jinn], were terrified, and they nearly ceased to exist. The angels became angry, Hell was kindled, the trees bristled, the earth became gloomy and dry, when they said: Allah has taken a son.

Muhammad ibn Ka'b said: The enemies of Allah almost established the Hour against us, by His saying: ﴿The heavens are almost rent asunder from it, and the earth splits open, and the mountains fall down in ruins, that they ascribe a son to the Most Merciful.﴾ Ibn al-'Arabi said: He spoke the truth. It is a grave saying, against which the decree and the destiny have already gone forth. Were it not that the Creator, blessed and exalted, is not diminished by the disbelief of the disbeliever and not exalted by the faith of the believer, and that this does not increase His kingdom just as that does not decrease His kingdom, such a thing would not have been spoken on the tongues. But He is the Holy, the Wise, the Forbearing, so after that He does not heed what the falsifiers say.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And it is not befitting for the Most Merciful to take a son.﴾ On this there are four issues.

The first: His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And it is not befitting for the Most Merciful to take a son.﴾ He negated from Himself, glorified and exalted, having a son, because a son implies kinship (jinsiyyah) and origination (huduth), as we have explained in al-Baqarah [see vol. 2, p. 85]. That is, this is not fitting for Him, He is not described by it, and it is not permissible concerning Him, because a son is only born of a father who has a father and an origin, and Allah, glorified, is exalted and sanctified above that.

He said [Ibn Ahmar al-Bahili, describing a mountain]:

"At the top of a smooth rock, from a lofty peak, no plain nor mountain is fitting beneath it."

(Ain kullu man fi al-samawati wal-ard illa atil-Rahmani 'abda) [verse 93]. "In" is negating, meaning "ma" (not). In the originals: al-idd is strength and hardness; the plural al-idd is also strength. The correct form, as in Lisan al-Arab, is: al-idd with a kasra is hardship, and al-add with a fatha is domination and strength.] The reciter said:

"They stripped from me hardship and weight, after I had been firm and sturdy."

End of his words. Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami read "addan" (أَدًّا) with a fatha on the hamza. Al-Nahhas said: One says adda yauddu adda, so he is addun, and the noun is idd, when he brings a great, monstrous thing. The reciter said:

"The rivals have met from me a horror, a calamity, a great and dreadful thing."

One says: "al-himl a'dahu, ya'uduhu, awdan," meaning the load made him heavy.

(yatafattarna minhu) [verse 90], that is, they split apart. Nafi', Ibn Kathir, Hafs and others read it with a taa' after the yaa' and with a shadda on the taa' from tafattur, here and in "al-Shura." His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed you have brought forth a thing that is idd (monstrous)﴾, that is, a grave evil, according to Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and others. In the originals: al-idd is strength and hardness; the plural al-idd is also strength. The correct form, as in Lisan al-Arab, is: al-idd with a kasra is hardship, and al-add with a fatha is domination and strength.] The reciter said:

"They stripped from me hardship and weight, after I had been firm and sturdy."

End of his words. Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami read "addan" (أَدًّا) with a fatha on the hamza. Al-Nahhas said: One says adda yauddu adda, so he is addun, and the noun is idd, when he brings a great, monstrous thing. The reciter said:

(yatafattarna minhu) [verse 90], that is, they split apart. Nafi', Ibn Kathir, Hafs and others read it with a taa' after the yaa' and with a shadda on the taa' from tafattur, here and in "al-Shura." His saying: (And the earth is split open (tanshaqqu)) [verse 90], that is, it cracks open.

"They are not weak in wars, when the belts are tied above the hips."

When they said it, the earth shuddered and the trees bristled.

It is a grave saying, against which the decree and the destiny have already gone forth. Were it not that the Creator, blessed and exalted, is not diminished by the disbelief of the disbeliever and not exalted by the faith of the believer, and that this does not increase His kingdom just as that does not decrease His kingdom, such a thing would not have been spoken on the tongues. But He is the Holy, the Wise, the Forbearing, so after that He does not heed what the falsifiers say.

The first: His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And it is not befitting for the Most Merciful to take a son.﴾ He negated from Himself, glorified and exalted, having a son, because a son implies kinship (jinsiyyah) and origination (huduth), as we have explained in al-Baqarah [see vol. 2, p. 85]. That is, this is not fitting for Him, He is not described by it, and it is not permissible concerning Him, because a son is only born of a father who has a father and an origin, and Allah, glorified, is exalted and sanctified above that.

He said [Ibn Ahmar al-Bahili, describing a mountain]:

"At the top of a smooth rock, from a lofty peak, no plain nor mountain is fitting beneath it."

(Ain kullu man fi al-samawati wal-ard illa atil-Rahmani 'abda) [verse 93]. "In" is negating, meaning "ma" (not). "Atin" is written with a yaa' in the script, and the original form has tanwin, which was dropped for lightness and then the word was made into a construct phrase (idafah).

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Certainly He has enumerated them﴾, meaning He knows their number, ﴿and counted them, a counting﴾. It is an emphasis, meaning that none of them is hidden from Him.

I say: In the names of Allah, glorified is He, we have found al-Muhsi (the Enumerator), namely in the Sunnah, in the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, which al-Tirmidhi recorded, and the derivation of this verb indicates it.

Al-Ustadh Abu Ishaq al-Isfara'ini said: Among the names is al-Muhsi, and it is distinguished by the fact that the multiplicity of things does not preoccupy Him from knowledge, like the light of illumination, the intensity of the wind, and the falling of leaves. So at that time He knows the parts of the movements in every leaf. And how would He not know, when He is the One who created? He has said: ﴿Should not He who created know? And He is the Subtle, the All-Aware﴾ [[See vol. 18, p. 213 onwards.]]. It occurs in the tafsir of Ibn Abbas that the meaning of ﴿Certainly He has enumerated them and counted them, a counting﴾ is: they acknowledged to Him servitude and bore witness to Him of lordship.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And all of them will come to Him on the Day of Resurrection, alone﴾, meaning singly, with no helper for him and no wealth with him to benefit him [[So it is in the originals except A: "yanfa'uhu" (benefit him).]], as He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿The Day when neither wealth nor children will benefit, except one who comes to Allah with a sound heart﴾ [[See vol. 13, p. 113 onwards.]]. So nothing benefits him except what he has sent ahead of good deeds. And He said: "And all of them will come to Him", following the wording, while considering the meaning, "they will come to Him."

Al-Qushayri said: In this there is an indication that you do not accept for yourselves that your children be enslaved, while all are His servants. So how do you accept for Him what you do not accept for yourselves? It has been refuted against them in a similar matter, in that they do not accept daughters for themselves, yet they say: "The angels are daughters of Allah", exalted is Allah above that, and their saying: "The idols are daughters of Allah." And He said: ﴿So what is for their associates does not reach Allah, and what is for Allah reaches their associates﴾ [[See vol. 7, p. 89 onwards.]].

Tafsir of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 19, verses 88–95 (part 2 of 2):

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Certainly He has enumerated them﴾, meaning He knows their number, ﴿and counted them, a counting﴾. It is an emphasis, meaning that none of them is hidden from Him.

I say: In the names of Allah, glorified is He, we have found al-Muhsi (the Enumerator), namely in the Sunnah, in the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, which al-Tirmidhi recorded, and the derivation of this verb indicates it.

Al-Ustadh Abu Ishaq al-Isfara'ini said: Among the names is al-Muhsi, and it is distinguished by the fact that the multiplicity of things does not preoccupy Him from knowledge, like the light of illumination, the intensity of the wind, and the falling of leaves. So at that time He knows the parts of the movements in every leaf. And how would He not know, when He is the One who created? He has said: ﴿Should not He who created know? And He is the Subtle, the All-Aware﴾ [[See vol. 18, p. 213 onwards.]]. It occurs in the tafsir of Ibn Abbas that the meaning of ﴿Certainly He has enumerated them and counted them, a counting﴾ is: they acknowledged to Him servitude and bore witness to Him of lordship.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And all of them will come to Him on the Day of Resurrection, alone﴾, meaning singly, with no helper for him and no wealth with him to benefit him [[So it is in the originals except A: "yanfa'uhu" (benefit him).]], as He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿The Day when neither wealth nor children will benefit, except one who comes to Allah with a sound heart﴾ [[See vol. 13, p. 113 onwards.]]. So nothing benefits him except what he has sent ahead of good deeds. And He said: "And all of them will come to Him", following the wording, while considering the meaning, "they will come to Him."

Al-Qushayri said: In this there is an indication that you do not accept for yourselves that your children be enslaved, while all are His servants. So how do you accept for Him what you do not accept for yourselves? It has been refuted against them in a similar matter, in that they do not accept daughters for themselves, yet they say: "The angels are daughters of Allah", exalted is Allah above that, and their saying: "The idols are daughters of Allah." And He said: ﴿So what is for their associates does not reach Allah, and what is for Allah reaches their associates﴾ [[See vol. 7, p. 89 onwards.]].

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 19, verses 88–95 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And they say, "The Most Merciful has taken to Himself a son."﴾ He means the Jews and the Christians, and whoever claims that the angels are the daughters of Allah.

Yahya, al-A'mash, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, 'Asim and Khalaf read "wuldan" (وُلْدًا) with a damma on the waw and sukun on the lam, in four places: in this surah, His saying, ﴿"Have I seen the Unseen, or have I taken a covenant with the Most Merciful?" ... "I will surely be given wealth and children (walad)."﴾ [Maryam: 77], which has already been discussed; His saying, "that they ascribe a son (walad) to the Most Merciful. And it is not befitting for the Most Merciful to take a son (walad)"; and in Surah Nuh, ﴿"his wealth and his children (waladuhu)"﴾ [Nuh: 21]. Ibn Kathir, Mujahid, Humayd, Abu 'Amr and Ya'qub agreed with them in "Nuh" specifically. The rest read all of them with a fatha on the waw and the lam. Both forms are dialectal variants, like "al-'arab" and "al-'urb" and "al-'ajam" and "al-'ujm." The poet said:

"And indeed I have seen people who have multiplied wealth and offspring (wuldan)."

Another said:

"Would that So-and-so had been in his mother's belly, would that So-and-so had been the offspring (wuld) of a donkey."

And al-Nabigha said, in the same sense:

"Gently! May all the people be ransomed for you, and may I not have accumulated wealth and offspring (walad)."

So he used the fatha. The Qays tribe use "wuld" with a damma as the plural and "walad" with a fatha as the singular. Al-Jawhari said: "Walad may be singular or plural, and likewise wuld with a damma." From the proverbs of the Banu Asad: "Your offspring is the one who bled your heels" [meaning: the one you bore in childbirth, whose afterbirth bled your heels, is your child]. Wuld may also be the plural of walad, like usd and asad. Al-Wild with a kasra is a dialect form of walad. Al-Nahhas said: Abu 'Ubayda distinguished between them, claiming that walad applies to the family and to offspring collectively. Abu Ja'far said: This is a rejected opinion that none of the lexicographers recognises. Walad and wuld refer only to a man's child and his child's child, except that walad is more common in the speech of the Arabs, as in the verse:

"Gently! May all the people be ransomed for you, and may I not have accumulated wealth and offspring (walad)."

Abu Ja'far said: I heard Muhammad ibn al-Walid say: It is permissible for wuld to be the plural of walad, as one says wathan and wuthn, and asad and usd. And it is permissible for walad and wuld to have one meaning, as one says 'ajam and 'ujm, and 'arab and 'urb, as mentioned earlier.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed you have brought forth a thing that is idd (monstrous)﴾, that is, a grave evil, according to Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and others. Al-Jawhari said: Al-idd and al-iddah mean a calamity and a dreadful matter, and from it is His saying: ﴿Indeed you have brought forth a thing that is idd.﴾ Likewise al-add, on the pattern of fa'il. The plural of iddah is idad. "A calamity afflicted So-and-so (addahu), so that it weighed heavily upon him" (adda, with a fatha). Al-add also means hardship. [Al-add: domination and strength. In the originals: al-idd is strength and hardness; the plural al-idd is also strength. The correct form, as in Lisan al-Arab, is: al-idd with a kasra is hardship, and al-add with a fatha is domination and strength.] The reciter said:

"They stripped from me hardship and weight, after I had been firm and sturdy."

End of his words. Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami read "addan" (أَدًّا) with a fatha on the hamza. Al-Nahhas said: One says adda yauddu adda, so he is addun, and the noun is idd, when he brings a great, monstrous thing. The reciter said:

"The rivals have met from me a horror, a calamity, a great and dreadful thing."

Al-Nahhas' statement, from al-Tha'labi: There are three forms. "Iddan" with a kasra is the reading of the common people. "Addan" with a fatha is the reading of al-Sulami. "Addun" on the pattern of madd is a dialect of some Arabs, transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas and Abu al-'Aliyah, and it seems to be derived from weight. One says: "al-himl a'dahu, ya'uduhu, awdan," meaning the load made him heavy.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿The heavens are almost rent (takadu)﴾. The common reading here and in "al-Shura" [see vol. 16, p. 4] is with the taa'. The reading of Nafi', Yahya and al-Kisa'i is "yakadu" with the yaa', because the verb comes first.

(yatafattarna minhu) [verse 90], that is, they split apart. Nafi', Ibn Kathir, Hafs and others read it with a taa' after the yaa' and with a shadda on the taa' from tafattur, here and in "al-Shura." Hamzah and Ibn 'Amir agreed with them in "al-Shura." Here they read "yanfatirna" from infitar. Abu 'Amr, Abu Bakr and al-Mufaddal read it in both surahs in this way too. This is the preference of Abu 'Ubayd, because of His saying: ﴿When the heaven is split asunder (infatarat)﴾ [al-Infitar: 1] and His saying: ﴿The heaven will be split asunder (munfatirun) by it﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 18].

His saying: (And the earth is split open (tanshaqqu)) [verse 90], that is, it cracks open.

(And the mountains fall down in ruins (hadda)) [verse 90]. Ibn 'Abbas said: Demolished, that is, they fall with a loud noise. In a hadith: "O Allah, I seek refuge in You from hadd and hadda." Shamir said: Ahmad ibn Ghiyath al-Marwazi said: al-hadd is demolition and al-hadda is subsidence. Al-Layth said: It is a severe collapse, like a wall that is brought down all at once. One says: "The matter hadda me, and hadda my pillar," meaning it broke me and reached me, as reported by al-Harawi. Al-Jawhari said: "Hadda al-bina' yahudduhu hadda" means he broke it and shattered it. "The calamity hadda him," meaning it weakened his support. "The mountain inhadda," meaning it broke. Al-Asma'i said: Al-hadd is a weak man. A man says to another, when threatening him: "I am not a weakling (hadd)," meaning I am not weak. Ibn al-A'rabi said: Al-hadd among men is the generous and noble one, while the cowardly and weak one is hid (with a kasra). He recited the line of al-'Abbas ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib, may Allah be pleased with him, [the lines mean: "They are not weak (yahudduna) in wars when the belts (nutuq) are tied above the hips (harqafat)."]:

"They are not weak in wars, when the belts are tied above the hips."

Al-hadda is the sound of a wall or the like falling. One says from it: "hadda yahiddu" (with a kasra) hadidan. Al-hadd is a sound heard by the people of the coast, coming to them from the sea, which has a resonance in the earth; sometimes an earthquake comes from it, and its resonance is its hadid. Al-Nahhas: "Hadda" [verse 90] is a verbal noun, because the meaning of "takharru" [verse 90] is "tuhaddu" (is demolished). Others said: it is a state (hal), that is, demolished.

(That they ascribe a son to the Most Merciful) [verse 91]. "An" (that) is in the accusative position according to al-Farra', because of "an da'aw" (that they ascribed), and from "an da'aw" the position of "an" is accusative by the removal of the preposition. Al-Farra' claimed that al-Kisa'i said: it is in the genitive position by the implied preposition.

Ibn al-Mubarak mentioned: Misar related to us from Wasil, from 'Awn ibn 'Abd Allah, who said: 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud said: "The mountain says to the mountain: 'O So-and-so, did anyone who remembers Allah pass by you today?' If he says yes, it rejoices." Then 'Abd Allah recited: ﴿And they say, "The Most Merciful has taken to Himself a son."﴾ and said: [that is, 'Awn said, as in al-Durr al-Manthur and elsewhere]: "Do you think they hear falsehood and do not hear good?"

He said: Awf related to me from Ghalib ibn 'Ajrad [so it is in the originals; probably Ghalib ibn Hujrah, and the text here is corrupted], who said: A man from the people of Syria related to me in the mosque of Mina: When Allah created the earth and created what is in it of trees, there was no tree on the earth to which the children of Adam came without obtaining some benefit from it, and they had benefit from it. The earth and the trees remained so until the wicked among the children of Adam uttered that great word: their saying "The Most Merciful has taken to Himself a son." When they said it, the earth shuddered and the trees bristled.

Ibn 'Abbas said: The mountains shuddered, and what is in them of trees, seas, and fish. From that came the thorns on the fish and the thorns on the trees. Ibn 'Abbas and Ka'b also said: The heavens, the earth, the mountains and all creatures, except the two weighty ones [humans and jinn], were terrified, and they nearly ceased to exist. The angels became angry, Hell was kindled, the trees bristled, the earth became gloomy and dry, when they said: Allah has taken a son.

Muhammad ibn Ka'b said: The enemies of Allah almost established the Hour against us, by His saying: ﴿The heavens are almost rent asunder from it, and the earth splits open, and the mountains fall down in ruins, that they ascribe a son to the Most Merciful.﴾ Ibn al-'Arabi said: He spoke the truth. It is a grave saying, against which the decree and the destiny have already gone forth. Were it not that the Creator, blessed and exalted, is not diminished by the disbelief of the disbeliever and not exalted by the faith of the believer, and that this does not increase His kingdom just as that does not decrease His kingdom, such a thing would not have been spoken on the tongues. But He is the Holy, the Wise, the Forbearing, so after that He does not heed what the falsifiers say.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And it is not befitting for the Most Merciful to take a son.﴾ On this there are four issues.

The first: His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And it is not befitting for the Most Merciful to take a son.﴾ He negated from Himself, glorified and exalted, having a son, because a son implies kinship (jinsiyyah) and origination (huduth), as we have explained in al-Baqarah [see vol. 2, p. 85]. That is, this is not fitting for Him, He is not described by it, and it is not permissible concerning Him, because a son is only born of a father who has a father and an origin, and Allah, glorified, is exalted and sanctified above that.

He said [Ibn Ahmar al-Bahili, describing a mountain]:

"At the top of a smooth rock, from a lofty peak, no plain nor mountain is fitting beneath it."

(Ain kullu man fi al-samawati wal-ard illa atil-Rahmani 'abda) [verse 93]. "In" is negating, meaning "ma" (not). That is: Not everyone in the heavens and the earth but comes to the Most Merciful on the Day of Resurrection, acknowledging His lordship, humbled and abased, as He said: ﴿And all of them will come to Him humbled (dakhirin)﴾ [al-Naml: 87], that is, lowly and abased. That is, all of creation are His servants, so how could one of them be a son to Him, exalted and majestic, far above what the wrongdoers and deniers say, with great exaltation?

"Atin" is written with a yaa' in the script, and the original form has tanwin, which was dropped for lightness and then the word was made into a construct phrase (idafah).

The second: In this verse there is evidence that a son cannot be owned by his father, contrary to those who said that he buys him, owns him, and he is not freed by him unless he frees him. Allah, may He be exalted, has made clear the incompatibility between children and ownership. So if the father owns his son through some kind of disposal, the son is freed by him. The evidence from this verse is that Allah, may He be exalted, made sonship and servanthood opposite poles of a contrast; He negated one and affirmed the other. If they were combined, this statement would have no benefit upon which an argument could be based. In the sound hadith: "A child cannot repay his father unless he finds him enslaved, buys him and frees him" (narrated by Muslim). So if the father does not own his son despite his rank over him, the son is even less owned by the father, because he is inferior to him.

The third: Ishaq ibn Rahawayh interpreted the saying of the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him: "Whoever frees his share in a slave" to mean male slaves only, not female slaves, so that the full obligation does not apply to one who frees a share in a female. This is contrary to the view of the majority of the early generations and those after them, for they did not distinguish between male and female, because the word "slave" ('abd) is intended in the generic sense, as He said, may He be exalted: "Not everyone in the heavens and the earth but comes to the Most Merciful as a servant ('abd)," for it certainly includes both male and female slaves. Ishaq relied on the report that "'abdah" is used for the feminine form.

The fourth: Al-Bukhari related from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "Allah, blessed and exalted, says: 'The son of Adam denied Me, and he had no right to do so, and he reviled Me, and he had no right to do so. As for his denying Me, it is his saying: He will not bring me back as He began me, and the first creation is not easier for Me than its return. As for his reviling Me, it is his saying: Allah has taken a son, while I am the One, the Eternal Refuge; I have not begotten, nor have I been begotten, and there is none comparable to Me.'" This has already been mentioned in al-Baqarah and elsewhere, and repeating it in a context like this is very good.

The angels became angry, Hell was kindled, the trees bristled, the earth became gloomy and dry, when they said: Allah has taken a son.

Muhammad ibn Ka'b said: The enemies of Allah almost established the Hour against us, by His saying: ﴿The heavens are almost rent asunder from it, and the earth splits open, and the mountains fall down in ruins, that they ascribe a son to the Most Merciful.﴾ Ibn al-'Arabi said: He spoke the truth. It is a grave saying, against which the decree and the destiny have already gone forth. Were it not that the Creator, blessed and exalted, is not diminished by the disbelief of the disbeliever and not exalted by the faith of the believer, and that this does not increase His kingdom just as that does not decrease His kingdom, such a thing would not have been spoken on the tongues. But He is the Holy, the Wise, the Forbearing, so after that He does not heed what the falsifiers say.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And it is not befitting for the Most Merciful to take a son.﴾ On this there are four issues.

The first: His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And it is not befitting for the Most Merciful to take a son.﴾ He negated from Himself, glorified and exalted, having a son, because a son implies kinship (jinsiyyah) and origination (huduth), as we have explained in al-Baqarah [see vol. 2, p. 85]. (Ain kullu man fi al-samawati wal-ard illa atil-Rahmani 'abda) [verse 93]. "In" is negating, meaning "ma" (not). (yatafattarna minhu) [verse 90], that is, they split apart. Nafi', Ibn Kathir, Hafs and others read it with a taa' after the yaa' and with a shadda on the taa' from tafattur, here and in "al-Shura."
