"Addun" on the pattern of madd is a dialect of some Arabs, transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas and Abu al-'Aliyah, and it seems to be derived from weight. One says: "al-himl a'dahu, ya'uduhu, awdan," meaning the load made him heavy.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿The heavens are almost rent (takadu)﴾. The common reading here and in "al-Shura" [see vol. 16, p. 4] is with the taa'. The reading of Nafi', Yahya and al-Kisa'i is "yakadu" with the yaa', because the verb comes first.

(yatafattarna minhu) [verse 90], that is, they split apart. Nafi', Ibn Kathir, Hafs and others read it with a taa' after the yaa' and with a shadda on the taa' from tafattur, here and in "al-Shura." Hamzah and Ibn 'Amir agreed with them in "al-Shura." Here they read "yanfatirna" from infitar. Abu 'Amr, Abu Bakr and al-Mufaddal read it in both surahs in this way too. This is the preference of Abu 'Ubayd, because of His saying: ﴿When the heaven is split asunder (infatarat)﴾ [al-Infitar: 1] and His saying: ﴿The heaven will be split asunder (munfatirun) by it﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 18].

His saying: (And the earth is split open (tanshaqqu)) [verse 90], that is, it cracks open.

(And the mountains fall down in ruins (hadda)) [verse 90]. Ibn 'Abbas said: Demolished, that is, they fall with a loud noise. In a hadith: "O Allah, I seek refuge in You from hadd and hadda." Shamir said: Ahmad ibn Ghiyath al-Marwazi said: al-hadd is demolition and al-hadda is subsidence. Al-Layth said: It is a severe collapse, like a wall that is brought down all at once. One says: "The matter hadda me, and hadda my pillar," meaning it broke me and reached me, as reported by al-Harawi. Al-Jawhari said: "Hadda al-bina' yahudduhu hadda" means he broke it and shattered it. "The calamity hadda him," meaning it weakened his support. "The mountain inhadda," meaning it broke. Al-Asma'i said: Al-hadd is a weak man. A man says to another, when threatening him: "I am not a weakling (hadd)," meaning I am not weak. Ibn al-A'rabi said: Al-hadd among men is the generous and noble one, while the cowardly and weak one is hid (with a kasra). He recited the line of al-'Abbas ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib, may Allah be pleased with him, [the lines mean: "They are not weak (yahudduna) in wars when the belts (nutuq) are tied above the hips (harqafat)."]:

"They are not weak in wars, when the belts are tied above the hips."

Al-hadda is the sound of a wall or the like falling. One says from it: "hadda yahiddu" (with a kasra) hadidan. Al-hadd is a sound heard by the people of the coast, coming to them from the sea, which has a resonance in the earth; sometimes an earthquake comes from it, and its resonance is its hadid. Al-Nahhas: "Hadda" [verse 90] is a verbal noun, because the meaning of "takharru" [verse 90] is "tuhaddu" (is demolished). Others said: it is a state (hal), that is, demolished.

(That they ascribe a son to the Most Merciful) [verse 91]. "An" (that) is in the accusative position according to al-Farra', because of "an da'aw" (that they ascribed), and from "an da'aw" the position of "an" is accusative by the removal of the preposition. Al-Farra' claimed that al-Kisa'i said: it is in the genitive position by the implied preposition.

Ibn al-Mubarak mentioned: Misar related to us from Wasil, from 'Awn ibn 'Abd Allah, who said: 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud said: "The mountain says to the mountain: 'O So-and-so, did anyone who remembers Allah pass by you today?' If he says yes, it rejoices." Then 'Abd Allah recited: ﴿And they say, "The Most Merciful has taken to Himself a son."﴾ and said: [that is, 'Awn said, as in al-Durr al-Manthur and elsewhere]: "Do you think they hear falsehood and do not hear good?"

He said: Awf related to me from Ghalib ibn 'Ajrad [so it is in the originals; probably Ghalib ibn Hujrah, and the text here is corrupted], who said: A man from the people of Syria related to me in the mosque of Mina: When Allah created the earth and created what is in it of trees, there was no tree on the earth to which the children of Adam came without obtaining some benefit from it, and they had benefit from it. The earth and the trees remained so until the wicked among the children of Adam uttered that great word: their saying "The Most Merciful has taken to Himself a son." When they said it, the earth shuddered and the trees bristled.

Ibn 'Abbas said: The mountains shuddered, and what is in them of trees, seas, and fish. From that came the thorns on the fish and the thorns on the trees. Ibn 'Abbas and Ka'b also said: The heavens, the earth, the mountains and all creatures, except the two weighty ones [humans and jinn], were terrified, and they nearly ceased to exist. The angels became angry, Hell was kindled, the trees bristled, the earth became gloomy and dry, when they said: Allah has taken a son.

Muhammad ibn Ka'b said: The enemies of Allah almost established the Hour against us, by His saying: ﴿The heavens are almost rent asunder from it, and the earth splits open, and the mountains fall down in ruins, that they ascribe a son to the Most Merciful.﴾ Ibn al-'Arabi said: He spoke the truth. It is a grave saying, against which the decree and the destiny have already gone forth. Were it not that the Creator, blessed and exalted, is not diminished by the disbelief of the disbeliever and not exalted by the faith of the believer, and that this does not increase His kingdom just as that does not decrease His kingdom, such a thing would not have been spoken on the tongues. But He is the Holy, the Wise, the Forbearing, so after that He does not heed what the falsifiers say.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And it is not befitting for the Most Merciful to take a son.﴾ On this there are four issues.

The first: His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And it is not befitting for the Most Merciful to take a son.﴾ He negated from Himself, glorified and exalted, having a son, because a son implies kinship (jinsiyyah) and origination (huduth), as we have explained in al-Baqarah [see vol. 2, p. 85]. That is, this is not fitting for Him, He is not described by it, and it is not permissible concerning Him, because a son is only born of a father who has a father and an origin, and Allah, glorified, is exalted and sanctified above that.

He said [Ibn Ahmar al-Bahili, describing a mountain]:

"At the top of a smooth rock, from a lofty peak, no plain nor mountain is fitting beneath it."

(Ain kullu man fi al-samawati wal-ard illa atil-Rahmani 'abda) [verse 93]. "In" is negating, meaning "ma" (not). That is: Not everyone in the heavens and the earth but comes to the Most Merciful on the Day of Resurrection, acknowledging His lordship, humbled and abased, as He said: ﴿And all of them will come to Him humbled (dakhirin)﴾ [al-Naml: 87], that is, lowly and abased. That is, all of creation are His servants, so how could one of them be a son to Him, exalted and majestic, far above what the wrongdoers and deniers say, with great exaltation?

"Atin" is written with a yaa' in the script, and the original form has tanwin, which was dropped for lightness and then the word was made into a construct phrase (idafah).

The second: In this verse there is evidence that a son cannot be owned by his father, contrary to those who said that he buys him, owns him, and he is not freed by him unless he frees him. Allah, may He be exalted, has made clear the incompatibility between children and ownership. So if the father owns his son through some kind of disposal, the son is freed by him. The evidence from this verse is that Allah, may He be exalted, made sonship and servanthood opposite poles of a contrast; He negated one and affirmed the other. If they were combined, this statement would have no benefit upon which an argument could be based. In the sound hadith: "A child cannot repay his father unless he finds him enslaved, buys him and frees him" (narrated by Muslim). So if the father does not own his son despite his rank over him, the son is even less owned by the father, because he is inferior to him.

The third: Ishaq ibn Rahawayh interpreted the saying of the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him: "Whoever frees his share in a slave" to mean male slaves only, not female slaves, so that the full obligation does not apply to one who frees a share in a female. This is contrary to the view of the majority of the early generations and those after them, for they did not distinguish between male and female, because the word "slave" ('abd) is intended in the generic sense, as He said, may He be exalted: "Not everyone in the heavens and the earth but comes to the Most Merciful as a servant ('abd)," for it certainly includes both male and female slaves. Ishaq relied on the report that "'abdah" is used for the feminine form.

The fourth: Al-Bukhari related from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "Allah, blessed and exalted, says: 'The son of Adam denied Me, and he had no right to do so, and he reviled Me, and he had no right to do so. As for his denying Me, it is his saying: He will not bring me back as He began me, and the first creation is not easier for Me than its return. As for his reviling Me, it is his saying: Allah has taken a son, while I am the One, the Eternal Refuge; I have not begotten, nor have I been begotten, and there is none comparable to Me.'" This has already been mentioned in al-Baqarah and elsewhere, and repeating it in a context like this is very good.

Tafsir of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 19, verses 88–95 (part 2 of 2):

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Certainly He has enumerated them﴾, meaning He knows their number, ﴿and counted them, a counting﴾. It is an emphasis, meaning that none of them is hidden from Him.

I say: In the names of Allah, glorified is He, we have found al-Muhsi (the Enumerator), namely in the Sunnah, in the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, which al-Tirmidhi recorded, and the derivation of this verb indicates it.

Al-Ustadh Abu Ishaq al-Isfara'ini said: Among the names is al-Muhsi, and it is distinguished by the fact that the multiplicity of things does not preoccupy Him from knowledge, like the light of illumination, the intensity of the wind, and the falling of leaves. So at that time He knows the parts of the movements in every leaf. And how would He not know, when He is the One who created? He has said: ﴿Should not He who created know? And He is the Subtle, the All-Aware﴾ [[See vol. 18, p. 213 onwards.]]. It occurs in the tafsir of Ibn Abbas that the meaning of ﴿Certainly He has enumerated them and counted them, a counting﴾ is: they acknowledged to Him servitude and bore witness to Him of lordship.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And all of them will come to Him on the Day of Resurrection, alone﴾, meaning singly, with no helper for him and no wealth with him to benefit him [[So it is in the originals except A: "yanfa'uhu" (benefit him).]], as He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿The Day when neither wealth nor children will benefit, except one who comes to Allah with a sound heart﴾ [[See vol. 13, p. 113 onwards.]]. So nothing benefits him except what he has sent ahead of good deeds. And He said: "And all of them will come to Him", following the wording, while considering the meaning, "they will come to Him."

Al-Qushayri said: In this there is an indication that you do not accept for yourselves that your children be enslaved, while all are His servants. So how do you accept for Him what you do not accept for yourselves? It has been refuted against them in a similar matter, in that they do not accept daughters for themselves, yet they say: "The angels are daughters of Allah", exalted is Allah above that, and their saying: "The idols are daughters of Allah." And He said: ﴿So what is for their associates does not reach Allah, and what is for Allah reaches their associates﴾ [[See vol. 7, p. 89 onwards.]].

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 19, verse 96:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, those who believe﴾, meaning those who affirm (saddaqu), "and do righteous deeds, the Most Merciful will appoint for them affection (wuddan)," meaning love in the hearts of His servants.

As al-Tirmidhi narrated from the hadith of Sa'd and Abu Hurayrah: the Prophet ﷺ said: "When Allah loves a servant, He calls Jibril, saying: 'Indeed I love so-and-so, so love him.' He said: 'So Jibril calls out in the heaven, then love for him is placed upon the people of the earth.' That is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿the Most Merciful will appoint for them affection﴾. And when Allah hates a servant, He calls Jibril, saying: 'Indeed I hate so-and-so,' so he calls out in the heaven, then hatred for him is placed upon the earth."

He said: this is a hadith that is ḥasan ṣaḥīḥ (good and sound). Al-Bukhari and Muslim narrated it in its meaning, and Malik in the Muwatta', and in Nawadir al-Usul.

Abu Bakr ibn Sabiq al-Umawi narrated to us, he said: Abu Malik al-Janbi narrated to us, from Juwaybir, from al-Dahhak, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Indeed Allah gives the believer al-ulfah [[In b, j, z, and t: al-mawaddah... The word "al-mqah" with a kasra on the mim and a ha' at its end means love. In k: al-shafaqah.]] and beauty and love in the breasts of the righteous and the honored angels." Then he recited: ﴿Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds, the Most Merciful will appoint for them affection.﴾

It has been disputed concerning whom it was revealed. It is said that it was revealed concerning 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him. Al-Bara' ibn 'Azib narrated: the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to 'Ali ibn Abi Talib: "Say, O 'Ali: O Allah, make for me a covenant with You, and place for me affection in the hearts of the believers." So the verse was revealed. Al-Tha'labi mentioned it.

Ibn 'Abbas said: it was revealed concerning 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf: Allah, Exalted is He, placed for him affection in the hearts of the servants; no believer meets him without honoring him, and no polytheist or hypocrite does so without exalting him.

Hiram ibn Hayyan used to say: "No one turns his heart toward Allah, Exalted is He, except that Allah, Exalted is He, turns the hearts of the people of faith toward him, until He grants him their affection and their mercy."

It is said: Allah, Exalted is He, will place for them affection in the hearts of the believers and the angels on the Day of Resurrection.

I say: If he is beloved in this world, then he is so in the Hereafter, for Allah, Exalted is He, loves only a believing and God-fearing person, and is pleased only with one who is sincere and pure. May Allah, Exalted is He, make us among them by His grace and generosity.

Muslim narrated from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Indeed Allah, Exalted is He, when He loves a servant, calls Jibril, peace be upon him, and says: 'Indeed I love so-and-so, so love him.' Jibril then loves him, then calls out in the heaven, saying: 'Indeed Allah loves so-and-so, so love him.' The inhabitants of the heaven love him." He said: "Then acceptance is placed for him on the earth. And when He hates a servant, He calls Jibril, peace be upon him, and says: 'Indeed I hate so-and-so, so hate him' [[from b, j, t, and k.]]. Jibril hates him, then calls out among the inhabitants of the heaven: 'Indeed Allah hates so-and-so, so hate him.' They hate him. Then hatred is placed for him on the earth..."

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 19, verse 97:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So We have made it easy in your tongue﴾, that is, the Qur'an, meaning: We have made it clear in your Arabic tongue and made it easy for whoever reflects upon it and contemplates it. It was also said: We revealed it to you in the language of the Arabs so that its understanding would be easy for them.

﴿That you may give glad tidings thereby to the mindful﴾ [that is, the believers [[from b, j, z, t and k.]]] ﴿and warn thereby a contentious people﴾. Ludd (لُدّ) is the plural of aladd (الْأَلَدّ), which is the one most intense in dispute, and from it is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿the most contentious of opponents﴾ [[See vol. 3, p. 14 onward.]]. The poet said:

I pass the night, confiding in my worries, as if I were
disputing with peoples of contention, fierce in argument.

Abu Ubayda said: the aladd is the one who does not accept the truth and claims falsehood. Al-Hasan said: ludd are those deaf to the truth. Al-Rabi said: deaf in the ears of the hearts. Mujahid said: wicked transgressors. Al-Dahhak said: those who dispute in falsehood. Ibn Abbas said: harsh in contention. It was also said: the unjust who do not go straight, and the meaning is one. They were singled out for warning because one who has no obstinacy in him is easily led to submit.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 19, verse 98:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿How many generations have We destroyed before them?﴾ That is, how many nations and communities of people before them, [who] warned the people of Makkah.

(﴿Do you perceive any one of them, or hear from them a faint sound?﴾) It is in the accusative position, meaning: do you see any of them, or find [any trace of them]? "Or hear from them a faint sound" means a voice. This is related from Ibn Abbas and others, meaning: they have died and gone to their deeds. It was also said: a sensation (hiss), as reported by Ibn Zayd. It was also said: al-rikz is what is not understood of a sound or a movement, as reported by al-Yazidi and Abu Ubaydah, like the rikz of an army division (kataybah). Abu Ubaydah recited the verse of Labid:

"She became alert to the rikz of a human presence, and it frightened her, from behind an unseen place, while the human presence was her destruction."

[[Tawajjasat: the cow heard the sound of people and it startled her, though she did not see the people. Wal-anis saqamaha means: and the human presence was her destruction, i.e., it hunted her.]]

It was also said: a hidden sound. From this comes "rakaza al-rumh" (he planted the spear), when he buried its tip in the ground. Tarafah said:

"And my two ears, which are truthful in listening for the stealthy approach, for a hidden rikz or a loud, resounding sound."

[[In this verse Tarafah describes the two ears of his she-camel, meaning that her ears do not deceive her about a sound. Al-munadd is an epithet of the sound, and a "munadd" sound is one that is intensely loud in its calling. It is also transmitted as "li-sawtin munaddin" with an idafah and a kasrah on the dal, but the first is the better transmission.]]

Dhu al-Rummah said, describing a bull that listened to the voice of a hunter and dogs:

"When a lean, alert one (muqfir nadus) senses a rikz, with the warning of a sound, there is no falsehood in its hearing."

That is, there is no falsehood in its listening; it is one of true listening. Nadus means skilful, and it is said nadis and nadus, as one says hadhir and hadhur, and yaqiz and yaqur. Al-nabah is a faint sound, and likewise al-rikz. Al-rikaz is buried wealth. And God knows best what is correct.
